**Summary.** This paper introduces a comprehensive quantum simulation architecture using alkaline-earth atoms to model the complex, multi-orbital physics found in correlated materials like nickelates. By combining various laser and lattice controls, the authors achieve programmable control over all necessary Hamiltonian terms, demonstrating a general route to simulate solid-state physics in an ultracold atom setting.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, general blueprint for realizing complex, multi-orbital Hamiltonians in ultracold atoms, bridging the gap between high-level condensed matter theory and programmable quantum hardware.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to faithfully reproduce the complex, multi-orbital Hamiltonians of correlated quantum materials, such as bilayer nickelates, using programmable quantum simulators.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate an integrated architecture using fermionic alkaline-earth atoms that can programmatically control all necessary ingredients—including orbital-selective tunneling, multi-orbital Hubbard/Hund couplings, and crystal field splitting—to simulate these complex models.

**Method.** The approach combines advanced atomic physics techniques (clock states, structured driving, Feshbach resonances) to engineer the effective Hamiltonian, which is then benchmarked against first-principles calculations from solid-state theory.

**Model / system.** The system uses fermionic alkaline-earth atoms in an optical lattice to simulate the low-energy physics of correlated materials, specifically targeting the four-band Hamiltonian of bilayer nickelates. The simulation controls hopping hierarchies, interaction strengths ($U, J_H, V$), and orbital energy offsets independently.

**Key observables.** Non-interacting band structure (e.g., $\alpha, eta, \gamma$ pockets), orbital-dependent hopping ratios, and the ability to reproduce microscopic parameters from first-principles modeling.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The simulation requires independent control over hopping ratios ($t_{\parallel}/t_{\perp}$), interaction strengths ($U, J_H, V$), and crystal field splitting ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method successfully encodes solid-state orbital symmetries into the effective Hamiltonian even when atoms are confined to simple $s$-wave Wannier orbitals. The realization requires a demanding combination of laser and lattice control.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the 'Toolbox' for simulation, mapping material requirements to atomic controls, and detail the specific hopping hierarchies and level schemes required to model the bilayer nickelate structure.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the general goal of simulating material Hamiltonians, details the specific physical ingredients (orbital encoding, coupling, detuning) available in the AEA platform, and validates this capability by applying it to the highly demanding benchmark of the bilayer nickelate model.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A long-term goal of quantum simulation is to faithfully reproduce the low-energy Hamiltonians of correlated quantum materials, establishing a direct connection between solid-state experiment, electronic-structure theory, and programmable many-body systems. Here, we introduce an integrated quantum-simulation architecture based on fermionic alkaline-earth atoms that enables programmable control over the key ingredients of multi-orbital material Hamiltonians. Long-lived clock states encode synthetic orbitals, their differential polarizabilities generate orbital-selective tunneling, and contact interactions provide multi-orbital Hubbard and Hund couplings. Spatially structured coherent driving on the ultra-narrow clock transition further realizes symmetry-selective inter-orbital hybridization, while the clock detuning independently controls orbital energy offsets. In this way, the spatial symmetries of solid-state orbitals can be encoded directly into the effective Hamiltonian, even though the atoms themselves remain in conventional $s$-wave Wannier orbitals of the lowest optical-lattice bands. We demonstrate the resulting integrated control using the four-band low-energy Hamiltonian of the bilayer nickelate La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ as a demanding benchmark. Self-consistent calculations show that the microscopic parameters obtained from first-principles modeling can be reproduced within a single experimentally accessible lattice configuration and independently programmed over substantial parameter ranges. Our results establish a general route for translating material-derived multi-orbital Hamiltonians into programmable ultracold-atom quantum simulators.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel, highly efficient 'magic state factory' designed for fault-tolerant quantum computation using quantum LDPC codes. It merges tricycle and quadcycle codes via a teleportation mechanism to generate high-fidelity magic states. The protocol is demonstrated on neutral-atom quantum computers, offering a practical, low-overhead pathway to scaling quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The integration of advanced quantum error-correcting codes (qLDPC) with a physical implementation platform (neutral atoms) to solve a fundamental resource bottleneck (magic state generation) is highly relevant for experimental quantum computing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is developing a space-time-efficient method to generate high-fidelity magic states required for fault-tolerant quantum computation using quantum LDPC codes.

**Main result.** The authors propose a factory combining tricycle and quadcycle codes that achieves logical error rates as low as $10^{-9}$ with 10-40 times lower space-time cost than existing methods.

**Method.** The approach uses an 'escape' mechanism to teleport postselected logical magic states from tricycle codes to more robust quadcycle codes via a depth-1 homomorphic CNOT.

**Model / system.** The protocol is demonstrated on reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computers, utilizing the algebraic structure of tricycle and quadcycle codes for state preparation and error correction.

**Key observables.** Logical error rate (achieving $10^{-9}$), space-time cost (showing 10-40x improvement), and fidelity of generated CCZ states.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical error rate ($p = 10^{-3}$), code distances ($d_{3D}$), and the number of available atoms/AODs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a standard circuit-level noise model at $p = 10^{-3}$, and the efficiency relies on the shared algebraic structure between the two code types.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the 'Transversal dimension-jump magic state factory' process, showing the flow from tricycle to quadcycle blocks, and detail the single-shot error correction capabilities of the quadcycle codes.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the need for efficient magic state generation for qLDPC codes. It then details the combination of tricycle and quadcycle codes, the teleportation mechanism, and finally presents a concrete, end-to-end implementation using neutral atoms.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can substantially reduce the qubit overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computation, but any useful architecture based on such codes also requires an efficient mechanism to implement non-Clifford gates in a fault-tolerant manner. We introduce a space-time-efficient magic state factory for high-rate qLDPC codes by combining the transversal non-Clifford gates of recently developed tricycle codes with single-shot four-dimensional balanced product quadcycle codes. The key ingredient is an efficient "escape" mechanism that teleports postselected logical magic states from tricycle codes to larger distance quadcycle codes. Under a standard circuit-level noise model at physical error rate $10^{-3}$, our factories produce $\mathrm{CCZ}$ states at logical error rates as low as $10^{-9}$ with 10-40 times lower space-time cost than state-of-the-art magic state generation methods. The resulting states are directly encoded in high-rate blocks suitable for computation. We identify the quadcycle codes by an AI-assisted search and show that they can serve as excellent memories capable of single-shot error correction. Finally, we present a concrete implementation of the entire factory with highly efficient atom transport on reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computers. Together, these results provide an end-to-end, practical protocol for producing and utilizing high-fidelity magic states within a high-rate qLDPC architecture, with the lowest space-time cost to date.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores how competing symmetry breaking and topological order manifest in 1D quantum spin chains. By mapping out the phase diagram, the authors identify multiple ordered and gapless phases, revealing exotic critical behavior. The research highlights unconventional mechanisms where symmetry and topology cooperate to generate complex quantum critical points.

**Why it may be interesting.** The findings on symmetry-enriched criticality and the breakdown of naive symmetry theorems in 1D systems provide deep insights into how topology and symmetry constrain quantum ground states, relevant for understanding exotic phases in correlated materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the complex interplay between spontaneous symmetry breaking and symmetry-protected topology in one-dimensional quantum spin-1/2 systems.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a rich phase diagram featuring six distinct gapped phases, two gapless phases, and exotic critical points, including a Lifshitz tricritical point that breaks continuous symmetry unexpectedly.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical analysis (e.g., Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory) with numerical techniques like DMRG and exact diagonalization to map out the phase diagram.

**Model / system.** The model consists of one-dimensional quantum spin-1/2 lattice Hamiltonians possessing $\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry. The analysis is performed on the coupling space $T^2$.

**Key observables.** Symmetry-breaking patterns (FM, Neel), topological attributes (SPT phases), gap status, central charge ($c=1$), and ground-state degeneracy.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling parameters $(\theta, \lambda)$ defining the Hamiltonian, and system size $2N$ for finite-size scaling analysis.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The classification of SPT phases relies on the change in ground-state degeneracy with boundary conditions; the analysis involves approximations for sums and limits for large system sizes.

**Figures summary.** Figures 1, 2, and 3 depict the phase diagrams in the coupling space $T^2$ and along specific cuts, illustrating the various ordered, topological, and critical regions.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically maps the phase diagram by analyzing fixed points, constructing the phase diagram across the $T^2$ coupling space, and then performing detailed theoretical analyses of the critical lines and boundary physics.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate how spontaneous symmetry breaking and symmetry-protected topology compete and cooperate in one-dimensional quantum spin-1/2 systems. We introduce two families of local Hamiltonians with $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}^{T}_{2}$ symmetry which host a zoo of broken-symmetry phases with and without gapless boundary spins, namely, six long-range-ordered gapped phases that differ by their $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}$-symmetry-breaking patterns (FM$^{\,}_{x,y,z}$ and Neel$^{\,}_{x,y,z}$), their partner symmetry-protected topological phases (FM$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x,y}$ and Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x,y}$), and two gapless phases (gFM$^{\,}_{z}$ and gNeel$^{\,}_{z}$) with incommensurate $\mathbb{Z}^{T}_{2}$-breaking magnetic long-range order and central charge $\mathsf{c}=1$. Direct transitions between competing gapped phases can be continuous or weakly first order. We demonstrate that continuous phase transition lines have exotic critical properties. For example, a line of deconfined quantum critical points (between the Neel$^{\,}_{x}$ and Neel$^{\,}_{y}$ phases) described by Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory is terminated by the gFM$^{\,}_{z}$ phase at a Lifshitz tricritical point which exhibits spontaneous breaking of the continuous U(1) symmetry despite the locality and one-dimensionality of the Hamiltonian, contrary to a naive expectation from the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner-Coleman theorem. Furthermore, critical lines between symmetry-protected topological phases with different $\mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}$-symmetry breaking (e.g., Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{x}$ and Neel$^{\mathrm{SPT}}_{y}$) additionally retain low-energy boundary degrees of freedom, realizing symmetry-enriched criticality (or a gapless SPT phase). Our results reveal unconventional mechanisms by which competing symmetry breaking and topology generate ordered critical phases and multicriticality.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a theoretical framework to engineer highly structured decoherence-free subspaces in open quantum systems by coupling matter to a dissipative bath. By leveraging representation theory of Lie algebras, the authors construct operators that enforce global constraints, leading to steady states with exotic symmetries and correlations. This method offers a controlled way to harness non-reciprocity and engineer complex quantum behavior in light-matter interactions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, systematic recipe for controlling quantum coherence in realistic, dissipative open systems, bridging concepts from group theory, quantum optics, and many-body physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a general framework to construct large and structured decoherence-free subspaces (DFSs) in open quantum systems.

**Main result.** They show that by coupling matter to a dissipative bosonic mode, one can engineer DFSs whose symmetries and properties are dictated by underlying Lie algebraic structures, leading to exotic quantum correlations.

**Method.** The construction relies on identifying 'matter null states' imposed by dissipation, utilizing representation theory of Lie algebras to build the necessary operators.

**Model / system.** The model is a hybrid quantum system coupling quantum matter (fermions or bosons) to a dissipative bosonic mode, exemplified by coupling to a lossy optical cavity and a directed tunneling operator.

**Key observables.** Long-range kinetic correlations, volume-law entanglement, symmetry-constrained Liouvillian skin effect, and the number of steady states.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The structure of the underlying Lie algebra (e.g., $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$) and the non-reciprocal nature of the coupling.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The construction assumes the ability to choose an operator $O$ whose symmetries are distinct from those of the full Liouvillian dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures sketch the central ingredients, including the coupling mechanism, the resulting DFS, and evidence of non-local conserved quantities and the Liouvillian skin effect.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the general framework, details the mathematical construction using Lie algebras, applies it to specific physical examples (like directed tunneling), and validates the results using analytical derivations and time-dependent MPS simulations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a framework to construct large decoherence-free subspaces with a non-trivial structure. The construction is based on hybrid quantum systems in which quantum matter is coupled to a dissipative bosonic mode. Dissipation imposes a global constraint on the matter by selecting the matter null states in the long-time limit. The decoherence-free subspaces spanned by matter null states can exhibit exotic quantum properties and emergent symmetries that do not characterize the full Liouvillian dynamics. We show how to construct many-body operators with physically interesting null states by employing representation theory of Lie algebras. This approach allows us to choose models based on their underlying algebraic structure. We consider explicitly the example of coupling a lossy optical cavity to the directed tunneling operator of quantum particles in one-dimension. In this case, the symmetries of the decoherence-free subspace originate in an $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C})$ algebra, leading to an exponentially large number of steady states. We characterize the null states for both fermionic and bosonic particles, employing analytical and numerical methods. The states exhibit several properties that underline their complex quantum nature: long-range kinetic correlations and volume-law entanglement. The nonreciprocal nature of the directed tunneling dynamics leads to the emergence in the many-body regime of a symmetry-constrained Liouvillian skin effect. The open light-matter system exhibits a strong symmetry stemming from spinless $η$-pairing algebras. We show how the non-trivial properties of the long-times states emerge in the dissipative dynamics from generic initial states, by performing time-dependent matrix product state simulations. Our framework opens avenues for dissipatively engineering complex quantum correlations and harnessing nonreciprocity in a controlled manner.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors propose a novel, chip-scale magnetometer using NV centers coupled to a defect-localized spin-wave mode in a magnonic crystal. By modeling the system dynamics using quantum master equations and analyzing the resulting homodyne response, they predict a substantial enhancement in magnetic field sensitivity. This work demonstrates a pathway to integrate quantum sensing with solid-state magnonics for practical quantum technology.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it combines cavity QED principles (cavity enhancement, coupling to quantum emitters) with solid-state magnonics, providing a roadmap for next-generation quantum sensors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a highly sensitive, chip-scale quantum magnetometer by coupling Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) center ensembles to a passive magnonic cavity.

**Main result.** The projected sensitivity reaches 72 pT/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ by combining the three hyperfine-resolved edges, representing a significant enhancement over single-resonance measurements.

**Method.** The system dynamics are modeled using a Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian coupled to a Lindblad master equation, analyzed via both ODMR and homodyne readout techniques.

**Model / system.** The platform uses a 1D YIG/CoFeB magnonic crystal with a structural defect creating a passive cavity mode. NV ensembles are coupled to this mode, which is biased by integrated permanent magnets.

**Key observables.** Hyperfine-resolved optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectrum and dispersive homodyne response ($\text{Re}\langle a \rangle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Optimal coupling strength ratio ($g_{\text{ens}}/2\pi \approx 0.2$-$0.4 \text{ MHz}$); thermal limits (e.g., 1.7 pT/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The sensitivity calculation relies on combining independent estimates in quadrature and assumes the system operates in a regime where the coupling is strong enough to yield measurable spectral features.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the band structure showing the defect-localized mode, the local dipolar field profile at the NV site, and the resulting ODMR/homodyne spectra showing multiple steep edges.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from characterizing the magnonic cavity mode via micromagnetics to developing the coupled quantum model (Tavis-Cummings/Lindblad) and finally calculating the enhanced sensitivity using both ODMR and homodyne readout formalisms.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre ensembles are leading room-temperature magnetometers, but their sensitivity is usually extracted from a single resonance and relies on external microwave and bias-field hardware. This work proposes a chip-scale NV magnetometer built around a one-dimensional YIG/CoFeB magnonic crystal, in which a single structural defect forms a passive magnonic cavity and integrated permanent magnets supply the bias field. Micromagnetic simulations show a defect-localised spin-wave mode at 2.910 GHz inside the 2.5-3.0 GHz magnonic band gap, 40 MHz from the NV zero-field splitting, with a band structure that matches an independent plane-wave calculation. A Tavis-Cummings/Lindblad model in which the microwave reaches the NV ensemble through this mode predicts a hyperfine-resolved optically detected magnetic resonance spectrum that is strong only within the mode linewidth, and a dispersive homodyne response with one steep edge per $^{14}$N hyperfine line. The master-equation solutions agree with the closed-form homodyne steady state ($R^2 > 0.9999$) and with an approximate analytic ODMR theory (peak positions within 0.012 MHz). For a critically coupled readout with room-temperature electronics, combining the three edges gives a projected sensitivity of 93 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$, a $\sqrt{3}$-fold gain over the best single edge. Mapping the sensitivity against the NV-magnon coupling reveals an optimum near $g_{\rm ens}/2π\approx 0.2$-$0.4$ MHz, where it reaches 72 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for a 0.64 MHz spin linewidth and 19 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for 0.17 MHz, with thermal limits of 6.6 and 1.7 pT/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$. The antenna-mode coupling, the NV-magnon coupling and the spin linewidth are therefore the main design levers.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tackles the difficulty of simulating chaotic quantum many-body systems by framing the problem as time-series forecasting. By comparing a nonlinear Transformer to a linear model (DLinear) on a Rydberg-atom-based PXP model, the authors show that the simple linear model maintains high accuracy across all dynamical regimes, even those exhibiting complex quantum scarring. This suggests that the underlying quantum complexity is not necessarily reflected in the complexity required for prediction.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, data-driven test case showing that linear ML methods can capture the essential dynamics of highly complex, non-integrable quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding information extraction from quantum chaos.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the computational challenge of simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics and investigates if Machine Learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting these complex time evolutions.

**Main result.** Simple linear forecasting models (DLinear) can accurately predict observables generated by complex quantum dynamics across various regimes, suggesting that the complexity of the evolution does not necessitate an equally complex forecasting model.

**Method.** The authors formulate quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, comparing the performance of a nonlinear Transformer against a simple linear model (DLinear) on simulated quantum trajectories.

**Model / system.** The study uses the paradigmatic PXP model, simulating dynamics on a few-qubit chain realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays. The system is tested across dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to non-ergodic quantum many-body scarring.

**Key observables.** Local magnetizations and connected two-point correlation functions are used as the feature vectors for time-series forecasting.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The initial state choice controls the dynamical regime, parameterized between fully polarized and Néel states. The analysis compares performance across these controlled initial conditions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework is benchmarked on a few-qubit PXP chain where exact time evolution is computable, but the methodology is claimed to be extendable to other systems with available time-series data.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the data preparation, training, and prediction stages for both the Transformer and DLinear models across different initial states.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by noting the difficulty of simulating chaotic dynamics, details the ML forecasting protocol using the PXP model, compares the Transformer and DLinear architectures across varying initial states, and concludes by demonstrating the superior performance of the linear model.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Accurately simulating chaotic quantum many-body dynamics remains a major computational challenge for classical methods, due to the rapid buildup and spatial spreading of entanglement during the evolution. This raises the question of whether machine learning can provide an effective alternative for predicting quantum dynamics. We address this question by formulating quantum dynamics as a time-series forecasting problem, using a few-qubit PXP chain, realizable with Rydberg-atom arrays, as a benchmark. By varying the initial state, the system spans dynamical regimes ranging from ergodic behavior to quantum many-body scarring, providing a controlled setting for testing forecasting models across qualitatively different dynamics. We compare two contrasting architectures: an expressive nonlinear Transformer and DLinear, a simple linear forecasting model. The Transformer accurately predicts dynamics in the more ergodic regime, but its performance progressively deteriorates as the initial state approaches the scarred limit. In contrast, DLinear remains accurate across the entire family of initial states, with its main deviations consisting of small high-frequency oscillations that have little effect on the overall prediction error. Remarkably, these results show that observables generated by complex quantum many-body dynamics can be forecast with high accuracy through a simple linear mapping from past to future observations. This reveals that the complexity of the underlying quantum evolution need not translate into an equally complex forecasting problem.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a deterministic polynomial chaos Galerkin method (DPCG) to solve the challenging non-Markovian quantum state diffusion problem. By replacing ensemble averaging with a single deterministic solve based on low-rank decomposition and polynomial expansion, the method drastically cuts computational costs. It proves to be highly accurate and efficient for simulating open quantum systems like the spin-boson model.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, deterministic alternative to computationally expensive stochastic methods for simulating open quantum dynamics, making complex, memory-dependent quantum processes accessible for routine simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing general-purpose and computationally efficient numerical methods for simulating non-Markovian quantum state diffusion (NMQSD) in open quantum systems.

**Main result.** The proposed deterministic polynomial chaos Galerkin method (DPCG) achieves accuracy comparable to stochastic hierarchy methods while drastically reducing computational cost by eliminating the need for large ensembles of trajectories.

**Method.** The method combines a low-rank decomposition of bath correlations with a Galerkin projection onto a polynomial chaos basis, transforming the stochastic evolution into a single, deterministic set of partial differential equations for the expansion coefficients.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on open quantum systems whose dynamics are governed by the NMQSD equation, exemplified by the spin-boson model and the Caldeira-Leggett model. The system interacts with an environment modeled by bath correlations.

**Key observables.** The reduced density matrix ($ho(t)$), spin polarization ($\langle\sigma_zangle_t$), and the state error ($\|\psi_t - \psi_{Q,P,t}\|_X$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low-rank truncation order ($Q$), polynomial chaos total degree ($P$), and the coupling strength ($\xi$ or $\varepsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary approximations involve truncating the infinite-dimensional bath correlation function via low-rank decomposition and truncating the polynomial chaos expansion at a finite total degree $P$.

**Figures summary.** Benchmark comparisons (e.g., for the spin-boson model) show the DPCG method maintaining accuracy comparable to reference solutions at strong coupling, while computational cost is significantly lower than stochastic methods.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the challenge of NMQSD and compares it to existing stochastic methods (HOPS/LRS). It then details the DPCG formulation, deriving the deterministic coefficient system via low-rank factorization and Galerkin projection. Finally, it presents convergence analysis and benchmarks on physical models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Developing general-purpose numerical methods for non-Markovian quantum state diffusion has long been a challenge in the simulation of open quantum systems. This paper proposes a deterministic polynomial chaos Galerkin method, which is easy to implement, accurate, and efficient. By combining a low-rank decomposition of bath correlations with Galerkin projection onto a polynomial chaos basis, the method yields a deterministic formulation compatible with standard numerical solvers for partial differential equations. The reduced density matrix is obtained from a single deterministic solve at a cost comparable to that of computing one stochastic hierarchy trajectory. Replacing an ensemble of $N_{\mathrm{traj}}$ trajectories therefore reduces the computational cost by approximately a factor of $N_{\mathrm{traj}}$ and eliminates statistical sampling error. Benchmark comparisons show that the proposed method achieves smaller errors at lower computational cost than the tested stochastic hierarchy methods. Applications involving nonquadratic potentials, diffraction and interference, and coupled three-dimensional dynamics demonstrate its ability to handle challenging problems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes a cavity-atom system by mapping its dynamics onto an effective 1D lattice model. It shows that the system exhibits two distinct regimes: a large-photon-number regime yielding SSH-type physics with controllable Bloch oscillations, and a small-photon-number regime inducing strong hopping deformation and localization. This highlights the tunability of quantum transport in cavity QED platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework for engineering synthetic quantum transport landscapes using cavity QED, demonstrating how non-RWA terms lead to rich physics like SSH models and localization.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates emergent SSH physics and localization in a cavity-atom system by analyzing its dynamics beyond the rotating-wave approximation.

**Main result.** The system can realize both emergent ladder spectra (in the large-photon-number regime) and hopping-induced localization (in the small-photon-number regime) using the same physical platform.

**Method.** The dynamics are recast into an effective tight-binding problem in the excitation-number basis, analyzed using perturbation theory and by examining different parameter regimes.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a superconducting microwave resonator coupled to an effective two-level artificial atom (Cavity-QED platform). The dynamics are modeled by a generalized quantum Rabi Hamiltonian projected onto effective 1D lattice Hamiltonians.

**Key observables.** Bloch and Bloch-Zener oscillations, anomalous diffusion, density of states reshaping, and return probability $R(t)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Photon number ($ar{n}$), Stark frequency ($\omega$), and coupling strengths ($\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \Omega$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis involves projecting the dynamics onto invariant subspaces ($\mathbb{Z}_2$ parity) and analyzing distinct limits, such as the large-photon-number limit ($ar{n} \gg 2N$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the energy structure for different oscillation regimes ($\gamma=0, \gamma=\omega/2, \gamma
eq 0, \omega/2$) and compare the time evolution of probability distributions $P_n(t)$ across small, intermediate, and large Stark frequency regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from deriving the effective Hamiltonian by projecting the full Rabi model, analyzing the large-$ar{n}$ limit to show SSH-type behavior and Bloch oscillations, and finally examining the small-$ar{n}$ limit to reveal hopping-induced localization and anomalous diffusion.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate a cavity--atom system beyond the rotating-wave approximation and recast its dynamics as an effective tight-binding problem in the excitation-number basis. The same experimentally relevant light--matter platform exhibits two distinct regimes controlled by the photon number. In the large-photon-number regime, the hopping amplitudes become nearly uniform and the effective lattice reduces to a dimerized SSH-type chain subject to a linear energy gradient. The spectrum then organizes into one or two Wannier--Stark ladders, giving rise to controllable Bloch and Bloch--Zener oscillations and quantitatively explaining the observed revival patterns. In the small-photon-number regime, the intrinsic $\sqrt{\bar n+(\cdots)}$ dependence produces a pronounced hopping deformation, namely dimerized couplings that increase along the excitation-number lattice. This deformation reshapes the density of states, enhances collective localization, and generates an energy-resolved spatial bias of the eigenstates. The corresponding real-time dynamics displays direction-dependent anomalous diffusion together with Bloch-like revivals and beat phenomena in selected parameter windows. Our results show that the same cavity--atom platform can realize both emergent ladder spectra and hopping-induced localization in excitation-number space.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors develop a method using building-block construction to find exact many-body eigenstates in coupled cavity-atom systems. They demonstrate that these states exhibit a dual nature: they can manifest as quantum scars that violate thermalization, or they can form robust polariton condensates characterized by long-range order. This framework is valuable for engineering quantum phases in light-matter devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a versatile theoretical framework for engineering coherent quantum phases (condensates) and non-thermalizing states (scars) in controllable light-matter architectures, which is central to quantum simulation and quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To identify and characterize exact many-body eigenstates in hybrid light-matter systems, demonstrating their dual physical nature as quantum scars or polariton condensates.

**Main result.** The constructed exact states exhibit a dual nature: they act as quantum scars violating ETH when embedded in a chaotic spectrum, and they form polariton condensates with Off-Diagonal Long-Range Order (ODLRO) when they are ground states in fixed-excitation sectors.

**Method.** The study employs a building-block construction method based on imposing specific resonance conditions on the system's Hamiltonian to analytically find exact eigenstates.

**Model / system.** The system is a hybrid of coupled cavities (light) and two-level atoms (matter), modeled by a lattice Hamiltonian incorporating JC coupling and nonlinear Stark interactions.

**Key observables.** Quantum scars (violation of ETH), Off-Diagonal Long-Range Order (ODLRO) via correlation functions ($A_r, S_r$), and local excitation-number fluctuations for MI-SF transitions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Resonance conditions ($g_l = \pm rac{\Omega_l}{2}(\omega_l - \kappa)$, etc.), coupling strengths ($g, U_R$), and fixed total excitation number ($\mu$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The construction relies on imposing specific resonance conditions on the building blocks, and the analysis of ODLRO assumes fixed, non-zero filling ($ho > 0$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the building-block construction, spectral statistics (comparing to GOE/Poisson), bipartite entanglement entropy, and Loschmidt echo dynamics for the identified scar tower.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the building-block construction and resonance conditions to find exact states. It then analyzes the dual nature of these states by examining spectral properties (scars) and coherence (condensates). Finally, it rigorously proves ODLRO and characterizes the MI-SF transition using correlation functions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study a hybrid system of coupled cavities, with or without two-level atoms doped inside. By employing a building-block construction facilitated by nonlinear Stark coupling, we identify a manifold of exact many-body eigenstates that remain analytically tractable across arbitrary lattice geometries and atom distributions. We demonstrate that these exact states exhibit a dual physical nature depending on their spectral positioning: when embedded within the chaotic many-body spectrum, they manifest as quantum scars that violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis and undergo weak ergodicity breaking; conversely, as ground states within fixed-total-excitation sectors, they exhibit off-diagonal long-range order and form polariton condensates. Furthermore, numerical calculations of local excitation-number fluctuations suggest that negative Stark coupling shifts the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition toward weaker inter-cavity hopping. Our findings provide a versatile framework for engineering both coherent quantum phases and non-thermalizing states in diverse light-matter architectures.

</details>

**Summary.** This experiment demonstrates the direct measurement of quantized mechanical energy in a nanomechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit. By performing repeated quantum nondemolition measurements, the researchers observed clear quantum jumps between the ground and first excited states. This work marks a significant step in applying quantum control techniques to macroscopic mechanical systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a direct, high-fidelity demonstration of quantum measurement backaction on a macroscopic mechanical oscillator, extending quantum control concepts from superconducting circuits and trapped ions to mechanical systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal was to observe the quantized nature of mechanical energy (phonon number discreteness) in a massive, vibrating object, which is otherwise hidden when measuring displacement.

**Main result.** The authors successfully observed quantum jumps between the resonator's first excited state and ground state, and heralded a single-phonon state with 85% fidelity.

**Method.** They used repeated quantum nondemolition (QND) measurements of the phonon number, implemented by coupling a superconducting qubit to a nanomechanical resonator.

**Model / system.** The system involves a nanomechanical resonator (e.g., in lithium niobate) dispersively coupled to a superconducting transmon qubit. The dynamics are governed by an effective Hamiltonian allowing QND measurement of the phonon number ($\hat{n}$).

**Key observables.** Phonon number distribution $P(n)$, quantum jumps between $|n=1angle$ and $|n=0angle$, and the mechanical lifetime ($T_1$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Mechanical lifetime ($T_1 \approx 2.1$ ms or $645 \mu$s), dispersive shift ($2\chi/2\pi = 328$ kHz/phonon), and single-shot parity assignment fidelity (0.68 to 0.912).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The measurement process is significantly faster than the phonon lifetime, and the forward-backward algorithm is used to estimate the true state evolution from noisy measurement records.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the device architecture, postselected qubit spectra showing phonon number peaks, and individual measurement trajectories demonstrating abrupt quantum jumps between energy levels.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical need to measure energy directly, details the superconducting qubit/nanomechanical resonator platform, presents the QND measurement protocol using parity checks, and finally reports the observation of quantum jumps and state preparation fidelity.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum mechanics predicts that a vibrating object's energy comes in discrete packets, yet no measurement of its position reveals this discreteness. Resolving individual energy levels requires a qualitatively different measurement, one coupling to the resonator's energy rather than its displacement. We use a superconducting qubit dispersively coupled to a nanomechanical resonator to perform repeated quantum nondemolition measurements of the phonon number. An aligned transfer-print technique integrating the qubit and resonator yields a mechanical lifetime of $T_1 = 2.1$ milliseconds and a dispersive shift of $2χ/2π= 328$ kilohertz per phonon. We heralded single-phonon states with 85% fidelity and observed quantum jumps between the resonator's first excited state and ground state. These discontinuous transitions are a striking manifestation of quantum mechanics in a massive, vibrating object.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on a hybrid quantum networking protocol that entangles a trapped ion with a solid-state $	ext{SiV}^-$ memory using photon mediation. By integrating multiple quantum optical components, the researchers achieved a high entanglement rate of 1.03 kHz. This result is significant because it matches the operational speed required for next-generation trapped-ion quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the scalability bottleneck in quantum networking by demonstrating a high-rate, solid-state memory interface for trapped-ion qubits, which is crucial for realizing modular quantum computers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is achieving rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits housed in separate physical modules for scalable distributed quantum computing.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated an entanglement generation rate of 1.03 kHz between a trapped ion and a solid-state memory, matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.

**Method.** The entanglement is heralded by detecting a single photon resulting from a complex process involving ion-photon entanglement, quantum frequency conversion, basis encoding, and spin-dependent reflection from the solid-state memory.

**Model / system.** The system is a heterogeneous quantum architecture combining a trapped $^{138}	ext{Ba}^+$ ion with a silicon-vacancy ($	ext{SiV}^-$) center embedded in a diamond nanophotonic cavity.

**Key observables.** Average entanglement rate (1.03 kHz), Fidelity (87.9%), and measured two-qubit correlators ($\langle	ext{XX}angle, \langle	ext{YY}angle, \langle	ext{ZZ}angle$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Entanglement rate of 1.03 kHz (one Bell pair per millisecond); fidelity of 87.9%; the process is limited by photon loss and heralding efficiency.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The rate is limited by the heralding scheme and remaining loss; the fidelity is subject to error accumulation from multiple components (Ion, QFC, Memory, Detection).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the overall process flow from ion-photon entanglement to heralded ion-$	ext{SiV}^-$ entanglement. Figure 2 details the experimental sequence, showing the time-to-success histogram confirming the measured rate.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical setup, describes the multi-step entanglement protocol (including frequency conversion and basis encoding), presents the measured rate and fidelity, and analyzes the error budget across the various components.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Distributed quantum computing requires rapid, high-fidelity entanglement between qubits in separate processor modules. Photonic links between single-atom qubits provide switchable, long-range connections, but photon loss limits their entanglement rate. Here we entangle a trapped $^{138}$Ba$^{+}$ ion with a silicon-vacancy (SiV$^{-}$) center in a diamond nanophotonic cavity. A photon emitted by the ion is converted in wavelength and encoding, reflected from the SiV$^{-}$--cavity system and detected, so that a single detected photon heralds entanglement. Including all conversion losses, we generate ion--SiV$^{-}$ Bell pairs at an average rate of 1.03(1)\,kHz with a fidelity of 87.9(7)\%. This is four times the rate of the fastest photonic link between two trapped ions and corresponds to one Bell pair per millisecond, matching the cycle time of planned trapped-ion processors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates the use of Subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) to calculate excited state energies using photons whose quantum states are encoded in orbital angular momentum (OAM) qudits. By implementing this on a photonic platform, the authors show a scalable and resource-efficient method for simulating complex molecular and quantum chain Hamiltonians beyond ground state calculations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the challenge of excited state simulation in quantum chemistry using photonic hardware, establishing a resource-efficient pathway for high-dimensional quantum simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Accurately estimating excited state energies is crucial for interpreting photochemical processes, but variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) are typically limited to ground states.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated Subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) on a photonic platform, estimating excited state energies for molecular and quantum chain systems.

**Method.** They use SSVQE, a NISQ-friendly approach, by encoding quantum information in the orbital angular momentum (OAM) of single photons to estimate multiple eigenenergies simultaneously.

**Model / system.** The experiment is performed on a photonic platform using single photons whose quantum states are encoded in OAM qudits. They apply this method to model a four-dimensional HeH+ molecule and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain.

**Key observables.** Estimated excited state energies ($\langle E_j angle$) for the target Hamiltonians, and the convergence of these energies over optimization iterations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The variational parameters ($\vec{\alpha}$) controlling the shared variational unitary circuit, and the dimension of the Hilbert space ($d=4$ or $d=8$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method avoids ancilla-based overlap measurements, relying instead on the coherent preparation and measurement of orthogonal OAM qudit states.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the iterative SSVQE cycle between the QPU, CPU, and classical optimizer. Figure 2 shows the experimental setup using SLMs for state preparation and measurement. Figures 3 and 4 show the calculated energy spectra for HeH+ and the Heisenberg chain, respectively.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the SSVQE algorithm, describes the photonic implementation using OAM qudits and SLMs, presents the experimental setup, and finally reports the successful estimation of excited state energies for the molecular and chain models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Accurate excited state energies are essential for interpreting fluorescence and photochemical processes, yet variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware have largely been confined to ground states. Subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) offers a NISQ-friendly route to excited states without ancilla-based overlap measurements, however it has lacked an experimental demonstration since it requires the coherent preparation and manipulation of multiple orthogonal basis states under a shared variational unitary. Here we realize SSVQE on a photonic platform by encoding orthogonal qudit states in the orbital angular momentum of single photons and optimizing a shared variational circuit. We estimate excited state energies for a four-dimensional $\rm{HeH^+}$ molecule and an eight-dimensional Heisenberg chain, thereby demonstrating scalable excited state eigensolving in a high-dimensional Hilbert space. Our results establish photonic qudits as a resource-efficient pathway to excited state quantum simulation.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the role of multi-photon interference in photonic quantum machine learning by comparing the feature space generated by indistinguishable versus distinguishable photon statistics. The authors show that interference creates a quantifiable geometric separation in the kernel space, which confirms a potential quantum advantage. This protocol allows researchers to test for this advantage computationally before building complex quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, computable, and pre-experimental diagnostic tool (kernel geometry) to predict the potential quantum advantage in photonic quantum machine learning before large-scale hardware investment.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine if multi-photon interference provides a task-independent advantage for quantum machine learning implemented with photonic reservoirs, resolving conflicting experimental reports.

**Main result.** Interference creates a measurable geometric separation between the feature kernels ($K_Q$ vs $K_C$), which is learnable for adversarially constructed tasks, though the advantage on natural tasks is gated by kernel-task alignment.

**Method.** The analysis treats the reservoir as a kernel machine, quantifying the geometric separation between the indistinguishable-photon kernel ($K_Q$) and the distinguishable-photon kernel ($K_C$) using kernel geometry metrics.

**Model / system.** The system is photonic reservoir computing using a linear interferometer where classical inputs are encoded into phases. The process involves injecting $N$ photons and post-selecting on detection events, comparing interference statistics ($P_Q$) to classical statistics ($P_C$).

**Key observables.** Kernel geometry separation ($g$), feature variance distribution, and task-level accuracy advantage ($\Delta A$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hong–Ou–Mandel visibility ($V$), number of photons ($N$), and the sampling budget (number of shots).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on treating the reservoir as a kernel machine and assumes that the geometric separation can be computed and measured robustly.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the reservoir kernel estimation and the distinguishability dial, contrasting the spectral contrast (variance spread) between $K_Q$ and $K_C$.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical framework by defining the kernels based on photon statistics, quantifies the geometric separation, demonstrates its dependence on visibility, and finally tests the learnability of this advantage on both designed and natural task sets.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Multi-photon interference is the resource most native to photonic quantum machine learning, yet experiments on photonic reservoirs have reported advantages, null results, and train-only effects. These outcomes cannot be compared: each measures task-dependent accuracy on different tasks and platforms. Here we resolve the question task-independently through the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps. Interference redistributes feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable-particle statistics, generating a large geometric separation between the corresponding kernels. The separation grows superlinearly with indistinguishability, is linear in Hong--Ou--Mandel visibility at small visibility for two to four photons, and retains approximately 80% of its magnitude at the source quality of current quantum processors. Under experimental sampling budgets the separation is learnable on adversarially constructed tasks (accuracy advantage +0.22 plus or minus 0.05) and an order of magnitude smaller on natural tasks, gated by kernel--task alignment. The results reconcile the existing experimental record and supply a pre-experimental protocol: kernel geometry establishes that an interference-specific learning resource exists, and task alignment determines whether a given task can access it; both are computable before committing significant hardware resources.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using a superconducting transmission line as an analog quantum simulator for $(1+1)$-dimensional $\phi^4$ field theory. By tuning circuit parameters, the system can mimic both simple particle scattering (single-well) and complex topological dynamics like kink-antikink collisions (double-well). This offers a powerful, experimentally accessible platform for studying interacting quantum field dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, hardware-based realization of simulating complex, interacting quantum field theories, bridging superconducting circuit QED with fundamental condensed matter physics problems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is understanding the real-time dynamics of strongly interacting quantum field theories, which is difficult using current computational or experimental methods.

**Main result.** The superconducting transmission line successfully emulates $(1+1)$-dimensional $\phi^4$ field theory, allowing for the simulation of both particle scattering and topological kink-antikink collisions.

**Method.** The authors use analog quantum simulation by engineering a superconducting circuit whose time evolution mimics the field theory dynamics, validated by lattice Monte Carlo calculations.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a Non-linear Transmission Line (NLTL) built from fluxonium-like superconducting circuits. This system is tuned to emulate the Lagrangian of a $\phi^4$ field theory, allowing access to both single-well and symmetry-broken double-well potentials.

**Key observables.** Scattering cross-sections for particle wave packets, and the dynamics of topological kinks and anti-kinks.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio of circuit parameters ($E_{JA}/E_J$ vs $n$) controls the potential regime (single-well vs. double-well). The simulation requires the continuum limit approximation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on the ability to fabricate a sufficiently large, controlled superconducting circuit, and approximations are used to derive the effective continuum action.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the free-field structure, the nonlinear circuit components, the resulting potential wells (single-well and double-well), and the convergence of the dispersion relation to the continuum theory.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical system (NLTL) and its Hamiltonian, confirms its equivalence to the continuum $\phi^4$ theory via lattice calculations, and then details how tuning parameters allows access to different physical regimes (single-well for scattering, double-well for solitons).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum fields remains a fundamental challenge. We propose a superconducting transmission line for analog quantum simulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional $φ^4$ field theory. The transmission line comprises fluxonium-like circuit elements whose continuous and unbounded phase variables encode a scalar field without Hilbert-space truncation. Their anharmonic potentials provide strong interactions. Tuning the circuit parameters provides access to two distinct regimes. In the first, the transmission line emulates $φ^4$ field theory with a single-well potential. We confirm this correspondence through lattice Monte Carlo calculations of the low-energy spectra of both the circuit and lattice $φ^4$ theory. This regime enables scattering experiments between counter-propagating particle wave packets. The second parameter set yields a double-well potential that emulates $φ^4$ theory in the symmetry-broken phase and hosts degenerate vacua. Interfaces between the two vacua form topological kinks, and the transmission line can simulate kink-antikink collisions. We present state preparation and measurement protocols for both collision experiments, enabling spatially resolved, real-time studies of particle and soliton scattering in an interacting quantum field theory.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the experimental demonstration of a high-rate, deterministic source for large-scale photonic GHZ states using semiconductor quantum dots. The key innovation is leveraging a 'natural spin echo' effect to maintain coherence and generate entanglement among more than a dozen photons. This work significantly advances the feasibility of solid-state quantum light sources for quantum information technologies.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses scalable quantum information processing by providing a high-rate, solid-state source of highly entangled photonic states, which is crucial for quantum networking and computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The deterministic generation of large-scale photonic Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states is demonstrated using a solid-state quantum light source.

**Main result.** The authors achieved deterministic generation of photonic GHZ states containing more than a dozen indistinguishable photons at a rate exceeding 1 GHz.

**Method.** The process utilizes a novel 'natural spin echo' mechanism in a semiconductor quantum dot to establish spin-photon entanglement, followed by repeated entangling gates.

**Model / system.** The platform is a semiconductor quantum dot (QD) embedded in a planar microcavity. The mechanism relies on the opposite precession directions of electron and hole spins to nullify accumulated phase.

**Key observables.** GHZ state visibility ($\langle\omega_Nangle$), Localizable Entanglement ($\zeta_{LE}$), and the ZZ-witness ($	ext{ZZ}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Photon generation rate (>1 GHz), number of entangled photons (>12), and the optimal excitation rate ($\Gamma_{	ext{opt}}^{	ext{exc}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The process is limited by electron spin decoherence ($	au_{	ext{dec}}$), and ideal operation requires tuning the excitation rate to nullify the accumulated phase.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup schematic, the temporal sequence for GHZ generation (involving E-CNOT gates), and plots showing the dependence of entanglement witnesses and process fidelity on external magnetic fields and excitation rates.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical mechanism using spin echo, outlines the multi-step process for generating the GHZ state via entanglement gates, presents quantitative measurements of state fidelity and entanglement length, and discusses optimization parameters.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum technologies witness rapid contemporary developments transitioning from abstract scientific ideas and fundamental demonstrations, into systems of sufficient quality and scale, enabling real applications. Photonic quantum technologies are playing a pivotal role in these developments, since photons are robust, easily controlled, detect and measured, thus qualify as flying carriers of quantum information and entanglement distributers. The efforts to develop photonic quantum technologies benefit from the maturity of the classical optical technologies. It was shown that even a source of heralded three entangled photons is sufficient for building large scale quantum computers using otherwise classical optical elements. Here, we demonstrate a novel semiconductor quantum dot based device, which deterministically generate at GHz rates, indistinguishable single photons in a robust Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state of more than a dozen photons. The device utilizes novel natural spin echo concept, provided by the opposite precession directions of the negative and positive carriers' spins in the excited and ground levels of the periodically excited dot, respectively. The excitation rate is finely tuned to nullify the phase acquired by both spins' precession. Our record long GHZ state producing device can yet be feasibly improved to provide higher-rate, brighter and more robust deterministic GHZ source, significantly reducing the overhead requirements for photonic quantum technologies.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports an experimental MDI-QKD system that successfully maintains high security and performance over distances exceeding 300 km. The key innovation is the rigorous incorporation of State-Preparation Uncertainty (SPU) into the security analysis using the operator dominance method. This work significantly advances the practical feasibility of long-haul quantum communication networks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work pushes the boundaries of practical quantum communication by providing a concrete, long-distance demonstration of QKD security under realistic, imperfect source conditions, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum information theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of implementing secure Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when quantum sources are imperfect, specifically by accounting for State-Preparation Uncertainty (SPU).

**Main result.** The authors achieved a record secure key distribution distance of over 300 km while rigorously accounting for the general form of SPU, demonstrating robust performance.

**Method.** They utilized the operator dominance method to derive tight theoretical bounds and performed a complex MDI-QKD experiment involving characterization of phase and intensity fluctuations.

**Model / system.** The system is an experimental Measurement-Device-Independent QKD (MDI-QKD) setup using free-running continuous-wave lasers at 1550.12 nm. Encoding uses time-bin and phase encoding, and the setup includes multiple modulators and single-photon detectors.

**Key observables.** Secret Key Rate (SKR), secure key distribution distance, counting rates ($Q[\mu,\mu]$), and bit error rates ($E_z$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Distance (up to 303.57 km), detection efficiency ($\approx 55\%$), and the degree of State-Preparation Uncertainty (SPU).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the prepared states are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), though the method is designed to handle general SPU forms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the MDI-QKD setup, separate characterization schemes for phase and intensity, and plots showing the SKR versus transmission distance.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the experimental setup, describes the characterization of SPU sources, develops the theoretical framework using operator dominance, and presents the measured SKR results over increasing distances.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum key distribution (QKD) promises theoretically secure communication. However, it encounters challenges in implementation security and performance due to inevitable device imperfections. Since the proposal of measurement-device-independent (MDI) QKD, the critical step toward practical security is to secure QKD with imperfect sources. The source imperfections manifest as state-preparation uncertainty (SPU) in various aspects, e.g., encoding uncertainty, intensity fluctuation, and imperfect vacuum states. Here, we perform an MDI-QKD experiment and achieve both high practical security and superior performance. We address the general form of SPU and guarantee a tight estimation of the secret key rate based on the operator dominance method. We achieve secure key distribution over 303.37 km, which not only represents the farthest distance in experiments involving SPU but also considers the most SPU scenarios. Our experimental results represent a significant step toward promoting practical and secure quantum communication.

</details>

**Summary.** This work studies how a quantum scalar field evolves after its mass is suddenly changed (a quench) in a finite system. Using advanced quantum field theory techniques, the authors predict a unique, measurable anomaly in the effective mass at a specific time related to the system size. This effect is shown to be a consequence of wave interference dictated by the system's periodic boundaries.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides a concrete theoretical framework for understanding finite-size effects in non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, which is highly relevant for interpreting results from ultracold atom experiments in periodic traps.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper theoretically investigates the non-equilibrium evolution of correlation functions for a quantum scalar field following a sudden change (quench) in its mass.

**Main result.** A strong, characteristic disturbance in the effective mass is observed at a time corresponding to half the system size, which is attributed to the interference of counter-propagating fluctuations due to periodic boundary conditions.

**Method.** The analysis employs the Keldysh–Schwinger formalism, solving the Dyson equations numerically in the one-loop approximation (Hartree–Fock).

**Model / system.** The model is a one-dimensional real scalar quantum field theory ($\phi^4$ theory) confined to a finite system of length $L$ with periodic boundary conditions. The system undergoes a mass quench from $m_0$ to $m_1$ at $t=0$.

**Key observables.** Keldysh (statistical) Green’s function, spectral function, and the self-consistently determined effective mass $M_{eff}(t)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size $L$ (varied), coupling constant $\lambda$, and the initial/final masses $m_0, m_1$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a spatially uniform distribution with zero mean field ($\langle\varphiangle=0$) and requires a counterterm to handle vacuum divergences.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 shows the time evolution of $M_{eff}(t)$ for varying $L$. Figure 2 illustrates the light cone structure of the retarded Green’s function. Figure 3 compares results obtained on a ring versus an infinite line.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the formalism using the Keldysh approach, solves the equations numerically in the one-loop approximation, and then confirms the key findings by comparing results obtained using different computational methods (e.g., ring vs. line boundary conditions).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we theoretically investigate the non-equilibrium evolution of the correlation functions of a quantum scalar field following a mass quantum quench in a finite-size system. The self-consistent equation for the Keldysh (statistical) correlation function is solved numerically in the one-loop approximation. A specific spatio-temporal effect is observed: at a point in time approximately equal to half the system size, the effective mass experiences a strong disturbance. It is shown that this effect is driven by the interference of counter-propagating wave fronts of fluctuations that propagate within the light cone and is induced by periodic boundary conditions.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in optimizing nonlinear Josephson microwave circuits by proposing a nonlinear feedback extension to the standard optimization workflow. The method uses the difference between linear and pumped simulation results as a diagnostic observable to guide subsequent, more accurate optimization cycles. This allows for the efficient design of high-performance parametric amplifiers by incorporating complex nonlinear physics into the initial design phase.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges advanced circuit simulation techniques with quantum optics/AMO concepts by treating the optimization of nonlinear quantum devices (like parametric amplifiers) as an iterative, feedback-controlled process, which has parallels in quantum control theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Optimizing Josephson-based nonlinear microwave devices is computationally expensive because standard methods fail to account for pump-induced nonlinear effects during initial linear parameter sweeps.

**Main result.** The authors introduce a nonlinear feedback mechanism using the discrepancy between linear and pumped response metrics, showing this observable contains crucial information about amplifier performance missed by linear optimization.

**Method.** They developed a two-stage optimization framework, extending the initial linear search with an iterative feedback loop that incorporates nonlinear simulation results back into the linear metric update.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifier (JTWPA) utilizing a reversed-Kerr architecture. The model is implemented using a lumped-element circuit description.

**Key observables.** Input reflection coefficient ($S_{11}$) in the signal band, third-harmonic suppression ($S_{11,dB}(3f_p)$), and the discrepancy ($\Delta M$) between linear and pumped metric values.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Circuit parameters like inductive bias ($I_0$) and ground capacitance ($C_g$), and operating frequencies (5–9 GHz signal band).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial linear optimization ignores nonlinear effects like impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced dispersion modifications; the feedback observable must mimic the gain landscape features.

**Figures summary.** Figure 3 validates the model by comparing simulated and measured signal gain. Figure 4 compares the linear metric, nonlinear metric, discrepancy ($\Delta M$), and average gain across the parameter space, highlighting the difference between linear and maximum-gain configurations.

**Paper structure.** The paper outlines the limitations of the standard two-stage optimization (JCO), introduces the nonlinear feedback extension, validates the model against experimental gain measurements, and finally demonstrates the use of the discrepancy ($\Delta M$) as the candidate feedback observable for iterative optimization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Optimizing Josephson-based nonlinear microwave devices is computationally demanding because the straightforward approach requires exploring broad circuit parameter spaces through expensive nonlinear simulations. Josephson Circuits Optimizer addresses this problem by using harmonic balance simulations in two stages: fast linear simulations to select promising circuit configurations according to properties such as impedance and phase matching, followed by nonlinear simulations to optimize their operating conditions. However, pump-induced effects such as impedance renormalization and Kerr-induced modifications of phase matching are not captured during the initial linear stage. We therefore introduce a nonlinear feedback extension that transfers information from the pumped response back to the linear optimization. The approach is investigated using a Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifier with a reversed-Kerr architecture, whose model is validated against experimental gain measurements. We then evaluate the difference between the linear and pumped response values of a metric based on the input reflection coefficient, while excluding configurations with insufficient third-harmonic suppression. This discrepancy is considered a candidate feedback observable, as it exhibits features similar to the gain landscape, supporting its use in subsequent optimization cycles.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors experimentally demonstrate a quantum key distribution protocol using a six-qubit entangled state generated from two photons. They encode the state using an even-parity code, allowing both parties to perform local error checks round-by-round. This method provides a quantum-secure alternative to classical cryptography by leveraging fundamental quantum correlations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, hardware-implementable demonstration of quantum key distribution that moves beyond simple entanglement swapping by incorporating error-correcting code structures into the key exchange protocol itself.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the need for quantum-secure, physics-based asymmetric key generation, providing an alternative to cryptosystems relying on computational hardness assumptions.

**Main result.** They experimentally demonstrated a key generation scheme using a six-qubit photonic entangled state, achieving a high Bell-CHSH parameter ($S = 2.798 \pm 0.008$) and demonstrating built-in error detection.

**Method.** The protocol utilizes a six-qubit state derived from two photons, encoding the qubits into a classical [3,2,2] even-parity code, and uses local parity checks for error filtering.

**Model / system.** The system is a photonic platform using two photons, each carrying polarization and path qubits. The state is generated via a Sagnac-based type-II SPDC source, and the key relies on the correlations within the parity-constrained six-qubit state.

**Key observables.** Bell-CHSH parameter ($S = 2.798 \pm 0.008$), Fidelity ($F = 0.987$), Raw key rate ($\approx 131$ kbit/s), and Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER $\approx 4.61\%$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key rate is doubled by generating two private bits per round. The security relies on the difficulty of guessing the random $t$-bit string, requiring $O(2^t)$ runs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The security is based on the monogamy of shared entanglement, and the local self-check mechanism assumes that errors are independent noise sources.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the quantum circuit for state preparation, the experimental setup using SPDC, and measurements confirming polarization entanglement and the Bell-CHSH parameter.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical construction of the six-qubit state using the [3,2,2] code, outlines the key generation protocol involving public announcement and private reconstruction, and concludes with experimental measurements verifying entanglement and key rate.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose and experimentally demonstrate an asymmetric key-generation scheme in which public and private keys are derived from a six-qubit photonic entangled state. A six-qubit entangled state is generated from two photons, each carrying one polarization and two path qubits. The state is prepared in an equal superposition of eight of the sixty-four six-qubit basis states, in which each photon's three qubits form a codeword of the classical [3,2,2] even-parity code, and are distributed between the two parties, Alice and Bob. This ensures, each triple is a uniformly random codeword and the two codewords are locked together through the correlation. The parity constraint is a local stabilizer, so each party verifies it on its own data every round, and eliminates the bit flip errors arising from imperfections, detector dark counts and multiple occupancy before it enters the raw key. A single publicly announced bit, chosen at random from either of the path qubits, allows each party to reconstruct the other's full triple while leaking no information to third party. We realize the desired six-qubit state using a Sagnac-based type-II SPDC source, reporting a Bell-CHSH parameter S = 2.798 +/- 0.008, by implementing gate operation on polarization and path degree's of freedom. This approach provides a physics-based alternative to public-key cryptosystems built on computational hardness assumptions. A t-bit string generated from multiple rounds for encryption will be intrinsically random. Without the private key, one needs at least O(2^t) runs on an t-qubit quantum system to find the matching bit to decrypt.

</details>
