**Summary.** This paper tackles the scaling bottleneck in superconducting quantum processors by quantifying the impact of parallel operations and parameter drift. It establishes measurable operating rules—such as minimum coupler separation for CZ gates and error-budget-driven refresh schedules—that automate calibration. These rules enable high-fidelity quantum operations on large-scale devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides concrete, experimentally grounded protocols for maintaining coherence and fidelity in large superconducting quantum systems, which is critical for scaling quantum computation beyond current proof-of-concept stages.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenges of scaling superconducting quantum processors by developing quantitative rules to manage crosstalk from parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters during automated calibration.

**Main result.** The derived rules allow for high-fidelity state preparation (e.g., 89.64% fidelity for a six-qubit GHZ state) and significantly reduce single-qubit error rates on large processors.

**Method.** The authors used Cross-Entropy Benchmarking (XEB) to quantify gate fidelity under varying parallel densities and implemented continuous monitoring to derive error-budget-based refresh priorities.

**Model / system.** The work is performed on superconducting quantum processors, specifically utilizing a 66-qubit device with a tunable-coupler architecture, which is tested up to 337 qubits.

**Key observables.** Zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity, single-qubit error rate ($\epsilon$), and the minimum required coupler-graph distance ($d_C$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority assigned to individual control parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes that calibration choices can be converted from heuristic guidelines into measurable, quantitative operating rules based on error budgets.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the full calibration workflow, comparing XEB Pauli error distributions under different parallel densities, and showing the time evolution of key control parameters exhibiting measurable drift.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes system-level limitations (crosstalk and drift), develops quantitative metrics for these limitations, and concludes by implementing an automated framework based on these derived rules.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

As superconducting quantum processors scale toward hundreds of qubits, manual calibration becomes increasingly costly and difficult to sustain. Here we address two system-level factors governing automated calibration, namely, crosstalk induced by parallel operations and temporal drift of control parameters. On a 66-qubit superconducting processor, cross-entropy benchmarking shows that single-qubit calibration tolerates full-chip concurrency with minimal fidelity loss, whereas CZ calibration requires a minimum coupler-graph distance of four to avoid elevated control errors. Continuous monitoring of representative qubit and coupler parameters further yields quantitative refresh rules that assign refresh priority by error-budget consumption. These results turn two conventionally heuristic choices, the concurrency density of calibration tasks and the refresh priority of each control parameter, into measurable operating rules. Implemented within an automated calibration framework, the rules support a six-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state with a zero-noise-extrapolated fidelity of 89.64%, distance-dependent logical-error suppression in a single-cycle repetition-code benchmark, and a reduction of the mean single-qubit error from 0.023 to 0.011 on a 337-qubit processor, providing an experimentally grounded reference for the automated calibration and maintenance of current and future large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This research addresses the vulnerability of superconducting qubits to quasiparticle poisoning from optical fields. By engineering the superconducting material's energy landscape beyond the Josephson junction, the authors developed a Niobium-based transmon that resists optical power-induced relaxation significantly better than standard aluminum devices. This demonstrates a crucial pathway for building more robust, scalable quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses hardware limitations in superconducting quantum computing by providing an experimental method to enhance qubit coherence against environmental noise sources like optical fields, which is critical for scaling quantum processors.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Superconducting qubits are highly susceptible to decoherence and errors caused by quasiparticle (QP) poisoning from high-energy radiation and optical fields.

**Main result.** Engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the Josephson junction, using a Niobium ground plane, increased the qubit's resilience to optical power by over an order of magnitude compared to all-Aluminum devices.

**Method.** The study involves fabricating and characterizing superconducting transmon qubits under varying levels of near-infrared optical illumination, measuring coherence times and frequency shifts.

**Model / system.** The platform is superconducting transmon qubits, comparing an all-Aluminum (Al) device against a novel Niobium (Nb)/Au device. The engineering focuses on controlling the QP energy landscape surrounding the Josephson junctions.

**Key observables.** Relaxation time ($T_1$), coherence time ($T^*$), QP-induced frequency shift ($\delta\omega_q$), and the onset of excess relaxation as a function of optical power.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Near-infrared optical power ($P_o$), gap engineering parameters ($\delta\Delta$), and the material choice (Al vs. Nb).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that engineering the QP energy landscape can physically separate the qubit from the sources of poisoning, although dephasing remains vulnerable.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare $T_1$ and $T^*$ degradation versus optical power for Al and Nb transmons, demonstrating the superior resilience of the Nb device. Simulations also model resonator quality factor ($Q$) dependence on QP sheet resistance.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of QP poisoning, details the novel Nb/Au device structure, presents comparative measurements showing enhanced resilience, and concludes that gap engineering beyond the junction is crucial for robust quantum processors.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Superconducting quantum circuits underpin large-scale quantum processors and are increasingly interfaced with optical systems, yet they are vulnerable to quasiparticle poisoning from high-energy radiation and optical fields. Gap engineering of Josephson junctions suppresses quasiparticle-induced relaxation, but quasiparticles near the junction can still shift the qubit frequency and cause phase errors. Here, we extend gap engineering beyond the junction using a flux-tunable transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and strongly gap-engineered aluminum junctions designed to keep quasiparticles away from the junction leads. Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, we demonstrate that the niobium device withstands more than an order of magnitude higher near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appears. The Nb transmon shows no resolvable quasiparticle-induced frequency shift over the same power range. At the same time, we observe that dephasing and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity increase with optical power even while relaxation remains protected. These results suggest that engineering the quasiparticle energy landscape beyond the junction can substantially increase qubit resilience, not only to radiation-induced error bursts, but also to nearby optical fields.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on an advanced SWAP spectroscopy technique to study TLS defects in superconducting qubits. By using fast flux pulses, the researchers achieved unprecedented sensitivity, detecting coherent TLS dynamics at very low coupling strengths. This work significantly advances the understanding of decoherence mechanisms, which is crucial for building reliable quantum computers.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly sensitive experimental platform for characterizing decoherence sources in superconducting qubits, directly impacting the feasibility and fidelity of quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is mitigating energy loss from Two-Level System (TLS) defects in superconducting qubits while achieving high-resolution spectroscopy of these defects.

**Main result.** The authors successfully detected coherent TLS dynamics at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, revealing TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds.

**Method.** They introduced a fast flux pulse sequence for SWAP spectroscopy, allowing for fine frequency resolution and long interaction times to probe weak coupling regimes.

**Model / system.** The system involves flux-tunable superconducting qubits coupled to TLS defects. The dynamics are analyzed using a dressed-state picture, fitting the coherent swap oscillations to extract relaxation times.

**Key observables.** Rabi chevrons, swap rates (0.1 MHz), TLS energy-relaxation time ($T_{relax}$), and swap coherence time ($T_{osc}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Sub-MHz frequency resolution, detection of coherence at rates an order of magnitude lower than previously reported.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on fitting the time-domain population decay ($P_1(	au)$) to a three-component model involving oscillation, relaxation, and background decay.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the SWAP spectroscopy technique, comparing previous detection limits ($\gtrsim 5$ MHz) to the new capability ($\downarrow 0.1$ MHz), and show the fitted time traces revealing oscillations and exponential decay.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from introducing the problem of TLS loss to detailing the novel fast-flux pulse sequence, presenting the measurements of low-rate Rabi chevrons, and finally analyzing the extracted coherence and relaxation times.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

An outstanding challenge in superconducting quantum circuits is mitigating loss from two-level system (TLS) defects. SWAP spectroscopy with flux-tunable qubits can detect individual TLSs, but the Rabi chevrons that signal coherent exchange have been observed only for the most strongly coupled defects. Here, we introduce a sequence with fast flux pulses only at state preparation and readout, switched off during the energy-relaxation delay for finer frequency resolution and longer interaction times. We detect Rabi chevrons at swap rates as low as 0.1 MHz, an order of magnitude lower than previously reported. In the dressed-state picture, we fit the coherent swap oscillations to extract the TLS energy-relaxation time. These Rabi chevrons reveal coherent TLSs with a median energy-relaxation time of 10 microseconds, at coupling strengths previously associated with incoherent TLSs. The swap coherence times exceed the qubit T2* limited by flux noise, indicating that the dressed gap protects them from low-frequency 1/f noise.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a new classical post-processing technique, the trace filter function, to overcome systematic biases in randomized benchmarking measurements. By suppressing transient decay modes, the method allows for accurate extraction of fidelity decay rates even when experimental circuits are too short for standard estimators to converge. This significantly extends the reliable characterization window for quantum hardware performance.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial algorithmic tool for characterizing decoherence in near-term quantum hardware, directly impacting the ability to benchmark quantum processors against theoretical limits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of obtaining accurate, unbiased estimates of fidelity decay rates from randomized benchmarking (RB) experiments when transient modes bias standard short-depth measurements.

**Main result.** A novel 'trace filter function' post-processing technique is introduced that provably suppresses these transient modes, enabling reliable fidelity characterization at circuit depths inaccessible to conventional estimators.

**Method.** The authors develop and analyze a one-parameter family of estimators, culminating in the trace filter function, which is applied to the measured expectation values from random circuits.

**Model / system.** The work is validated using experiments on a superconducting processor (Rigetti) for one-dimensional circuits up to 12 qubits, utilizing random Clifford circuits generated via brickwork patterns.

**Key observables.** Fidelity decay rate ($eta$), transient modes, and the variance of the estimators.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The filter parameter $\alpha$, the circuit depth ($m$), and the qubit number ($n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumptions include time-stationary Markovian gate-dependent noise and local-symmetry assumptions for the noise model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup (simulated and physical circuits), the comparison of different methods for determining the mixing length, and the theoretical scaling of moment calculations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the bias caused by transient modes in RB, introducing the interpolating estimator family, deriving the theoretical properties of the trace filter function (including its efficiency for local circuits), and validating the method with superconducting hardware experiments.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Randomized benchmarking (RB) with structured circuits is experimentally scalable, but gives biased short-depth fidelity estimates because incomplete ensemble mixing introduces transient modes. Waiting for these transients to decay in deeper circuits can push the signal below the noise floor. This is a well-established obstacle, e.g. in linear cross-entropy benchmarking (LinXEB). Here we overcome this obstacle solely through classical post-processing. We introduce a one-parameter family of estimators that interpolate between the standard LinXEB-type post-processing and a new post-processing technique we call the trace filter function. Under practical assumptions, the trace filter function provably suppresses transient modes, exposing an interpretable fidelity decay at short depth, with theoretical guarantees comparable to standard RB, at the cost of an increased variance. We bound the variance, analyze the evaluation complexity of the new estimators, and develop practical post-processing algorithms. Experiments on a Rigetti superconducting processor validate the method for one-dimensional circuits of up to 12 qubits: where the standard estimator requires depth beyond a 40-layer experimental window, the trace filter function yields consistent estimates below 10 layers. Trace-filtered randomized benchmarking therefore extends reliable fidelity characterization to relevant structured circuit ensembles and short-depth regimes that are inaccessible to conventional estimators.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents Residual-Guided Drive Design (RGDD), a novel optimization protocol for engineering arbitrary interaction graphs in trapped-ion quantum simulators. RGDD iteratively adds laser tones to synthesize a target Hamiltonian while minimizing infidelity and controlling motional excitation errors. This scalable framework significantly expands the programmable capabilities of trapped-ion quantum computing platforms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of controlling complex many-body interactions in trapped ions, providing a scalable, systematic method for designing the required laser fields.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge is designing a compact set of global drive spectra to synthesize a target interaction Hamiltonian in trapped-ion quantum simulators with high fidelity.

**Main result.** The Residual-Guided Drive Design (RGDD) protocol systematically achieves near-theoretical fidelity bounds using a number of laser tones that scales nearly linearly with system size.

**Method.** RGDD is an incremental optimization strategy that iteratively adds global laser tones, guided by the residual error, to minimize the cosine infidelity between the synthesized and target interaction.

**Model / system.** The system is trapped-ion quantum simulators, where interactions are modeled using long-range Ising-type Hamiltonians generated by multi-tone global drive laser fields.

**Key observables.** Cosine infidelity ($I$), minimum number of tones ($M_{min}$), and residual motional excitation ($\alpha_k$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate time ($t_g$), penalty coefficient ($\lambda_a$), and the ratio of gate time to baseline time ($s = t_g/t_{g0}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The accessible interaction space is fundamentally constrained by the native motional modes of the ion crystal.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare tone-count scaling (RGDD vs. NNLS) and closure error across different power-law targets; Figure 6 compares infidelity vs. tone count for RGDD versus equal-spacing placement.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the RGDD protocol, details the optimization objective incorporating a closure penalty, and then analyzes its performance by comparing it against baseline methods (like NNLS) and by investigating the trade-off between infidelity and closure error as a function of gate time.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Trapped-ion quantum simulators are powerful platforms for exploring many-body physics, yet engineering of arbitrary interaction graphs remains a central challenge. To leverage the intrinsic structure of native motional modes and thereby enhance programmability, a residual-guided optimization protocol is introduced for the systematic design of multi-tone global drive spectra. While the achievable interaction fidelity is fundamentally bounded by the available motional modes, this adaptive strategy converges on the theoretical limit using a number of laser tones that scales nearly linearly with system size. The versatility of this method enables the synthesis of both long-range and traditionally difficult short-range coupling topologies. Additionally, by incorporating a penalty for residual motional excitation, the algorithm effectively mitigates errors associated with incomplete closure of phase-space trajectories. Overall, this scalable framework significantly expands the programmable capabilities of trapped-ion architectures while maintaining low computational overhead and high potential for experimental implementation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on advanced error correction techniques applied to a large superconducting quantum processor. The researchers successfully implemented the dynamic compass code while actively compensating for hardware imperfections like underperforming qubits. By using noise-informed decoding and defect mitigation, they demonstrated that high-fidelity fault-tolerant memory and logic operations are achievable on monolithic, imperfect quantum chips.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, hardware-aware roadmap for scaling quantum computation by directly addressing the practical limitations of superconducting chip fabrication, which is highly relevant to experimental quantum information scientists.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is achieving high-fidelity, fault-tolerant quantum computation and memory using superconducting qubits while accommodating unavoidable component heterogeneity.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated that by combining noise-informed decoding, defect exclusion, and leakage post-selection, they maintained high performance, achieving logical error probabilities improvements of up to 35% and Bell fidelities above 97% for lattice surgery.

**Method.** They employed advanced noise-informed quantum error correction strategies, including using ACES-derived Pauli noise models and implementing defect exclusion and leakage pre-selection filtering.

**Model / system.** The work is performed on a superconducting-qubit processor with 156 qubits arranged on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, utilizing the dynamic compass code for error correction.

**Key observables.** Logical error probabilities (for memory), failure probability (for stability), and Bell fidelities (for lattice surgery).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The performance improvements are quantified relative to baseline measurements, showing gains up to 56% in stability experiments.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The performance gains rely on the successful combination of multiple advanced noise-informed quantum error correction strategies to mitigate component imperfections.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the dynamic compass code layout on the 156-qubit processor, detailing the syndrome extraction schedule and how underperforming qubits are excluded.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the implementation of the dynamic compass code on the physical hardware, presents results comparing various noise-informed decoding strategies (including defect exclusion and leakage post-selection), and demonstrates high-fidelity operations like lattice surgery.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Large quantum computations require high-fidelity error-corrected memory and fault-tolerant logical operations. To achieve these with superconducting circuits, quantum processors will need many components operating with low error rates. In practice, fabrication of monolithic superconducting devices produces unavoidable heterogeneity in component performance, which the quantum computer must accommodate. We implement strategies to operate a large dynamic compass code on an array of 156 superconducting qubits arranged on a heavy-hexagonal lattice, making use of the entire monolithic quantum processor and redesigning our measurement schedule to exclude underperforming components. We demonstrate improvements of up to $35\%$ in logical error probabilities for a memory experiment by using a noise-informed decoder combined with strategies to exclude the worst-performing qubits and couplers, along with post-selecting on shots with a low probability of leakage errors. In addition to these memory results, we also observe performance gains of up to $56\%$ when these strategies are applied to measurement-based logic, demonstrated by stability experiments. We furthermore demonstrate high-fidelity fault-tolerant logic through lattice surgery. Through pre-selection filtering techniques, we can obtain Bell fidelities above $77\%$, and further logical gap post-selection using exclusive decoding increases these fidelities to above $97\%$. Our experiments demonstrate that high performance can be maintained in key elements of fault-tolerant quantum memory and logic when working on monolithic superconducting quantum processors with underperforming components, by using a suite of noise-informed quantum error correction strategies.

</details>

**Summary.** This work characterizes a novel class of topologically distinct superradiant quantum critical points in cavity-mediated spin chains. By analyzing edge degeneracies and comparing bulk versus boundary critical behavior, the authors prove that this criticality is fundamentally different from conventional transitions. This has implications for understanding topological order in open quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** It bridges concepts from quantum optics (superradiance) with topological quantum matter, showing how topological invariants can characterize critical points in open quantum systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To investigate if superradiant phase transitions can exhibit topological universality classes distinct from conventional light-matter coupled systems.

**Main result.** The critical line separating the superradiant phase from the cavity topological phase is topologically nontrivial, evidenced by robust symmetry-protected edge degeneracies, and this criticality is generic for cluster-qudit chains.

**Method.** Numerical simulations, including Finite-size Density-Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) and analysis of entanglement entropies and energy spectra.

**Model / system.** The study uses cavity-mediated cluster-Ising chains (and generalizes to cluster-qudit chains) coupled to a single photon mode, described by a specific Hamiltonian involving cavity and spin interactions.

**Key observables.** Photon occupation number, entanglement entropies ($S_{	ext{spin}}$, $S_{	ext{photon-spin}}$), Binder cumulant, and boundary/bulk spin correlations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling strengths ($g, J, f$), photon frequency ($\omega_0$), and system size ($L$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on comparing bulk critical properties with boundary/edge properties to diagnose topological differences.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing three distinct phases (FM, Superradiant, SPT), and show finite-size scaling of entanglement entropies and correlation functions confirming topological differences between models.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the phase diagram, using DMRG and finite-size scaling to distinguish between topologically trivial and non-trivial critical points in the superradiant transition.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Superradiant phase transitions are fundamental phenomena in light-matter coupled systems. Here, we uncover a novel class of superradiant criticality that is topologically distinct from previously known superradiant transitions. Using cavity-mediated cluster-Ising chains as an illustrative example, we numerically demonstrate that the critical line separating the superradiant phase from the cavity topological phase hosts robust symmetry-protected edge degeneracies, a feature absent in conventional superradiant transitions. Remarkably, although its local bulk critical properties are indistinguishable from those of the previously identified topologically trivial superradiant transition, the two criticalities cannot be smoothly connected without breaking the protecting symmetries or passing through a multicritical point. We further show that such topological superradiant criticality is generic, also occurring in cavity-mediated $\mathbb{Z}_{n}^{}$ cluster-qudit chains, as supported by complementary lattice simulations.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study proposes a controllable method to generate remote nonreciprocal entanglement between magnons in a coupled cavity system. By leveraging the Barnett effect and implementing coherent quantum feedback, the authors show that the entanglement can be selectively generated for one direction of the applied magnetic field while suppressing it in the opposite direction. This offers a versatile platform for quantum information processing using magnonic circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it combines several advanced topics: cavity quantum electrodynamics (magnonics), non-Hermitian physics (via feedback), and the study of quantum correlations (entanglement) in solid-state systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the generation and control of remote nonreciprocal magnon-magnon entanglement in a coupled cavity magnonic system.

**Main result.** They demonstrate that nonreciprocal entanglement can be achieved by tuning the system parameters, specifically showing that entanglement exists for one direction of the bias magnetic field while vanishing for the opposite.

**Method.** The analysis uses Quantum Langevin Equations (QLEs) to model the system dynamics and quantifies entanglement using the logarithmic negativity of the magnon covariance matrix.

**Model / system.** The system consists of two microwave cavities coupled to YIG spheres (one rotating, one stationary) and driven by squeezed vacuum fields, incorporating the Barnett effect and a coherent feedback loop.

**Key observables.** Magnon-magnon entanglement ($E_N$), Asymmetry Contrast ($\xi_E$), and critical temperatures for entanglement vanishing.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cavity detuning, feedback phase, relative squeezing phase, squeezing factors ($R_1, R_2$), and the sign of the Barnett shift ($\Delta B$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes a lossless feedback loop and neglects propagation delay.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dependence of entanglement ($E_N$) on the relative squeezing phase, feedback reflectivity ($r_b$), squeezing factors ($R_1$), and temperature ($T$) for both positive and negative Barnett shifts.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical model using QLEs, derives the necessary steady-state covariance matrix equations, and then systematically analyzes the entanglement measure ($E_N$) as a function of control parameters to establish the nonreciprocal control scheme.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a scheme for generating and controlling remote nonreciprocal magnon--magnon entanglement in a cavity magnonic system with coherent feedback.The two microwave cavities are driven by independent single-mode squeezed vacuum fields, with a rotating YIG sphere in the left cavity and a stationary one in the right cavity. For a fixed rotation direction, reversing the bias magnetic field applied to the rotating sphere changes the sign of the Barnett shift, leading to nonreciprocal magnon--magnon entanglement. By tuning the cavity detuning and feedback phase, entanglement can be generated for one direction of the bias magnetic field while it vanishes for the opposite direction, yielding complete nonreciprocity. Coherent feedback enhances the entanglement at an appropriate reflectivity, whereas stronger feedback can reduce it. The relative squeezing phase provides additional control, and an appropriate choice of unequal squeezing factors improves the entanglement at fixed total input photon occupation. With the squeezed inputs kept fixed, moderate feedback also increases the critical temperature for magnon entanglement.Our results provide a controllable approach to preparing remote nonreciprocal quantum correlations in cavity magnonic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This review surveys how strong-field Terahertz and Mid-infrared radiation are used to probe and manipulate emergent phenomena in quantum materials. By employing nonlinear spectroscopy, researchers can access complex dynamics related to coupled electronic, lattice, and superconducting orders. The work highlights the potential of these techniques to control material properties by driving systems far from equilibrium.

**Why it may be interesting.** The techniques described—using intense, tunable THz/MIR fields to drive systems nonlinearly—are highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics, as they represent coherent, non-equilibrium driving protocols for many-body systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is identifying and controlling emergent phenomena in quantum materials by understanding the complex interactions among various degrees of freedom (charge, spin, orbital, lattice). This control is crucial for tailoring material properties.

**Main result.** Strong-field THz and MIR radiation can drive quantum materials far from equilibrium, allowing for the transient reshaping and manipulation of ordered electronic and lattice states.

**Method.** The work reviews techniques using nonlinear THz/MIR spectroscopy, including 2D spectroscopy and time-resolved measurements, to probe these complex dynamics.

**Model / system.** The study covers diverse quantum materials, including superconductors (cuprates, $	ext{MgB}_2$), topological insulators, ferroelectrics ($	ext{SrTiO}_3$), and semiconductors (GaAs). The physics involves coupled electronic, lattice, and superconducting order parameters.

**Key observables.** Nonlinear conductivity, order-parameter dynamics (e.g., Higgs mode), gap/spectral-weight transfer, and symmetry-sensitive responses.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strong-field THz and Mid-infrared radiation intensity, frequency, and phase coherence.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Linear spectroscopy is insufficient for disentangling complex interactions, and the analysis often relies on semiclassical or anharmonic potential expansions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the frequency coverage of intense THz sources and detection methods. Figure 2 summarizes nonlinear THz spectroscopy paradigms, linking techniques (like THz-pump/THz-probe) to physical information (like gap dynamics).

**Paper structure.** The review surveys progress by first establishing the need to probe coupled degrees of freedom. It then details the experimental platforms (THz/MIR sources, detection) and progresses through specific physical phenomena, such as nonlinear electronic dynamics, collective mode coupling, and symmetry-sensitive responses.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Emergent phenomena in quantum materials arise from interactions among different degrees of freedom. Identifying these interactions and establishing their roles in ordered states are central problems in condensed-matter physics and provide a basis for controlling material properties. Many relevant low-energy excitations and gaps lie in the terahertz (THz) and mid-infrared (MIR) range, where intense phase-stable fields can both interrogate nonlinear dynamics and drive selected degrees of freedom far from equilibrium. This review surveys recent progress in probing and manipulating quantum materials with strong-field THz and MIR radiation, with emphasis on nonlinear electronic dynamics, collective-mode coupling, symmetry-sensitive responses and field-induced changes in electronic structure and ordered states. Particular attention is given to developments enabled by the Synergetic Extreme Condition User Facility (SECUF).

</details>

**Summary.** This research introduces a method to control transitions between non-equilibrium steady states by actively engineering the noise correlations of the surrounding bath. Using a trapped particle model, the authors derive analytical protocols that allow for faster state changes than natural relaxation. The work is significant because it treats the bath's temporal correlations as a controllable parameter, enabling optimization of both speed and energy dissipation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses non-equilibrium dynamics far from equilibrium, providing a quantitative method to steer system states using engineered environmental correlations, which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems and dissipation engineering.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops and demonstrates control protocols for achieving finite-time transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states (NESSs).

**Main result.** By actively engineering the temporal correlations (noise color) of the bath, transitions can be achieved substantially faster than natural relaxation times, while also allowing optimization of thermodynamic costs.

**Method.** The core method involves reverse-engineering the required time-dependent correlation rate ($\omega_c(t)$) by solving the coupled differential equations governing the system's second moments (variance and covariance) based on a desired trajectory.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a particle undergoing an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process (AOUP) confined in a harmonic trap. The active bath is controlled by modulating the noise correlation rate $\omega_c(t)$.

**Key observables.** Normalized variance ($\hat{s}(t)$), excess heat ($\hat{Q}_{ex}$), and the transition duration ($t_f$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Trap relaxation rate ($\omega_0$), active diffusion coefficient ($D_a$), and the control parameter $\omega_c(t)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on polynomial fitting (e.g., third- or fifth-order) to define the admissible control trajectories, and the system dynamics are analyzed via second moments.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison between polynomial control protocols ($p_3$, $p_5$) and instantaneous step protocols for achieving faster transitions, and show the optimization of excess heat and minimum transition time.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by deriving the moment equations and the required control law $\omega_c(t)$. It then develops and analyzes polynomial protocols ($p_3, p_5$) to achieve specific trajectories, followed by optimization procedures to minimize time or excess heat, culminating in experimental validation using a trapped colloidal particle.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a family of control protocols for finite-time transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states using the noise-color (correlation rate) as the sole control parameter. By reverse-engineering the second moment dynamics of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, we determine the time-dependent correlation rate required to realize a prescribed evolution of the system's state. We experimentally implement these protocols with a micrometer-sized optically trapped particle coupled to an engineered active bath, demonstrating transitions substantially faster than the natural relaxation while keeping the confining potential, noise amplitude, and temperature fixed. Our approach extends engineered swift-equilibration methods to far-from-equilibrium steady states by directly controlling the temporal correlations of an active environment. We show how physical constraints impose a speed limit on finite-time transitions, while the freedom in choosing the prescribed system evolution can be exploited to eliminate control discontinuities, minimize the admissible transition time, or optimize a thermodynamic cost.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes a qubit interacting with a coherent environment through repeated collisions. It demonstrates that environmental coherence acts as a powerful resource, allowing the system to achieve steady states with enhanced purity and even cool below the bath temperature. Furthermore, it shows that this coherence can induce anomalous heat flow, controlled by the relative phase between system and ancilla coherence.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and open quantum systems, showing how environmental correlations (coherence) can violate simple thermal assumptions to control energy flow and state preparation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how environmental coherence influences the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit interacting with a coherent environment via repeated interactions.

**Main result.** Environmental coherence acts as a quantum resource, enabling cooling below the bath temperature and allowing for anomalous heat flow whose direction depends on the relative phase of the coherence.

**Method.** The authors derive an exact analytical solution for the dynamics using the Markovian repeated-interaction (RI) framework, analyzing the evolution map $ho^{(n+1)}_S = 	ext{Tr}_A \{ \hat{U}(	au) ho^{(n)}_S \otimes ho_A \hat{U}^\dagger(	au) \}$.

**Model / system.** The model consists of a single qubit (System, S) interacting sequentially with an ancillary qubit (Ancilla, A) via a flip-flop interaction Hamiltonian. The dynamics are treated as a Markovian process.

**Key observables.** System ground-state population ($p^{(n)}_S$), coherence ($c^{(n)}_S$), steady-state purity, and the direction/amount of heat transfer.

**Important parameters / regimes.** System-ancilla coupling strength ($J$), interaction time ($	au$), environmental coherence magnitude ($|c_A|$), and the relative phase between system and ancilla coherence.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the system and ancilla are resonant ($\omega_S = \omega_A$) and that the process is Markovian (no memory effects between collisions).

**Figures summary.** The notes mention figures illustrating the required number of iterations ($n^*$) to reach steady state, showing it increases with environmental coherence, and plots showing the steady-state coherence and $l_1$-norm as a function of environmental coherence.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the model and derives the exact solution (Section II), investigates cooling below bath temperature and purity enhancement (Section III), and analyzes the thermodynamics and anomalous heat flow (Section IV).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the relaxation dynamics and steady state of a qubit interacting with a coherent environment through an energy-conserving flip-flop interaction within the Markovian repeated-interaction framework. We derive an exact analytical solution for the evolving and stationary state, nonperturbative in the environmental coherence. We show that environmental coherence provides a resource for dissipative state preparation by expanding the set of accessible steady states. In particular, coherent ancillas can increase the system ground- state population beyond that of the bath, corresponding to an effective temperature below the bath temperature, and enhance its steady-state purity, with these effects controlled by the interplay between the system energy scale and the system-ancilla coupling. Nevertheless, we prove that the purity of the system can never exceed the purity of the ancilla. We further analyze the thermodynamics of the protocol and show that environmental coherence can modify and even reverse the natural direction of heat transfer, giving rise to anomalous heat flow. Remarkably, for fixed interaction parameters, the direction of the coherence-induced heat transfer is governed by the relative phase between the system and ancilla coherence, whereas their magnitudes determine the amount of heat exchanged. Our results establish environmental coherence as a resource for controlling steady-state preparation and energy transfer in repeated-interaction dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors show that in systems with ultrastrong light-matter coupling, the formation of polaritons and the dressing of the quantum vacuum are not equivalent. By utilizing helicity control in a chiral cavity coupled to a 2DEG, they can independently access these two regimes, proving that a large Rabi splitting alone does not guarantee a dressed vacuum state.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a clean, experimentally addressable platform (chiral cavities) to decouple two closely related, yet distinct, quantum phenomena (polaritons vs. vacuum correlations) in the regime of ultrastrong coupling, which is highly relevant to cavity QED.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To demonstrate that polariton formation (spectral hybridization) and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct physical phenomena arising from ultrastrong light-matter coupling.

**Main result.** By controlling the helicity of the cavity field relative to the cyclotron motion, the system can be tuned to exhibit either conventional polariton anticrossings or vacuum dressing effects, proving the two are distinct.

**Method.** Theoretical modeling using Hamiltonian approaches and advanced numerical techniques like the Transfer Matrix Method (TMM) and full-wave finite-element simulations.

**Model / system.** The system involves cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circular mode, realized in a 2DEG coupled to a photonic crystal cavity.

**Key observables.** Rabi splitting, polaritonic anticrossing, ground state squeezing, virtual excitation populations, and polarization-resolved magnetotransmission spectra.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Helicity ($\chi$), magnetic field direction ($B$), cyclotron frequency ($\omega_c$), and coupling strength ($g$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on a single-mode approximation for the cavity and assumes the ability to fix the cavity helicity while reversing the magnetic field on the 2DEG.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spectral reorganization, showing a clear avoided crossing when the cavity and cyclotron motion co-rotate ($B<0$), and the disappearance of this crossing with the acquisition of vacuum correlations when they counter-rotate ($B>0$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical setup using chiral cavities, develops the Hamiltonian based on helicity control, and then analyzes two distinct regimes ($B<0$ vs $B>0$) to spectroscopically and correlationally separate the effects of hybridization from vacuum dressing.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Polaritons and quantum vacuum dressing are usually regarded as intertwined consequences of ultrastrong light-matter coupling. Here we show that they can be controlled independently through helicity. We consider cyclotron resonance coupled to a chiral cavity supporting a single circular mode. When the helicity of the cavity field matches the cyclotron motion, energy is exchanged resonantly between light and matter, producing a large Rabi splitting and conventional polaritons, while the ground state remains the bare vacuum. Reversing the magnetic field reverses the cyclotron motion without changing the cavity. The same mode then couples through anomalous processes that create and annihilate light and matter excitations in pairs: the conventional polaritonic anticrossing disappears, while the ground state acquires squeezing and virtual excitations. These two regimes show that spectral hybridization and quantum vacuum dressing are distinct manifestations of ultrastrong coupling, and that a large Rabi splitting alone does not imply a dressed quantum vacuum. Helicity therefore provides a route to controlling polariton formation and quantum correlations as distinct resources in cavity quantum materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a comprehensive, unified framework for building and validating effective quantum models from complex dynamics. It moves beyond simple derivation by enforcing a three-step consistency check—encoding, evolution, and reconstruction—to ensure physical predictions are robust. This methodology is vital for accurately modeling systems like cavity QED or driven lattices where approximations are common.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial methodological toolkit for AMO physicists working with open quantum systems, offering rigorous diagnostics to distinguish between a mathematically derived effective Hamiltonian and one that yields physically consistent predictions.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to develop a unified and rigorous framework for constructing and validating effective quantum models that accurately predict measurable physical quantities.

**Main result.** It establishes a three-step, order-consistent process (encoding, evolution, reconstruction) for physical predictions, systematically exposing failures in approximations like leakage or inconsistent observables.

**Method.** The framework unifies multiple projection techniques, including Schrieffer-Wolff transformations, Magnus expansions, Floquet theory, and adiabatic elimination, to derive effective dynamics.

**Model / system.** The Quantum Rabi Model serves as a recurring benchmark, allowing the systematic comparison of different effective descriptions derived under varying physical regimes (e.g., near vs. far from resonance). Applications include light-matter coupling and driven lattices.

**Key observables.** Control parameters, virtual processes, spectral corrections, and the reconstructed physical observable ($\hat{ho}_{	ext{rec}}(t)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Detuning ($\Delta$), coupling strength ($g$), and the ratio of coupling to spectral gaps, which dictate the validity of approximations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core challenge is ensuring consistency across all components (manifold, observables, dissipation) when eliminating high-energy or fast degrees of freedom.

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured around developing the unified framework, benchmarking it using the Rabi model, and detailing the three-step process for generating and validating physical predictions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Effective models make complex quantum dynamics tractable by retaining only the states, processes, and timescales relevant to a given physical question. Their predictive power, however, depends on treating the retained manifold, initial state, observables, micromotion, dissipative channels, and eliminated degrees of freedom consistently. We develop a unified framework for constructing and validating effective descriptions using projection methods, Schrieffer--Wolff transformations, Magnus expansions, adiabatic elimination, small rotations, time coarse graining, and Floquet theory. The quantum Rabi model and its dispersive limits serve as recurring benchmarks for identifying control parameters, virtual processes, spectral corrections, observable dressing, and breakdown. Higher-order resonances and applications to collective light--matter coupling, Raman processes, spin-chain buses, lossy mediators, and driven lattices illustrate how effective interactions can be interpreted and designed. A physical prediction is organized into three order-consistent steps: encoding into the retained description, evolution under the effective dynamics, and reconstruction of the physical observable. This viewpoint exposes failures caused by leakage, small denominators, neglected micromotion, inconsistent observables, memory effects, or incorrectly transformed dissipation, while linking derivation, physical interpretation, and mechanism-guided discovery. Companion notebooks provide QuTiP implementations, convergence tests, and microscopic-to-effective comparisons.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel technique to independently control the polarization of light at every site within an optical tweezer array using a spatial light modulator. By achieving this site-resolved polarization control, the researchers successfully homogenized light shifts on trapped strontium atoms, enabling high-fidelity sideband cooling and controlled transport across the array. This technique is vital for building scalable, multi-zone quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial experimental tool—local polarization control—that directly addresses a major bottleneck in scaling up quantum simulation and quantum computing architectures based on optical tweezers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is achieving independent, site-resolved control over the polarization of individual optical tweezers within an array, which is necessary for advanced quantum state engineering.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated site-resolved linear polarization rotation using a spatial light modulator, enabling sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition and dynamic atom transport across polarization zones.

**Method.** They exploit the local birefringence tunability of a liquid-crystal spatial light modulator (SLM) to imprint controlled phase retardations, thereby rotating the polarization at each trapping site.

**Model / system.** The experiment uses optical tweezer arrays trapping ultracold strontium atoms ($^{88}	ext{Sr}$). The system relies on the polarization dependence of light shifts on atomic transitions, specifically the ${^1	ext{S}_0}\leftrightarrow{^3	ext{P}_1}$ intercombination line.

**Key observables.** Differential light shifts ($
u$), polarization rotation angle ($	heta$), cooling laser frequency offset ($f$), and atomic coherence during transport.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Magic-angle condition ($	heta_M$), mrad-level polarization noise stability, and the ability to program arbitrary polarization patterns across the array.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that the polarization-dependent light shift can be accurately mapped to the local birefringence tunability of the SLM.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup for local polarization control using the SLM, the tuning of the tensor light shift, the application of local polarization correction for efficient sideband cooling, and the programming of various polarization patterns for sequential operations.

**Paper structure.** The work progresses from establishing the fundamental technique of site-resolved polarization control to applying this control to homogenize light shifts for sideband cooling, demonstrating dynamic transport, and finally characterizing the stability of the polarization control system.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Optical tweezer arrays trapping ultracold atoms and molecules are a versatile quantum science platform with broad impact in quantum simulation, quantum computation, and quantum metrology. The polarization dependence of anisotropic vector and tensor light shifts offers a degree of freedom for precise quantum state engineering of trapped particles. Similarly, state-selective operations depend on the polarization of the addressing light through the atom--light coupling strength. Yet, methods for controlling the polarization of individual tweezers or local addressing beams remain an experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate independent, site-resolved linear polarization rotation across an optical tweezer array by exploiting the local birefringence tunability of a spatial light modulator. Applying this capability to an array of $^{88}\rm{Sr}$ atoms, we homogenize differential light shifts imparted by the 813-nm tweezers to the narrow ${^1{\rm S}_0}\leftrightarrow{^3{\rm P}_1}$ transition, enabling sideband cooling under a magic-angle condition. Furthermore, we show dynamic transport of trapped atoms across distinct polarization zones with high survival and preserved coherence. Finally, we characterize tweezer polarization noise and demonstrate closed-loop stabilization referenced to the atomic transition frequency, reaching mrad-level stability. Our work establishes a technique for manipulating polarization-sensitive atomic and molecular transitions in tweezer architectures, with immediate applications to optical tweezer clocks and multi-zone quantum processors.

</details>

**Summary.** This work models the decoherence of the early universe's background degrees of freedom due to thermal cosmological perturbations using open quantum systems theory. By deriving a master equation that includes cosmological backreaction, the authors find that decoherence can occur rapidly, potentially faster than the expansion rate. This offers a theoretical framework to use decoherence as a criterion for selecting semiclassical states in quantum cosmology.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, albeit toy, example of applying open quantum system techniques (master equations, backreaction) to a fundamental problem in cosmology—the quantum-to-classical transition.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how the thermal bath provided by cosmological perturbations can induce decoherence in the homogeneous degrees of freedom of the early universe.

**Main result.** The characteristic decoherence timescale can be found to be shorter than the Hubble timescale for representative parameters, suggesting rapid decoherence.

**Method.** It employs the open quantum systems formalism to derive a master equation, incorporating cosmological backreaction via an effective second-order coupling.

**Model / system.** The model is a toy system describing a spatially flat semiclassical inflationary universe with a clock field, where scalar perturbations act as the environment bath.

**Key observables.** The decoherence timescale ($	au_{	ext{decoherence}}$) and the induced pointer-state structure.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coupling constant derived from thermal correlation functions, the Hubble timescale ($H^{-1}$), and the effective temperature ($T$) of the perturbations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The environment (perturbations) is assumed to be in a thermal-like state, and the analysis explicitly avoids the Markov approximation in its full treatment.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the master equation by treating the perturbations as an environment, deriving the non-unitary decoherence term, and analyzing the resulting time evolution of the density matrix.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study, within a toy model, how a thermal bath of cosmological perturbations can decohere the homogeneous degrees of freedom of the universe, treating the perturbations as an environment in the framework of open quantum systems. In contrast to several earlier approaches, instead of tracing out the perturbations from a semiclassical ansatz for the total wave function, we incorporate their cosmological backreaction through an effective second-order coupling and derive a master equation. Our toy model consists of a spatially flat semiclassical inflationary universe with a clock field in the slow-roll regime, while scalar cosmological perturbations in an assumed thermal-like state constitute the environment. One of the features of the model is the absence of the Markov approximation. The resulting coupling constant is determined by thermal correlation functions of the quantized perturbation modes. Within this framework, we find that, for a representative set of parameter estimates, the characteristic decoherence timescale corresponding to the thermal contribution can be shorter than the Hubble timescale. In addition, we address the question of whether the pointer-state structure induced by the decoherence in such a framework could provide a criterion for the choice of semiclassical states in the early universe.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper connects two primary theoretical methods—Absorbing Boundary Conditions (ABCs) and Complex Absorbing Potentials (CAPs)—used to model quantum particle detection. The authors prove that ABCs can be derived as a limit of CAPs using a Dirichlet boundary condition, offering a more practical and rigorous mathematical framework for calculating detection probabilities in open quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial mathematical bridge between two standard, but distinct, theoretical tools (CAPs and ABCs) used to model open quantum systems and particle detection, offering a more physically grounded derivation for one approach.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the theoretical challenge of calculating the probability distribution of a quantum particle's detection time and location at a boundary or within a volume.

**Main result.** It rigorously demonstrates that Absorbing Boundary Conditions (ABCs) can be obtained as a limit of Complex Absorbing Potentials (CAPs) by using a Dirichlet boundary condition, which is argued to be more physically relevant than previously assumed Neumann conditions.

**Method.** The authors employ asymptotic analysis by taking the limit of a finite-thickness CAP layer ($L 	o 0$) and showing the convergence of the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and the resulting probability distributions to those derived from the ABC model.

**Model / system.** The system involves the time evolution of a quantum particle governed by the Schrödinger equation, comparing the CAP model (with a complex potential) to the ABC model (with a specific boundary condition at $x=0$).

**Key observables.** Detection time distribution ($P_{CAP}$ vs $P_{ABC}$), survival probability, eigenvalues, and eigenfunctions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The limit parameter $L 	o 0$, and the complex parameters $\alpha$ and $eta$ defining the potentials/boundary conditions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is performed for a single particle in 1D but is argued to generalize to higher dimensions and curved surfaces due to the local nature of the PDEs.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the physical context by comparing ABCs and CAPs. It then develops the mathematical machinery by analyzing the convergence of the Hamiltonian and its spectral properties in the limit $L 	o 0$, culminating in the proof of convergence for the detection probability.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In quantum mechanics, among the proposals for how to compute the probability distribution of detection time and place along a given spatial surface or in a given volume, two leading candidates involve absorbing boundary conditions (ABCs) and complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) for the Schrödinger equation. Here, we extend earlier results on how the two are related. It was previously shown that ABCs arise as a limiting case of CAPs, but for that a (reflecting) Neumann boundary condition was assumed at the end of the region with the CAP. Here, we obtain ABCs in a different limit using a Dirichlet boundary condition at the end of the CAP region, which seems more practically relevant and realizable.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a theoretical framework for generating highly entangled states in atomic ensembles coupled to an optical cavity. By moving beyond simplified two-level approximations and incorporating nematic tensor dynamics, the authors show a method to accelerate entanglement generation significantly. This advancement is crucial for developing faster and more robust quantum sensing and quantum information devices based on cold atoms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the engineering of quantum resources (entanglement) in complex atomic platforms, providing a concrete pathway to significantly enhance the speed of quantum information processing protocols in AMO physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to achieve fast generation of multi-body entanglement in atomic ensembles, overcoming the slow dynamics associated with traditional two-level system models.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that by utilizing the full ground-state hyperfine manifold and operating under specific detuning conditions, entanglement generation can be achieved over a hundred times faster than typical experiments.

**Method.** The analysis employs cavity Quantum Electrodynamics (cQED) theory, deriving effective Hamiltonians and master equations through sequential adiabatic elimination of the excited atomic states and the cavity mode.

**Model / system.** The system involves $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms coupled to an optical cavity. The model is described by an effective Hamiltonian involving collective spin and nematic tensor operators, derived from the full atomic and cavity interaction.

**Key observables.** Spin-nematic squeezing parameter ($\xi^2_x$), entanglement generation rate, and the comparison between spin-based and nematic-based squeezing.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Detuning ($\Delta$), cavity decay rate ($\kappa$), and the ratio of rates ($\Phi/\Lambda$) which dictates the speedup.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on adiabatic elimination approximations for the excited states and the cavity mode, and the analysis assumes the system is driven by off-resonant laser fields.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the physical setup involving $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms coupled to an optical cavity, detailing the relevant detunings.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the full system Hamiltonian, through adiabatic elimination to derive effective Hamiltonians for both spin and nematic dynamics, and finally compares the resulting squeezing generation rates and speed advantages.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Many-body entanglement in atomic ensembles offers the potential for enhanced sensing devices. Entanglement can be generated by interfacing atoms with a cavity. Traditional methods use effective two-level systems isolated from more complex atomic level structures. However, alternative strategies allow entanglement to be generated in atoms confined to a single hyperfine manifold. These strategies enable entanglement in ways fundamentally not available to two-level systems but feature extremely slow dynamics due to requiring strongly off-resonant laser fields. Here, I show that equivalent squeezing dynamics can be achieved much closer to resonance, offering entanglement generation over a hundred times faster than typical experiments. Furthermore, the Hamiltonian can be used to speed up the creation of maximally entangled states via adiabatic passage.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a framework using Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) to diagnose spatial non-Markovianity in physical systems. The authors demonstrate that even when systems flow to the same fixed point, perturbations can induce power-law CMI tails that are cutoff-suppressed. This provides a precise theoretical tool to distinguish between truly non-Markovian physics and artifacts of the lattice cutoff.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous connection between CMI decay rates and the underlying Markovian nature of the steady state is a powerful diagnostic tool for characterizing complex, non-equilibrium phases in statistical mechanics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how spatial non-Markovianity can be probed using Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) and distinguishes between different types of power-law decay in CMI.

**Main result.** It shows that irrelevant perturbations breaking detailed balance can generate cutoff-suppressed, algebraically decaying CMI, leading to an infinite Markov length at any finite lattice cutoff but vanishing in the continuum limit.

**Method.** The analysis employs the Renormalization Group (RG) framework, perturbative expansions in the perturbation strength ($\epsilon$), and scaling arguments for Gaussian distributions.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes critical Gibbs states of finite-range local classical Hamiltonians, using Langevin dynamics to model the time evolution. Specific examples include the Ising-symmetric critical point of Toom's cellular automata and the long-range Ising paramagnet.

**Key observables.** Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), Markov length ($\xi_M$), and the decay rate of CMI.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Lattice cutoff ($a$), perturbation strength ($\epsilon$), and relative length scales ($l, l_B, \xi_{	ext{cross}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the CMI is UV-finite in the continuum limit and relies on the perturbation being RG-irrelevant.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the geometry of CMI calculation in both annular (2D) and 1D settings.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining CMI to probing non-Markovianity, develops the RG framework for analyzing decay types, and applies these tools to specific models like the Ising paramagnet and Gaussian systems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Conditional mutual information (CMI) probes spatial non-Markovianity and plays a central role in a recently developed framework for defining mixed-state phases based on local reversibility. This framework sharply distinguishes exponentially decaying from algebraically decaying CMI, since the latter obstructs equivalence to a state with finite Markov length. Here we show that states that flow to the same renormalization-group (RG) fixed point can nevertheless exhibit qualitatively different CMI. Starting from a critical Gibbs state of a finite-range local classical Hamiltonian, whose CMI vanishes beyond the interaction range, we show that an RG-irrelevant perturbation that breaks detailed balance generically generates algebraically decaying CMI. Crucially, these power-law tails are cutoff-suppressed: although they lead to an infinite Markov length at every fixed lattice cutoff, they vanish as a positive power of the cutoff in the continuum limit. We construct solvable models that exhibit this phenomenon and predict that the Ising-symmetric critical point of Toom's cellular automata generically exhibits such behavior. We also find analogous cutoff-suppressed CMI in the high-temperature paramagnetic phase of the long-range Ising paramagnet, in contrast with the genuine power-law CMI at the finite-temperature critical point in this same model that survives the continuum limit. We also derive a general result that in one spatial dimension, CMI decays faster than the inverse square of the buffer length if and only if the long-distance physics is Markovian.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a response matrix technique to diagnose environmental memory in open quantum systems without requiring full system-environment tomography. By analyzing the spectrum of this matrix, researchers can quantify how past system history influences future measurements across a temporal cut. This offers a practical diagnostic tool for characterizing correlated noise in quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, operational tool for diagnosing correlated noise and memory effects in open quantum systems, which is crucial for understanding decoherence in quantum computation and simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing environmental memory in open quantum systems, where past interactions affect future measurements even after system resets.

**Main result.** A novel response matrix approach allows for the diagnosis of environmental memory structure by analyzing its spectrum, circumventing the need for full process tomography.

**Method.** The authors introduce a response matrix constructed from controlled interventions and system observations across a causal break, whose spectrum characterizes temporal memory structure.

**Model / system.** The framework is applied theoretically to general quantum stochastic processes and benchmarked on interacting spin systems and two-qubit platforms.

**Key observables.** Response matrix, singular spectrum, response entropy, and quantum-memory witnesses.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The degree of environmental correlation (memory strength $\epsilon$), probe budget ($m$), and environment size.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The diagnostics are probe-dependent, meaning the detected memory is only characterized for the specific set of measurements performed.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the construction of the response matrix across a causal break and show how the response entropy varies with probe budget and environment size.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from the general theory of quantum stochastic processes to the construction of the response matrix, followed by spectral diagnostics and concrete demonstrations on Ising and two-qubit models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum systems are rarely isolated from their surroundings. These hidden environments can retain information and return it later, producing correlated errors in quantum computers and complicating the interpretation of experiments.On a quantum processor, for example, one job can therefore leave an environmental trace that affects the next, even after the qubits themselves have been reset. Learning how this hidden influence persists and affects later behavior is therefore important, but the environment is often impossible to measure directly, and fully reconstructing its effects through tomography rapidly becomes impractical. Here, we introduce a response matrix that uses controlled interventions and observations of the system alone to reveal the temporal structure of environmental memory. The matrix records how future observations change across different controlled histories. Its spectrum characterizes how memory is structured and how it persists under specified system resets, while suitable linear combinations of its entries can rule out specified classical models of that memory. Because its history-future queries can be evaluated independently, numerical response matrices can be assembled in parallel. We establish the framework theoretically, characterize response spectra in an interacting spin process, and certify quantum memory in a two-qubit benchmark. This approach turns system observations into a probe of inaccessible environments and could support the diagnosis of correlated noise, tests of open system models, and memory-aware control design.

</details>

**Summary.** This research tackles the challenge of noise in OAM-encoded quantum communication by modeling turbulence-induced degradation as structured leakage. The authors propose and validate a novel distributed quantum feature-extraction technique that uses quantum convolutional operations to extract robust signatures of this structured leakage, linking channel dynamics directly to quantum machine learning principles.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges quantum optics (OAM modes, turbulence) with quantum information processing (feature extraction, robust encoding), providing a physics-informed method to characterize decoherence in high-dimensional photonic quantum channels.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the vulnerability of Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM)-encoded qubits to environmental noise, specifically atmospheric turbulence, and seeks to characterize the structured information loss beyond the ideal quantum subspace.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that turbulence causes structured leakage, which can be robustly extracted using a novel distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme employing quantum convolutional operations.

**Method.** The methodology combines theoretical modeling of OAM propagation through noisy channels with experimental validation using controlled turbulence and quantum convolutional processing.

**Model / system.** The system uses OAM modes for high-dimensional quantum communication, modeled as logical qubits propagating through channels characterized by turbulence (Kolmogorov phase screens). The analysis employs a logical-qubit representation and quantum convolutional operations (QConv) for feature extraction.

**Key observables.** Structured leakage magnitude, Quantum-State Fidelity, Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), and the evolution of the scattering matrix.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Turbulence strength (quantified by Strehl Ratio, SR), OAM order ($\ell$), and the size of the simulated OAM basis ($\ell_{	ext{max}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the structured leakage signatures are physically meaningful and can be captured by mapping intensity distributions into quantum feature spaces, requiring the use of an erasure operator to maintain trace-preservation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the overall pipeline (simulation/experiment/QConv), the evolution of the scattering matrix showing leakage trends with turbulence, and comparisons between reconstructed states under various noise models.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes a framework by modeling OAM propagation through noisy channels, quantifying structured leakage via the scattering matrix, and then developing a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme using QConv to robustly extract these leakage-related signatures.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes have emerged as an important platform for high-dimensional quantum communication but remain vulnerable to environmental noise and channel imperfections. Here we introduce a logical-qubit representation of OAM propagation in which modes evolve as qubits through noisy quantum channels. In this representation, turbulence manifests as leakage from the logical OAM subspace into turbulence-induced leakage components, providing a unified description of degradation in both single-photon and coherent-beam regimes. We show that turbulence-induced leakage exhibits systematic dependence on turbulence strength and OAM order, revealing structured signatures of information redistribution beyond the logical subspace. Leveraging this insight, we develop a distributed quantum feature-extraction scheme that encodes high-dimensional OAM states into quantum representations and employs quantum convolutional operations to extract turbulence-robust features. Simulations and experimental measurements demonstrate robust extraction of these features across a broad range of turbulence strengths, OAM orders, and propagation conditions. Our results establish a direct link between OAM-channel dynamics, structured leakage, and quantum learning, providing a physics-informed framework for characterizing turbulence-degraded high-dimensional optical states and extracting robust signatures of turbulence-induced information redistribution.

</details>
