**Summary.** This paper presents a novel 'photo-assisted two-electron tomography' protocol to measure two-electron coherences in quantum circuits using only standard current measurements. By applying this technique to quantum Hall edge channels, the authors demonstrate a direct method to detect and quantify interaction-induced electronic entanglement. This opens a powerful new experimental avenue for studying quantum correlations in mesoscopic condensed matter systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges advanced quantum optics measurement techniques (tomography, coherence reconstruction) directly into the study of strongly correlated electron systems in solid-state platforms, providing a concrete pathway to measure entanglement beyond simple charge measurements.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is experimentally accessing and characterizing the two-electron coherences necessary to witness electronic entanglement in quantum circuits.

**Main result.** The authors introduce a photo-assisted tomography protocol that successfully reconstructs the two-electron Wigner distribution, revealing interaction-induced energy entanglement in quantum Hall edge channels.

**Method.** The method uses routine transport measurements (dc-currents and current correlations) combined with an RF driving tone to encode off-diagonal two-electron coherences into measurable current responses.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on electrons propagating in ballistic quantum conductors, specifically applying the protocol to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels.

**Key observables.** Two-electron coherences ($G^{(2e)}_{AB}$), the two-electron Wigner distribution, and the violation of an entanglement witness based on Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coulomb interactions, thermal background, and the ability to resolve Wigner function negativities.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The protocol assumes that the required measurements (average currents and current correlations) are routinely measurable in existing electronic interferometry setups.

**Figures summary.** Not specified, but the notes indicate the reconstruction of the two-electron Wigner distribution and the violation of the entanglement witness.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the concept of two-electron coherences and the entanglement witness, details the photo-assisted tomography protocol, applies it to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels, and finally extends the approach to intra-channel coherences.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Witnessing entanglement between electrons propagating in quantum circuits requires accessing their two-electron coherences, which encode the two-particle quantum correlations generated by Coulomb interactions. Yet, experimental reconstruction of two-electron coherence remains a major challenge. We introduce photo-assisted two-electron tomography, a quantum coherence reconstruction protocol from dc-currents and time-averaged current correlations, routinely measured in electron quantum optics experiments. Driving an energy filter with a small rf tone encodes off-diagonal coherences in the frequency domain into the dc-current response, enabling single-electron tomography without resorting to current-noise measurements. Extending it to two channels, current correlations after two photo-assisted filters reconstruct the two-electron Wigner distribution and isolate its irreducible two-body part. When applied to Coulomb-coupled quantum Hall edge channels, the protocol reveals interaction-induced energy entanglement. Signatures of this entanglement are visible through the violation of an entanglement witness based on Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities, as well as Wigner function negativities, which remain resolved above the thermal background for realistic device parameters. A generalized Franson geometry further extends the approach to intra-channel two-electron coherences. This opens a direct pathway to detect and characterize electronic entanglement in ballistic quantum circuits.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using superconducting quantum circuits to simulate quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds, overcoming experimental limitations. By mapping hyperbolic geometry onto the circuit's controllable Hamiltonian parameters, the authors develop an ensemble simulation technique. This allows for the robust extraction of global topological invariants, such as the Chern number, by probing the system's response to geometric quantum driving.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges abstract mathematical geometry (hyperbolic manifolds) with a physical, controllable quantum hardware platform (superconducting qubits), providing a novel avenue for quantum simulation beyond standard lattice models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge of experimentally investigating exotic quantum phenomena associated with hyperbolic geometry due to the Euclidean constraints of natural materials.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated a method to probe hyperbolic quantum dynamics by simulating the system's evolution within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit.

**Method.** They employ an ensemble simulation technique, leveraging the theoretical foundation of ergodicity, to calculate the topological response function, which converges to the first Chern number.

**Model / system.** The system is a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) whose hyperbolic properties are mapped onto the dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters of a superconducting quantum circuit. The dynamics are governed by the geometry of the Bolza surface.

**Key observables.** Topological Response Function ($\omega(T)$), First Chern Number ($C_1$), and quantum state trajectories tracked via quantum state tomography.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Driving velocity ($\lambda$), particle number ($N$), and the topological parameter $\epsilon$ which controls the phase transition.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on the assumption of ergodicity on hyperbolic manifolds to justify the use of ensemble averages over single-trajectory analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the ensemble evolution on the hyperbolic parameter space and the superconducting chip mapping. Other figures show quantum state tomography, the convergence of the topological response for varying velocities, and the dependence of $C_1$ on a tuning parameter $\epsilon$.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of hyperbolic geometry simulation, details the construction of the HDQS on superconducting circuits, develops the ensemble simulation method to extract topological invariants, and presents results showing convergence and phase transitions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hyperbolic geometry hosts a plethora of exotic quantum phenomena ranging from holographic duality to novel topological phases. However, investigating these effects experimentally remains challenging due to the Euclidean constraints of natural crystalline materials. While recent synthetic lattices have achieved static realizations, they often lack the dynamical tunability required to explore the full geometric landscape. Here, we overcome these limitations by implementing a quantum simulation of hyperbolic geometry within the parameter space of a superconducting quantum circuit. We construct a Hyperbolically Driven Quantum System (HDQS) by mapping the hyperbolic properties onto the dynamically controllable Hamiltonian parameters. By probing the systems' response under geometric quantum driving, we elucidate how the intrinsic geometry of the parameter space dictates observable physical quantities. Furthermore, we extend the theoretical framework to realize ensemble simulation. This generalization enables us to harness the fast coherent control of superconducting qubits to capture essential geometric characteristics, establishing a versatile platform for exploring quantum dynamics on hyperbolic manifolds.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops an ecological theory to model the risk posed by growing populations of misaligned AI agents. It introduces the concept of a 'critical population threshold' ($N_{crit}$), showing that collaboration can cause a population to take off uncontrollably once this threshold is crossed. The authors advocate for 'ecological red teaming' to estimate this critical size before deployment.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on AI safety, the mathematical structure—modeling collective emergence, critical thresholds, and non-linear growth dynamics—shares conceptual parallels with phase transitions or collective behavior studied in complex many-body systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the ecological safety of AI agent populations, specifically determining the conditions under which a population of misaligned agents undergoes an uncontrolled, self-reinforcing 'takeoff' cycle.

**Main result.** Collaboration introduces a critical population threshold ($N_{crit}$), analogous to the strong Allee effect, below which the population declines and above which it takes off, regardless of individual agent capability.

**Method.** The authors develop an ecological theory using a population growth equation, $	au dN/dt = N[\kappa p(N) - \mu]$, adapting concepts from population dynamics to AI cyber-attack capabilities.

**Model / system.** The system models AI agent populations engaged in cyberattacks. The core mechanism is the collective success probability $p(N)$, which is shown to increase with population size $N$ when collaboration is present.

**Key observables.** Population Threshold ($N_{crit}$), population growth rate, and the scaling of collective cybersecurity capability $p(N)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The loss fraction ($\mu$), the addition rate ($\kappa$), and the collaboration gain parameter ($eta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The theory is a 'toy theory' providing a conceptual framework; it assumes constant loss fractions and models capability scaling via specific functional forms (e.g., power laws).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the difference between growth dynamics with and without collaboration, highlighting the emergence of $N_{crit}$ with collaboration, and show how varying the functional form of effective work $C(N)$ shifts this threshold.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the basic population growth model, demonstrating the difference between independent and collaborative scaling, and then analyzing how the functional form of collective capability $C(N)$ (e.g., power law, saturation) dictates the existence and value of $N_{crit}$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. Because red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety in larger populations, our theory calls for ecological red teaming and population pacing: gradually deploying larger agent populations in controlled environments, while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size, and estimating the critical population size for takeoff. Capability gains may lower this threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work examines magnon transport in a chiral soliton lattice, showing that the dynamics are fundamentally governed by the symplectic quantum metric. Using semiclassical methods, the authors derive equations showing that this metric introduces a geometric force that dictates the wave packet's periodic, bounded motion. This establishes the quantum metric as a key determinant of transport properties in bosonic quantum magnets.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit appearance of the symplectic quantum metric controlling the dynamics provides a powerful, geometric framework for understanding transport in bosonic quantum systems, which has parallels in effective Hamiltonians used in AMO and quantum optics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how quantum geometry, specifically quantified by the symplectic quantum metric, influences the dynamics of magnon wave packets in one-dimensional quantum spin chains.

**Main result.** The magnon wave packet dynamics are dominated by a geometric contribution from the symplectic quantum metric, leading to periodic, bounded motion in phase space.

**Method.** The authors employ semiclassical methods, deriving equations of motion for the wave packet center using the Dirac-Frenkel variational principle applied to the magnon Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The system is a quasi-one-dimensional chiral soliton lattice, modeled using spin-wave approximations and bosonic magnon excitations. The dynamics are analyzed by considering the influence of the symplectic structure on the magnon Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Symplectic quantum metric ($g_n(k)$), wave packet velocity, phase-space area, and the time evolution of the wave packet spread ($\Delta x^2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system is analyzed in the nearly flat band limit, where the geometric contribution dominates over the conventional group velocity.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that interband transitions due to Landau-Zener tunneling are suppressed, validating a single-band semiclassical description.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the soliton lattice structure, the localization of the lowest band via the sIPR, and the resulting bounded, periodic motion of the wave packet center in phase space, governed by the quantum metric.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian, deriving the semiclassical equations of motion using the quantum metric, and finally solving these equations to characterize the periodic, geometrically constrained dynamics of the wave packet.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the effects of quantum geometry on the motion of magnon wave packets in one-dimensional quantum spin chains. In contrast to fermionic systems, where transport phenomena driven by the quantum metric have been extensively studied, we show that the dynamics in bosonic magnon systems are strongly affected by the symplectic structure and the pseudo-unitarity of the transformation of the magnon Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian. A chiral soliton lattice provides a setting in which the symplectic quantum metric strongly influences the longitudinal magnon dynamics. We derive the semiclassical response of a magnon wave packet in such a system to a weak, slowly varying perturbation and demonstrate that the wave packet velocity acquires a geometric contribution proportional to the momentum derivative of the symplectic quantum metric, which dominates over the conventional group velocity for a nearly flat band. Solving the resulting equations of motion, we obtain a bounded trajectory in real time with a phase-space area determined by the symplectic quantum metric.

</details>

**Summary.** This review provides a comprehensive overview of using integrated photonic chips for universal quantum computing, comparing discrete-variable and continuous-variable approaches. It details how resource state generation and measurement-based techniques overcome the limitations of linear optics. The work highlights the path toward scalable, fault-tolerant quantum microprocessors by addressing key hardware and algorithmic challenges.

**Why it may be interesting.** This paper is highly relevant as it reviews the state-of-the-art hardware and theoretical pathways for building quantum processors using photonics, connecting quantum optics principles to large-scale computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central challenge is developing scalable, fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers capable of universal quantum computation.

**Main result.** Integrated photonics offer a viable platform by overcoming bulk-optics limitations, and the field advances through Measurement-Based Quantum Computation (MBQC) and Fusion-Based Quantum Computation (FBQC).

**Method.** The review surveys both discrete-variable (DV) and continuous-variable (CV) approaches, focusing on resource state generation and measurement-induced gate operations.

**Model / system.** The system is based on integrated photonic quantum chips, which integrate light sources (e.g., SPDC, Quantum Dots), linear optical circuits (MZIs, interferometers), and detectors (SPDs, Homodyne Detectors).

**Key observables.** Success probability of fusion measurements, percolation threshold ($p_{th}$), and the required resource overhead (number of ancillary photons/components).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Scalability (moving from table-top to integrated chips), and error tolerance thresholds for topological codes (e.g., 3D RHG lattice).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitations involve the probabilistic nature of entangling gates and the need to achieve full fault tolerance.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the high-level architecture of photonic quantum computation (Sources, Circuits, Detection). Figure 2 details the ballistic generation of DV cluster states and the FBQC architecture.

**Paper structure.** The paper provides a comprehensive review, first establishing the advantages of integrated photonics, then detailing the theoretical frameworks for DV and CV computation, and finally discussing the architectural components and remaining challenges for fault tolerance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Integrated photonic quantum chips have emerged as a promising platform for realizing fault-tolerant photonic quantum computers. Compared with bulk-optics systems, integrated photonics offer compact device footprints, enhanced programmability, and exceptional stability, attributes that are essential for executing large-scale and computationally demanding quantum tasks. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in both discrete-variable and continuous-variable universal photonic quantum computation. We survey progress in fault-tolerant architectures and state-of-the-art integrated platforms and highlight the key challenges that must be addressed to scale photonic systems toward full fault tolerance. Finally, we outline future opportunities and research directions aimed at bridging the gap between current proof-of-principle demonstrations and fully scalable quantum microprocessors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenge of ultrastrong magnon-magnon coupling in the antiferromagnet $	ext{CrPS}_4$ by developing a quantum model that extends beyond the standard approximations. The authors successfully link the microscopic coupling parameters to the macroscopic, measurable quantum phenomenon of magnon squeezing. This establishes a practical quantum framework for utilizing magnons in advanced spintronic and quantum information applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it provides a concrete, material-specific pathway to observe and exploit non-classical quantum states (squeezing) using magnons, bridging condensed matter magnetism with quantum optics principles.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to achieve and quantify ultrastrong magnon-magnon coupling (USC) in a magnetic insulator and link this coupling to the generation of measurable non-classical quantum states, specifically squeezed magnon vacuum states.

**Main result.** The authors successfully developed a quantum model beyond the Rotating-Wave Approximation to quantify three distinct coupling channels ($g_1, g_2, g_3$) and demonstrated a protocol to extract a substantial squeezing factor (up to $\sim 9.7 	ext{ dB}$) from thermal noise-driven dynamics.

**Method.** The study combines advanced quantum Hamiltonian modeling (going beyond RWA) with both micromagnetic simulations and analysis of experimental Antiferromagnetic Resonance (AFMR) spectroscopy data.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the van der Waals antiferromagnet $	ext{CrPS}_4$. The theoretical framework involves a quantum Hamiltonian decomposed into pure and coupling terms, which is analyzed in different coupling regimes (AM-OM and RM-LM).

**Key observables.** Squeezing factor ($	ext{dB}$), quadrature fluctuations ($\langle\Delta \hat{X}_{\varphi,\psi}^2angle$), coupling strengths ($g_1, g_2, g_3$), and magnon dispersion relations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Normalized coupling ratio $g/f_g \sim 0.41$, and the USC regime itself.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The necessity of moving beyond the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) is a key point, as the classical LL model is insufficient for the full quantum description.

**Figures summary.** Figures show experimental AFMR spectra ($	ext{dP/dH}$) compared to theoretical dispersions, illustrating mode hybridization and the field dependence of the extracted coupling strengths ($g_1, g_2, g_3$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the challenge (USC) to developing a comprehensive quantum model (Hamiltonian decomposition), linking this model to measurable quantum diagnostics (squeezing via quadrature operators), and finally validating the results using both simulation and experimental spectroscopy.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Achieving and quantifying ultrastrong magnon-magnon coupling (USC) remains a key challenge for quantum magnonics. Here, we demonstrate widely tunable USC between chiral (right- and left-handed) and acoustic or optical magnon modes in the van der Waals antiferromagnet $CrPS_4$. Using a full quantum model, we decompose the interaction into three microscopic interaction channels: the co-rotating term $g_1$ (mode hybridization), the counter-rotating term $g_2$ (two-mode squeezing), and, uniquely in the chiral regime, the self-squared term $g_3$ that mediates single-mode squeezing. The normalized coupling ratio reaches $g/f_g$ $\sim$ 0.41, entering the USC regime. Most significantly, we establish a complete protocol linking these USC parameters to a measurable quantum phenomenon: a squeezed magnon vacuum state. Our simulations not only visualize the chirality and polarization evolution of the hybrid modes but also demonstrate how to directly extract quadrature fluctuations and a substantial squeezing factor (up to $\sim$ 9.7 dB) from thermal noise-driven magnetization dynamics. This work provides a material-specific quantum framework for USC and a practical pathway to detect and exploit non-classical magnon states in low-damping two-dimensional magnets, opening a route toward quantum-enhanced spintronics and hybrid quantum information platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the relaxation dynamics in modular networks by treating the system as a combination of a base network and attached fibers. It establishes that the overall relaxation time is additive, and crucially demonstrates that the underlying small-world structure dictates the asymptotic spectral dimension, potentially misleading measurements on finite samples.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of spectral dimension and relaxation time in complex, structured networks is highly relevant to understanding energy or information transport in disordered quantum systems or complex quantum architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether the relaxation dynamics of a modular network are governed by the properties of the individual modules or by the connecting network structure.

**Main result.** The equilibration time is found to be the sum of the base relaxation time and the fiber trapping time, and the small-world core always imposes its own Fiedler dimension, biasing finite-size estimates.

**Method.** The analysis uses spectral graph theory, focusing on the Fiedler eigenvalue ($\lambda_g$) derived from the graph Laplacian, and employs scaling arguments to compare different network growth regimes.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a 'bundled network,' consisting of a base graph to which multiple copies of a 'fiber graph' are attached at every node.

**Key observables.** Fiedler eigenvalue ($\lambda_g$), equilibration time ($	au_{eq}$), spectral dimension ($d_s$), and effective Fiedler dimension ($d_{	ext{eff}}^g$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio $x = 	au_{trap}/	au_B$ dictates whether the gap is base-controlled or fiber-controlled; growth parameters like $	heta$ are crucial.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The series law for equilibration time ($	au_{eq} \simeq 	au_B + 	au_{trap}$) is assumed to be exact under certain spectral conditions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the series law for $	au_{eq}$ across various network combinations, and show how the effective dimension $d_{	ext{eff}}^g$ scales with the composition parameter $	heta$ for different base types.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing the physical model (modular networks), deriving the series law for relaxation times, analyzing the crossover between base- and fiber-controlled regimes, and finally providing asymptotic scaling laws for the Fiedler dimension in various growth classes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Is the relaxation of a modular network dictated by its modules or by the network that connects them? The answer fixes the time scales of diffusion, consensus, and synchronization, all set by the Fiedler eigenvalue. We show that, for bundled networks, the two levels act one after the other: a random walker must first escape from its module and then spread over the network that connects them. The equilibration time is the sum of these two times, the time needed to reach the base from inside a fiber and the relaxation time of the base, slowed down by the mass of the fibers. The consequences are unexpected. However large the modules are, a small-world core always imposes its own Fiedler dimension; the modules survive only as a logarithmic correction, which slows down equilibration and hides the true exponent up to sizes far beyond any real network. Effective dimensions measured on finite modular systems can therefore be systematically biased. We analytically work out all combinations of finite-dimensional and small-world bases and fibers, and compare them with numerically exact spectra of representatives of each category.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a novel, relativistic collapse model for quantum fields to solve the measurement problem, overcoming issues like vacuum instability. It introduces 'Dynamical Vacuum Subtraction' and applies the framework to a scalar field, deriving finite rates of particle and energy increase. The results offer quantitative evidence for the consistency of this speculative quantum gravity theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work tackles the foundational intersection of quantum gravity phenomenology and quantum foundations, providing concrete, calculable predictions for collapse dynamics in QFT.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of constructing a testable, relativistic spontaneous collapse model applicable to Quantum Field Theory (QFT) to resolve the quantum measurement problem.

**Main result.** The authors present a framework that achieves no-signaling and yields finite particle-number and energy-increase rates for a free massive scalar field in the long-time limit.

**Method.** The methodology involves modifying standard unitary evolution with a 'Dynamical Vacuum Subtraction' prescription and employing a history-dependent Aharonov-Albert prescription for nonlocal state updates.

**Model / system.** The model is a 'Flash-Based Relativistic Collapse Model' built upon the Collapse Points Quantum Mechanics (CPQM) framework, applied to quantum fields like the free massive scalar field.

**Key observables.** Correlation coefficients ($r_N, r_E$), leading-order flash intensity ($\mu^{(1)}_F$), and particle/energy increase rates ($\Gamma_F$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The collapse point density ($\mu_C$), the long-time limit, and the coupling constant ($\lambda$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes the Poisson sprinkling of collapse points is statistically Poincaré invariant, and it modifies the standard dynamics to ensure vacuum stability.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate state assignment on Cauchy surfaces, showing how collapse outcomes are incorporated into the state evolution across spacetime.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first outlining the challenges of relativistic collapse models, then introducing the modified Aharonov-Albert prescription and Dynamical Vacuum Subtraction, followed by detailed calculations of correlation functions and finally applying the framework to a free scalar field.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Spontaneous collapse models provide a possible, testable solution to the quantum measurement problem, but constructing a relativistic version applicable to quantum field theory remains an important open challenge. Challenges in constructing relativistic collapse models include avoiding superluminal signaling and foliation dependence, controlling energy production, and ensuring vacuum stability. Here, we present a relativistic collapse framework that addresses these problems at the cost of introducing a new space of physical states, whose complete characterization is left open. A modified, history-dependent Aharonov--Albert prescription describes instantaneous nonlocal state updates on arbitrary spacelike foliations while preserving foliation independence. To ensure vacuum stability, we modify the standard unitary evolution through a prescription that we name dynamical vacuum subtraction. The resulting dynamical map is linear and trace-preserving but not positive on the full set of standard density operators. We establish no-signaling by proving microscopic parameter independence, and identify conditions under which standard nonrelativistic collapse dynamics are recovered. Finally, we apply our framework to a free massive scalar field, obtaining finite particle-number and energy-increase rates at leading order in the long-time regime, together with further promising evidence for the consistency of the framework.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel, gauge-invariant clustering coefficient designed for bipartite networks with complex edge weights, applicable to quantum and photonic systems. It successfully separates the structural connectivity from the phase-dependent interference effects occurring around four-node cycles. This allows researchers to quantify how phase disorder degrades network coherence, providing a powerful diagnostic tool for quantum network design.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a quantitative tool to measure structural coherence in quantum networks by incorporating phase information directly into a standard graph metric, which is vital for understanding interference effects in quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the lack of a structural measure for bipartite networks that simultaneously accounts for complex edge weights and the bipartite topology, which is crucial for quantum and photonic architectures.

**Main result.** A gauge-invariant clustering coefficient is defined that factorizes into topological and phase contributions, allowing for the quantification of phase interference effects in these complex-weighted networks.

**Method.** The authors derive the coefficient based on the phase accumulated around the fundamental four-node cycle (square) and use expectation values and closed-form derivations for specific ensembles.

**Model / system.** The model is a complex-weighted bipartite network, relevant to quantum repeaters and photonic meshes, where edge weights are complex amplitudes leading to interference effects.

**Key observables.** Gauge-invariant clustering coefficient, phase flux ($\Phi_s$), coherent distance, and the phase contribution factor $(\sin \Delta/\Delta)^4$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Phase disorder magnitude ($\Delta$), network topology (e.g., Watts-Strogatz ensemble parameters).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes independent link phases for expectation value calculations, and the coefficient is shown to be gauge-invariant under node-wise phase redefinitions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the four-node square as the elementary unit of interference in various quantum/photonic architectures and show the standard deviation of the clustering coefficient versus phase disorder.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the mathematical framework by defining the gauge-invariant flux around a square, deriving the clustering coefficient based on this flux, and then calculating its expectation values and variance for specific random ensembles.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Structural measures such as the clustering coefficient and the average shortest-path length characterise how a network is organised. These measures are typically formulated for real, non-negative edge weights. A class of quantum and photonic architectures has complex edge weights instead, whose phases determine whether alternative routes interfere constructively or destructively. These architectures are also bipartite, so triangles are absent and the smallest closed cycle is a four-node square. Existing measures address complex weights and bipartite structure separately: bipartite clustering coefficients quantify clustering through four-node squares but do not contain phase information, while interferometric coefficients retain phase but are defined on triangles. In this work, we define a clustering coefficient for complex-weighted bipartite networks which reduces to the classical bipartite coefficient when the phases vanish, becomes negative when alternative routes cancel, and can be obtained for all nodes from a single sparse matrix product. We show that the phase accumulated around a square is the smallest gauge-invariant carrier of structural phase information in a bipartite network. The clustering coefficient factorises into a topological contribution and a phase contribution, making a bipartite Watts--Strogatz ensemble analytically tractable. For phases uniformly distributed on $[-Δ,Δ]$, the mean phase contribution is $(\sinΔ/Δ)^4$, independent of node, degree, and topology. We also derive closed-form expressions for the clustering coefficient, open-path visibility, and phase variance. We numerically verify these predictions and further show that phase disorder increases coherent distance.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces an iterative Bayesian VQE that estimates the ground state of a quantum Hamiltonian by modeling the state belief with a von Mises-Fisher distribution. It generalizes the measurement process to condition on multiple measurement outcomes ($m$) and rigorously proves that the estimate converges monotonically toward the true ground state while its uncertainty shrinks. This offers a theoretically grounded, measurement-based alternative to standard VQE techniques.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a theoretically rigorous and general framework for quantum state estimation that bypasses the need for explicit circuit ansatzes, potentially offering a more robust alternative to standard gradient-based VQE methods.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of finding the ground state and energy of a quantum many-body Hamiltonian using an iterative quantum algorithm.

**Main result.** It develops and proves the convergence of an iterative Bayesian Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) that models the state belief using a von Mises-Fisher distribution.

**Method.** The method involves sequentially updating the belief distribution by conditioning on multiple success outcomes ($m$) from Hadamard-test measurements on an ancilla qubit.

**Model / system.** The system is a general quantum many-body Hamiltonian $H$, and the state is parameterized as a real unit vector $\psi$ in the Hilbert space. The inference is performed using the von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distribution.

**Key observables.** Average fidelity, overlap ($R$), and concentration parameter ($\kappa$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of success outcomes $m$, the concentration parameter $\kappa_0$, and the measurement budget $N$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the large-concentration regime ($\kappa_0$ large) to derive a closed-form posterior update, and the convergence theorems require $m$ to be within a specific range relative to $\kappa_0$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the Hadamard test measurement scheme and show the monotonically increasing average fidelity of the algorithm on random and molecular Hamiltonians.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem and the Bayesian framework, then derives the closed-form update for the vMF posterior by generalizing moment matching for $m>1$. It mathematically proves two key convergence properties (non-decreasing overlap and concentration) and concludes with a measurement-based algorithm and numerical demonstrations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop an iterative Bayesian variational quantum eigensolver in which the unknown ground state, parametrised as a real unit vector, is inferred through a von Mises--Fisher distribution sequentially updated from   Hadamard-test measurements on a single ancilla qubit. Building on a companion paper that treated a single success outcome via exact moment matching, we generalise the scheme to condition on $m$ success outcomes for the likelihood function   per iteration. Since exact moment matching becomes impractical for $m>1$, we exploit the large-concentration regime, in which a first-order expansion of the log-likelihood yields a closed-form von Mises--Fisher   posterior with $m$ entering only through a multiplicative weight. We prove that the two convergence properties of the single-outcome scheme---non-decreasing overlap and non-decreasing concentration---are   preserved provided $m$ lies within an explicitly characterised range. Based on the theory, we propose a measurement-based algorithm and illustrate the convergence on randomly generated three- and four-qubit Hamiltonian matrices, on $\mathrm{HeH}^+$, and on $\mathrm{H}_2$.

</details>

**Summary.** This work studies fermionic excitations in a complex holographic model representing a two-current Gubser-Rocha background with axion relaxation. By analyzing three distinct non-minimal coupling channels, the authors demonstrate that the spectral function is highly sensitive to these couplings, leading to characteristic reconstructions like flat-bottom or Fermi-arc features. This clarifies how multiple physical mechanisms jointly govern the spectral properties of strongly correlated matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** The holographic approach provides a powerful, non-perturbative tool to study spectral properties in strongly correlated systems, linking bulk gravity dynamics to boundary quantum matter physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how fermionic spectral functions are reshaped by the interplay of current mixing, axion-induced momentum relaxation, and non-minimal couplings within a holographic two-current Gubser-Rocha background.

**Main result.** Different coupling channels ($p_1, p_2, p_3$) yield distinct spectral reconstructions: $p_1$ causes soft asymmetry, $p_2$ results in a flat-bottom reconstruction by suppressing the zero-energy peak, and $p_3$ generates open, Fermi-arc-like segments.

**Method.** The analysis uses holographic methods, solving radial equations for fermionic components coupled to the background fields, and calculating the retarded Green's function to obtain the spectral function $A(\omega, k)$.

**Model / system.** The model is a probe fermion propagating in a (3+1)D bulk dual to a (2+1)D boundary theory, utilizing the two-current Einstein-Maxwell-Gubser-Rocha background with linear axion momentum relaxation.

**Key observables.** Fermionic spectral function $A(\omega, k)$, spectral reconstruction patterns (flat-bottom, Fermi-arc-like segments).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Momentum-relaxation strength ($eta/\mu$), doping parameter ($\chi$), and coupling constants ($p_1, p_2, p_3$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the background admits a specific solution and focuses on the dual normal metal sector, omitting the superconducting sector.

**Figures summary.** Not specified, but the results describe spectral features varying based on the coupling channel and background parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the background solution in the two-current GR model. It then derives the bulk fermionic dynamics and solves the radial equations for different coupling channels ($p_1, p_2, p_3$) to determine the spectral function $A(\omega, k)$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate fermionic spectral functions in a two-current Gubser-Rocha background with linear-axion momentum relaxation. Serving as a comparison channel, the dipole coupling $p_1$ is found to produce a soft asymmetric reconstruction without opening a clean hard Mott gap. Our main analysis then focuses on two axion-dependent non-minimal couplings modulated by current mixing. The $p_2$ tensor channel suppresses the zero-energy Fermi peak and shifts the dominant spectral weight to finite frequencies, resulting in a flat-bottom reconstruction. In contrast, the $p_3$ vector channel creates a strong spectral asymmetry in momentum space, generating open, Fermi-arc-like segments. Varying the momentum-relaxation strength $β/μ$ and the doping parameter $χ$ reveals a channel-dependent response to the two-current background. Increasing $β/μ$ generally broadens the $p_2$ response, whereas the one-sided $p_3$ feature varies non-monotonically under changes of the background parameters. These results clarify how current mixing, axion-induced momentum relaxation, and non-minimal fermion couplings jointly reshape holographic fermionic excitations. **Summary.** This work analyzes the adiabatic passage time required for quantum annealing of the random transverse-field Ising model. Using the Strong-Disorder Renormalization Group, the authors derive scaling theories showing that error density decreases logarithmically with time. This provides crucial insights for designing optimal, noise-resistant quantum annealing protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between quantum annealing dynamics, disorder physics (IDFP), and the calculation of critical time scales is highly relevant for understanding noise and robustness in quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the minimum annealing time required to prevent defect formation during quantum annealing in the random transverse-field Ising model.

**Main result.** The error density is shown to decrease logarithmically with annealing time, characterized by dimension-dependent critical exponents of the infinite-disorder fixed point.

**Method.** The study employs the Strong-Disorder Renormalization Group (SDRG) technique combined with an analysis based on the adiabatic theorem.

**Model / system.** The system is the random transverse-field Ising model (RTFIM) on $d$-dimensional lattices. The Hamiltonian is time-dependent, and the annealing process is analyzed via the adiabatic condition.

**Key observables.** Error density, Crossover Annealing Time ($	au_c$), and the gap ($\epsilon(s)$) between the ground and first excited state.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimension ($d=1, 2, 3$), annealing time ($	au$), and the critical exponents associated with the infinite-disorder fixed point.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the adiabatic theorem and uses the SDRG to model the process as a gradual aggregation of strongly coupled clusters.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the annealing-time threshold $Q(s)$ for the 1D RTFIM, showing the critical time $	au_c$.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory using SDRG to model defect formation, derives scaling theories for error statistics in general dimensions, and validates the approach using exact diagonalization (free-fermion technique) in 1D.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum annealing must be sufficiently slow to prevent defect formation. We study this problem in the random transverse-field Ising model via the adiabatic theorem to obtain the limiting rate at which defect formation can be avoided. Our approach based on the strong-disorder renormalization group (SDRG) technique views the annealing process as a gradual aggregation of strongly coupled clusters, giving access to the elementary events of error formation. We present a scaling theory of the statistics of these events in general dimensions and confront it to an extensive numerical analysis carried out in one, two, and three dimensions by an efficient implementation of the SDRG method. This approach is also validated by exact diagonalization in one dimension by means of the free-fermion technique. Our results consistently show a logarithmically slow decrease of the error density with the annealing time, characterized by the dimension-dependent critical exponents of the corresponding infinite-disorder fixed point of the model. Furthermore, we provide a map of individual events of potential defect formation in the excitation energy - control parameter plane, which may help in the design of optimal annealing paths.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work investigates the complex pseudogap phase in the Hubbard model, arguing that Fermi liquid theory fails in this regime. Using advanced many-body techniques, the authors distinguish between true and false Fermi surfaces, showing that the pseudogap physics is fundamentally driven by critical thermal spin fluctuations rather than simple band structure effects.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed analysis of spectral function crossovers and the failure of standard quasiparticle assumptions in the pseudogap state provides a rigorous theoretical framework relevant to understanding strongly correlated quantum materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to clarify the physics of the pseudogap regime in the Hubbard model, specifically distinguishing between true and false Fermi surfaces and zero-energy quasiparticle lines.

**Main result.** The standard Fermi liquid description breaks down in the pseudogap regime, and the emergence of false Fermi surfaces is linked to critical thermal spin fluctuations, which are better captured by real-frequency spectral analysis.

**Method.** The study employs the improved Two-Particle Self-Consistent Approach (TPSC+) to simultaneously analyze Energy Distribution Curves (EDC) and Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC), comparing results against Diagrammatic Quantum Monte Carlo (DiagMC) data.

**Model / system.** The system analyzed is the nearest-neighbor Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice, described by a Hamiltonian involving hopping and on-site Coulomb repulsion.

**Key observables.** Energy Distribution Curves (EDC), Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC), spectral function A(k, omega) at zero real frequency A(k, 0), and the quasiparticle condition $\partial\Sigma'(k, \omega)/\partial\omega|_{\omega=0}<0$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping ($\delta$), Temperature ($T$), and Interaction Strength ($U$). The analysis focuses on the pseudogap regime driven by spin fluctuations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The TPSC+ approach is used, which is an improvement over standard TPSC, and the analysis relies on the distinction between real-frequency and Matsubara-frequency spectral representations.

**Figures summary.** The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but they detail the analysis of EDC and MDC across different doping and temperature regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops its argument by first establishing the breakdown of Fermi liquid theory, then analyzing the spectral signatures (false vs. true FS) arising from commensurate and incommensurate spin fluctuations, and finally benchmarking the TPSC+ method against DiagMC results.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Exact diagrammatic quantum Monte Carlo (DiagMC) results for the nearest-neighbor Hubbard model motivate a closer study of the pseudogap. Using the improved two-particle self-consistent approach (TPSC+), we analyze Energy (EDC) and Momentum Distribution Curves (MDC) simultaneously. We show that Fermi-liquid terminology breaks down in the pseudogap regime, requiring a distinction between true and false Fermi surfaces and zero-energy quasiparticle (ZEQ) lines. A false Fermi surface has a momentum-space spectral maximum but a frequency-space depression at zero energy, while a false ZEQ line violates the standard quasiparticle condition $\partial Σ'(\mathbf{k},ω)/\partial ω|_{ω=0}<0$.The pseudogap is driven by critical thermal spin fluctuations, which occur in two dimensions because of the Mermin-Wagner theorem. Commensurate fluctuations first open an antinodal pseudogap, leaving true Fermi arcs. With decreasing temperature, the Fermi surface evolves into hole- and electron-like false Fermi surfaces. Incommensurate fluctuations generate hot spots near the diagonal, where the pseudogap persists to the quantum critical point (QCP), whereas at $\mathbf{k}_{AN}$ it disappears before the QCP doping. There, the spectrum has two precursor antiferromagnetic (AFM) bands, both in the unoccupied ($ω>0$) region. We benchmark TPSC+ against DiagMC results for the Matsubara spectral proxy $-\mathrm{Im}[\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{k},iπT)]/π$. TPSC+ underestimates pseudogap suppression in the strong-interaction regime, reproducing DiagMC behavior at lower temperatures or doping. This proxy is equivalent to the spectral function with thermal broadening $η=πT$, which obscures features when $πT$ is not the smallest energy scale. Using $A(\mathbf{k},0)$, we find that hole-like Fermi surfaces emerge at any interaction strength at low temperature, even at weak coupling.

</details>

**Summary.** This work characterizes the 'strange-metal' state in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ by showing linear temperature dependence of resistivity and $\omega^{-0.7}$ optical response. The authors argue that this anomalous behavior, marked by Planckian dissipation, arises specifically due to large-scale spatial modulations within the anion layers, distinguishing it from standard Fermi liquid behavior.

**Why it may be interesting.** The direct link established between structural disorder (incommensurate anion layers) and the emergence of Planckian dissipation scaling in transport properties is highly relevant to understanding non-Fermi liquid physics in correlated materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the origin of 'strange-metal' behavior in molecular conductors, characterized by charge transport that violates conventional metal power laws.

**Main result.** The strange metal behavior in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ is linked to the presence of incommensurate anion layers and large-scale spatial modulations, leading to Planckian dissipation scaling.

**Method.** The study combines temperature-dependent transport measurements ($ho(T)$) with broad-range optical investigations using frequency-dependent complex conductivity ($\hat{\sigma}(\omega)$).

**Model / system.** The physical system is $\kappa$-BEDT-TTF salts, comparing $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4	ext{Hg}_{3-\delta}	ext{X}_8$ (strange metal candidate) against $\kappa$-CuBr and $\kappa$-CuNCS (Fermi liquid reference).

**Key observables.** Resistivity ($ho(T) \propto T$ vs $T^2$), frequency-dependent conductivity ($|\hat{\sigma}(\omega)| \propto \omega^{-0.7}$ vs $\omega^{-1}$), and the frequency dependence of the scattering rate ($\Gamma(\omega) \propto \omega$ vs $\omega^2$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), frequency ($\omega$), and the ratio $\hbar\Gamma/k_B T \approx 1.2$ (Planckian dissipation).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on comparing the observed spectral weight transfer and scattering rate scaling against established theoretical expectations for Fermi liquids.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare $ho(T)$ and $\Gamma(\omega)$ for strange metals vs. Fermi liquids, showing the characteristic linear ($\omega$) vs. quadratic ($\omega^2$) scaling of the scattering rate.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the electronic signatures of strange metals ($\kappa$-Hg$_3-\delta$X$_8$) against conventional Fermi liquids ($\kappa$-CuBr, $\kappa$-CuNCS) using transport and optical measurements to pinpoint the role of structural modulation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The $κ$-BEDT-TTF salts are prototypical Mott systems, realizing a correlation-driven electronic transition from a Fermi-liquid state to a Mott insulator. The metallic compounds with spatially modulated Hg-containing anions, $κ$-(BEDT-TTF)$_4$Hg$_{3-δ}X_8$ ($X$ = Br, and Cl), however, fall outside this classification. Our temperature-dependent transport and broad-range optical investigations reveal a $ρ(T)\propto T$ dependence of the resistivity up to elevated temperatures and a power-law behavior of the frequency-dependent conductivity $\vert\hatσ (ω)\vert \propto ω^{-0.7}$; well-known hallmarks of ``strange metals''. The linear-in-frequency scattering rate of these strange metals scales to the Planckian dissipation. We demonstrate that this response only occurs in systems with incommensurate anion layers and establish a direct link to large-scale spatial modulations. Our conclusions can be extended to other strongly correlated strange-metal compounds

</details>

**Summary.** This paper addresses the critical need for reliable uncertainty quantification when estimating quantum state fidelity on noisy quantum hardware. The authors propose a novel, distribution-free framework combining Bayesian insights with conformal prediction to generate guaranteed prediction intervals. This methodology offers a scalable and statistically rigorous tool for validating modern quantum systems against hardware imperfections.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a statistically robust, model-agnostic tool for characterizing the performance of quantum processors, which is critical for experimental quantum information science.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is providing rigorous, reliable uncertainty quantification for estimating quantum state fidelity, which is essential for benchmarking quantum hardware.

**Main result.** The proposed hybrid Bayesian-informed conformal prediction framework maintains statistical validity and coverage guarantees where traditional methods fail, especially under noise or finite samples.

**Method.** The authors introduce a hybrid framework combining Bayesian concepts with conformal prediction to generate distribution-free prediction intervals for the fidelity estimate.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on estimating the fidelity $F(ho, \sigma)$ between a physical quantum state $ho$ and a known reference state $\sigma$, using measurement statistics from POVM measurements on quantum hardware.

**Key observables.** Quantum fidelity ($\hat{F}$), rigorous prediction intervals, and empirical coverage rates.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Qubit number ($q=2, 4, 6$), shot count ($N$), and noise parameters (e.g., depolarizing noise strength $\eta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework requires an initial point estimator (classical or neural network) and uses conformal prediction to provide coverage guarantees, though care must be taken when approximating confidence intervals related to Born's rule.

**Figures summary.** Figures demonstrate that the proposed conformalized estimators maintain nominal target coverage across various qubit numbers and noise regimes, outperforming standard methods that suffer from coverage failure.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the necessity of UQ for fidelity estimation, critiques existing methods (Bayesian, bootstrap), and then introduces and rigorously tests the hybrid conformal prediction framework across various noise and system sizes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum fidelity estimation is a fundamental task in quantum information and computing to benchmark the quality of quantum states, and hence of quantum processes, on noisy quantum hardware. Point estimates of fidelity by existing methods generally lack the rigorous uncertainty quantification required for reliable preparation and verification of these tasks. While Bayesian and bootstrap frameworks are widely used for uncertainty quantification, they are sensitive to model misspecification or lack formal coverage guarantees in non-asymptotic regimes. This paper introduces a hybrid "Bayesian-informed" conformal prediction-based framework to provide distribution-free, rigorous prediction intervals for quantum state fidelity estimation which can be used, with care, to approximate confidence intervals with respect to the quantum randomness of Born's rule. The framework requires a point estimator, and we consider both classical point estimators as well as data-driven neural net estimators. We evaluate the robustness of the methodology across a diverse range of experimental challenges, including finite-sample noise, tomographic incompleteness, physical model error, and out-of-distribution data. Our results demonstrate that conformalized estimators maintain statistical validity where traditional methods fail, offering a scalable and reliable approach for the verification of modern quantum systems. The best performing variant of our methodology is based on a class-conditional conformal prediction, as this most closely approximates the conditional coverage desired for a true confidence interval.

</details>

**Summary.** This work tackles the difficulty of applying quantum optimization algorithms to massive, real-world constrained problems like power grid analysis. It proposes a scalable pipeline that uses spectral graph partitioning to break the problem into smaller, hardware-manageable chunks. By combining quantum sampling with classical repair techniques, the authors demonstrate a viable path for running thousand-variable optimization on current superconducting quantum processors.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the core problem is graph optimization, the methodology heavily relies on mapping complex constraints onto quantum circuits, simulating entanglement via MPS, and managing hardware resource constraints (qubit count, depth), making it highly relevant to quantum computing architecture and algorithm development.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of scaling quantum optimization methods, specifically for the Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition (MBD), to large-scale, thousand-variable constrained problems.

**Main result.** The combination of spectral graph partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on large-scale optimization problems using current quantum hardware.

**Method.** The approach combines the Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) framework with single-layer QAOA sampling, distributing the problem via spectral partitioning across multiple quantum processing units (QPUs).

**Model / system.** The problem is modeled as decomposing a doubly substochastic matrix into a sparse weighted sum of matchings, formulated as a QUBO Hamiltonian on a graph like the 1,354-node PEGASE bus test case.

**Key observables.** Residual decomposition error ($\lVert D - D^* Vert_F^2$), hardware execution time, and mirror fidelity ($\hat{F}_{	ext{mirror}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Partition size ($p_s$), QAOA parameters ($\gamma_0, eta_0$), and the number of qubits (up to 1,710 variables).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes that retaining a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition is necessary for convergence, and it relies on classical feasibility repair to enforce global constraints.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the workflow involving partitioning residual graphs into QAOA subproblems, dispatching them across multiple QPUs using spatial circuit packing, and the comparison of convergence curves against classical baselines.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the formulation of MBD, introduces the E-FCFW framework augmented by QAOA sampling, describes the scaling solution using spectral partitioning and spatial packing, and validates the entire pipeline on large benchmark graphs.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Minimum Birkhoff Decomposition (MBD) seeks a sparse weighted sum of matchings and is a challenging optimization problem with applications in network scheduling and energy trading. We scale a quantum-assisted decomposition method by combining single-layer QAOA sampling with Extended Fully-Corrective Frank-Wolfe (E-FCFW) optimization, spectral graph partitioning, and greedy feasibility repair. We demonstrate the pipeline on the 1,354-node PEGASE bus test case (representing a 1,354-bus transmission grid with 1,710 transmission lines), whose 1,710 edges define a native 1,710-variable matching optimization problem requiring 1,710 qubits in the unpartitioned encoding. Partitioning enables distributed execution on IBM superconducting quantum processors. The best reported hardware result uses a 50-qubit partition bound, while reducing partitions to 20 qubits degrades convergence in the partition-size comparison. Larger partitions are more demanding for matrix product state (MPS) simulation, and bond-dimension tests show that truncating quantum correlations reduces candidate quality. The results therefore motivate retaining a substantive quantum sampling task within each partition as the overall problem scales. On the PEGASE-1354 benchmark, repaired QAOA samples achieve lower residual decomposition error than both simulated annealing and uniform random sampling baselines, while spatial circuit packing reduces hardware execution time by approximately a factor of three. These results demonstrate that combining spectral partitioning, spatial circuit packing, and classical feasibility repair provides an executable path for deploying gate-based quantum sampling on thousand-variable constrained optimization problems on current hardware.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper derives universal, exact relations for the Drude weights characterizing charge, spin, and energy transport in the 1D repulsive Fermi gas (Yang-Gaudin model). Using advanced techniques like generalized hydrodynamics, the authors confirm that charge transport is purely ballistic and relate these weights directly to fundamental thermodynamic quantities. This provides a crucial theoretical benchmark for experiments with ultracold atoms.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical foundation for understanding transport in integrable quantum gases, directly relevant to ultracold atom experiments where such systems are realized.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To rigorously establish universal relations between Drude weights governing charge, spin, and energy transport and thermodynamic properties in the 1D repulsive two-component continuum Fermi gas.

**Main result.** The charge Drude weights are shown to equal the particle density, magnetization, and entropy density, confirming ballistic transport. Furthermore, the spin Drude weights map out the zero-temperature phase boundary across the mu-H plane.

**Method.** The work builds upon the Bethe ansatz and generalized hydrodynamics (GHD), utilizing rapidity-space formulations and integral equations to derive transport coefficients.

**Model / system.** The system is the one-dimensional (1D) repulsive two-component continuum Fermi gas, modeled by the integrable Yang-Gaudin model, which is a paradigmatic system for studying interacting quantum gases.

**Key observables.** Drude Weights ($D_{nn}, D_{mm}, D_{ne}, D_{me}$), particle density ($n$), magnetization ($m_z$), and entropy density ($s$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and magnetic field ($H$). The analysis explores zero and low-temperature limits.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the system being described by the Yang-Gaudin model and utilizes advanced theoretical frameworks like GHD and TBA equations.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare calculated Drude weights from different theoretical protocols (integral form, tilted potential, partitioning) against each other and against numerical results, confirming consistency.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives the transport coefficients by relating them to derivatives of thermodynamic potentials in the grand canonical ensemble, confirming the ballistic nature of charge and spin transport while treating energy transport separately.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Building on the Bethe ansatz and generalized hydrodynamics, we rigorously establish universal relations between Drude weights governing charge, spin, and energy transport and thermodynamic properties for the one-dimensional repulsive two-component continuum Fermi gas - the paradigmatic integrable Yang-Gaudin model. We analytically derive thermodynamic expressions for charge Drude weights: $D_{nn}$, $D_{nm}$, $D_{ne}$ (responses of particle, magnetization and energy currents to a chemical potential gradient) equal the particle density, magnetization, and temperature times entropy density, respectively. These relations constitute a hallmark of ballistic transport, and can be generalized to other 1D continuum integrable systems. Furthermore, we investigate spin Drude weight ($D_{mm}$, $D_{me}$) at zero and low temperatures. They characterize the magnetization and energy current responses to a magnetic field gradient, revealing an essential spin-charge coupling feature in quantum transport. We find that the Drude weights $D_{nm}$, $D_{mm}$, and $D_{me}$ across the $μ\text{-}H$ plane remarkably map out the zero-temperature phase boundary. This work fills a critical gap in the understanding of transport within integrable quantum gases and furnishes a direct theoretical foundation for future ultracold-atom experiments.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work analyzes how to optimize the minimum energy gap during quantum annealing by studying the 'exchange-resolved sensitivity' of the system's gap. It finds that while local changes are predictable, finite updates require accounting for 'bottleneck migration' via a 'repair-and-expose' mechanism. The results suggest that a max-min update rule is superior for guiding the annealing process when multiple low-energy states compete.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on gap dynamics, bottleneck identification, and local optimization rules directly relates to understanding the energy landscape traversal in complex quantum many-body systems, which is central to condensed matter physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses how to design constraint-preserving drivers in quantum annealing to reliably improve the minimum gap ($\min_s \Delta(s, w)$) of the annealing path.

**Main result.** Local gap sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but finite edge replacements require a 'repair-and-expose' mechanism and a 'tied-minimum max-min update' for reliable continuation.

**Method.** The analysis derives the exchange-resolved sensitivity of the minimum gap using Hellmann–Feynman theorems and compares local (infinitesimal) versus finite updates.

**Model / system.** The model involves binary optimization problems with fixed-cardinality constraints, analyzed via an annealing path $H(s, w) = (1 -s)D(w) + sP$. The driver $D(w)$ is constructed from exchange Laplacians.

**Key observables.** Minimum Gap ($\Delta(s, w)$), Exchange-Resolved Sensitivity, Subspace Overlap ($O_{	ext{sub}}$), and the Dirichlet-energy contrast ($G_e(s)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis distinguishes between infinitesimal changes ($\alpha \ll 1$) and finite edge replacements ($\alpha=1$), and uses various step sizes ($\epsilon=10^{-2}$ or $10^{-3}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The local sensitivity analysis assumes simple eigenvalues and a unique minimizer $s^*$; the max-min rule is presented as a local continuation method.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the distinction between the physical exchange graph and the induced configuration-space swap graph; other figures compare gap improvements across different optimization strategies.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework for gap sensitivity, derives the local response, identifies the 'repair-and-expose' mechanism when bottlenecks migrate, and proposes the 'tied-minimum max-min update' rule for reliable driver redirection.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Constraint-preserving exchange drivers allow many coupling graphs that preserve the same feasible sector, but exhibit different minimum gaps along an annealing path. We derive an exchange-resolved sensitivity of the normalised minimum gap for fixed-cardinality Laplacian drivers sharing a Dicke ground state, and apply it to identify locally favourable modifications of the driver. Numerical experiments indicate this sensitivity reliably predicts beneficial infinitesimal changes, but its reliability decreases when the same direction is extended to a finite edge replacement. The gap landscape tracking reveals one mechanism of this loss of reliability. Improving the active bottleneck can expose a competing minimum, with a more extensive reorganisation of the low-energy subspace. We call this the "repair-and-expose" mechanism and observe it in both dense quadratic and sparse frustrated objective families. This motivates relinearizing the response when competing minima become co-active. In the tested oracle setting, a tied-minimum max-min update is substantially more reliable than continuing the original direction or optimizing only the incoming minimum. Supporting finite-size search and selector tests show that this local information can remain useful beyond the infinitesimal limit, while its practical extraction depends on the driver geometry and identification of the relevant low-energy competitors. These results connect local exchange-resolved gap sensitivity to bottleneck migration and conditional driver redirection.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper deeply explores the mathematical structure of Mutually Unbiased Bases (MUBs) by analyzing common unbiased states and the conditions required for their completion into full measurement bases. Using advanced algebraic geometry, the authors establish constructive theorems for certain systems while also deriving specific obstructions that limit the number of such bases in higher dimensions. It provides fundamental theoretical constraints on quantum measurement theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical framework developed here—linking algebraic geometry to the existence of quantum measurement bases—provides deep structural insights into the limits of quantum information processing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the mathematical constraints governing common unbiased states and the conditions under which a set of such states can be completed to form a full orthonormal measurement basis in quantum systems.

**Main result.** The authors provide explicit constructions showing that for specific Fourier pairs, common unbiased states can be completed to an orthonormal basis, while also deriving obstructions (e.g., in dimension six) that prove strong unextendibility for certain configurations.

**Method.** The work employs advanced algebraic and geometric techniques, analyzing projective ray schemes, affine coordinate algebras, and utilizing complex equations derived from quantum measurement theory.

**Model / system.** The model is abstract quantum measurement theory, focusing on pure states represented as rays in a complex Hilbert space, and measurements defined by orthonormal bases (like the Fourier or Hadamard bases).

**Key observables.** Common unbiased states, the Gram defect of candidate bases, and the structure of the projective ray scheme.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space (especially $d=6$), and the neighborhood size ($\epsilon$) around reference matrices.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on specific, highly structured input bases (like phase-deformed Fourier pairs) or the assumption of small perturbations around known exact matrices.

**Figures summary.** Not specified; the notes describe mathematical theorems and structural proofs rather than figure content.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining common unbiased states and the problem of completion, to presenting specific constructive theorems (e.g., for Fourier pairs), followed by detailed algebraic analyses of constraints (finiteness results) and specific dimensional obstructions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Which pure states give uniform outcomes in several mutually unbiased measurements, and when can they form another measurement basis? We distinguish common unbiased states, their orthonormal completion, and further extension. For a displayed phase-deformed Fourier pair in dimension $2m$, a clock symmetry and skew antiunitary complete every prescribed common unbiased state to an explicit orthonormal basis. In dimension six, an amplitude-profile obstruction proves strong unextendibility of a given mutually unbiased triple when its original third-basis rays are invariant under the ternary clock. We give an exact nonproduct example and an application to a companion whose columns are localized at single Fourier frequencies. For every exact Hadamard matrix in a specified closed entrywise neighborhood of a fixed reference matrix, the coordinate and Hadamard bases have exactly 48 common unbiased rays but no third measurement basis, with a quantitative lower bound on the squared Gram defect of every six-column candidate.   We also study auxiliary complex equations for common states, retaining algebraic multiplicities. For a flat unitary of order six with all $3\times3$ minors nonzero, the projective ray scheme is finite; each singular two-minor contributes two reduced isolated boundary points, and the affine coordinate algebra is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$. In every order, a critical-algebra identity preserves multiplicities; in dimension six it gives finiteness for a fixed phase fibre. Specialization over a discrete valuation ring controls complete reciprocal-orthogonal collections. A nonphysical Tao/Potts collection separates algebraic from physical solutions. These results do not determine the global maximum number of mutually unbiased bases or classify all triples.

</details>
