**Summary.** This paper develops a theoretical framework to find the optimal pupil function for maximizing the intensity of vortex beams (carrying OAM) focused onto a ring. By solving a variational eigenvalue problem, the authors derive the optimal pupil structure, which combines Fresnel and Bessel modulations. They validate these theoretical limits through both detailed analysis and experimental implementation using SLMs.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a fundamental, analytically derived upper bound for energy concentration in structured light beams, which has direct implications for designing high-performance optical elements and understanding wave propagation limits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the optimization problem of achieving the maximum possible intensity concentration when focusing paraxial beams carrying Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) through a finite circular aperture.

**Main result.** The optimal pupil profile combines Fresnel phase structure with an OAM-dependent Bessel radial modulation, establishing a rigorous upper bound on achievable ring intensity for structured waves.

**Method.** The problem is formulated as a variational optimization problem leading to an integral-kernel eigenvalue problem, which is solved analytically.

**Model / system.** The system involves paraxial beams with OAM ($\ell$) propagating through a circular aperture. The analysis is conducted in the paraxial wave regime, modeling the focusing objective as maximizing intensity at a specific ring radius.

**Key observables.** Maximum achievable ring intensity ($\Lambda(\ell)$), optimal pupil function ($\psi^+_\ell$), and focusing efficiency ($\eta_\ell(\psi)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Topological charge ($\ell$), aperture radius ($R$), target ring radius ($ho^*$), and propagation distance ($	au_f$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the paraxial approximation and assumes the input field is aperture-limited.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the OAM dependence of the optimal eigenfunction and relative focusing strength, and compare experimental peak focal ring intensities for various mask types across different OAM orders.

**Paper structure.** The paper first formulates the optimal focusing problem variationally, deriving the optimal pupil structure. It then compares this theoretical optimum against practical mask designs (binary vs. amplitude-weighted) and experimentally tests these predictions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We formulate diffractive ring focusing of paraxial beams carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM) through a finite circular aperture as a variational optimization problem. For a fixed topological charge, we determine the real-valued radial pupil that maximizes the intensity at a prescribed ring radius and propagation distance under a normalization constraint on the input field. The resulting problem admits an exact analytical solution: the optimal pupil combines the familiar Fresnel phase structure with an OAM-dependent Bessel radial modulation, and the associated eigenvalue yields a rigorous upper bound on the achievable ring intensity. We further analyze the lens-assisted configuration and derive a simple bound that allows direct comparison between diffractive and refractive vortex focusing. The theory also provides a quantitative framework for evaluating the performance of practical mask designs, including binary Fresnel-Bessel zone plates and amplitude-weighted pupils. We have experimentally tested our predictions in the optical domain by implementing the corresponding vortex beam pupils and comparing their propagation and focusing performance with the optimal solution. Our results establish the vortex-beam analogue of optimal amplitude-only focusing and identify the fundamental limits governing diffractive concentration of structured waves

**Summary.** This paper develops structural criteria to ensure that measuring only a subset of Pauli observables on $n$ qubits is sufficient to uniquely determine the quantum state. It introduces a 'quartic certificate' based on the omitted observables and proves that avoiding certain commuting sets of four operators guarantees unique determination for $n \ge 3$. This provides a powerful, testable tool for quantum tomography protocols.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous, checkable mathematical criteria directly applicable to experimental quantum information protocols, linking algebraic constraints (quartic identities) to fundamental physical properties (state distinguishability).

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to derive structural criteria to guarantee that quantum state tomography, performed using restricted Pauli measurements on $n$-qubit systems, uniquely determines the quantum state (either among pure states or among all possible states).

**Main result.** It establishes that for $n \ge 3$, universal unique determination among all states (UDA) is guaranteed if the set of omitted Pauli observables avoids containing four distinct operators that commute pairwise and multiply to $\pm I$ (the 'four-set-free' condition).

**Method.** The analysis converts the uniqueness problem into spectral conditions on the measurement kernel operator, deriving a 'quartic certificate' based on the fourth elementary symmetric polynomial of the operator's eigenvalues.

**Model / system.** The system is an $n$-qubit quantum system, and the measurements are restricted to expectation values of a subset of Pauli observables. The ambiguity is characterized by the kernel operator $K_A$ acting on the space of state differences.

**Key observables.** Expectation values of Pauli observables, the measurement kernel operator $A$, and the fourth elementary symmetric polynomial $e_4(A)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of qubits ($n$), the structure of the omitted Pauli observables (e.g., 'four-set-free'), and the spectral properties of the kernel operator (e.g., number of positive/negative eigenvalues).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on relating the ambiguity to the spectral properties of the kernel operator $A$, and specific results are derived for $n=3$ qubits where the four-set-free condition is necessary.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the uniqueness notions (UDP/UDA), deriving the quartic certificate from the spectral analysis of the kernel, establishing the structural criterion (four-set-freeness) for $n \ge 3$, and finally analyzing the necessary and sufficient conditions for $n=3$ and the general commuting case.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Full Pauli-basis tomography of an arbitrary $n$-qubit state uses the expectation values of all nonidentity Pauli observables. For multiqubit systems, prior knowledge that the state is pure allows some of these observables to be omitted while retaining uniqueness. We study two resulting notions of uniqueness: whether every pure state is uniquely determined among pure states (UDP), and whether every pure state is uniquely determined among all states, including mixed states (UDA). We derive quartic uniqueness certificates from the fourth elementary symmetric polynomial of operators in the real span of the omitted Pauli observables. An exact quartic identity shows that, for $n$-qubit systems with $n\geq 3$, every pure state is UDA whenever the omitted Pauli observables contain no four distinct operators that commute pairwise and multiply to $\pm I$. For three qubits, this condition is also necessary for UDP, yielding an exact characterization of both UDP and UDA. We further prove that UDP and UDA coincide for any number of qubits whenever the omitted Pauli observables commute pairwise. These results provide directly checkable structural criteria for certifying pure-state tomography from restricted Pauli measurements.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes how initial entanglement between two particles (B and C) affects the measurement uncertainty of a third particle (A) during Bhabha scattering. By quantifying memory-assisted entropic uncertainty, the authors show that the spectator particle C acts as a quantum memory, whose initial entanglement can reduce the overall uncertainty in the scattering process near backscattering angles.

**Why it may be interesting.** It applies advanced quantum information concepts (uncertainty relations, entanglement) to a high-energy particle physics process, providing insights into how quantum correlations govern measurement limits in scattering experiments.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates spin-outcome correlations and memory-assisted entropic uncertainty in Bhabha scattering when one particle is initially entangled with a spectator.

**Main result.** Initial entanglement between the scattering positron and the spectator can lower the total memory-assisted uncertainty in high-energy backscattering by strengthening spin-outcome correlations with the spectator.

**Method.** The analysis uses quantum information diagnostics, including entanglement entropy, memory-assisted entropic uncertainty, and outcome-memory mutual information sums.

**Model / system.** The system is tree-level QED Bhabha scattering ($e^-e^+ 	o e^-e^+$) where the positron (B) is initially entangled with a spectator electron (C). The analysis focuses on the post-selected three-particle scattering state.

**Key observables.** Entanglement entropy $S(ho_A)$, total memory-assisted uncertainty $U_A$, outcome-memory mutual-information sums $G_B$ and $G_C$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Initial entanglement weight $\eta$, scattering angle $	heta$, and high-energy backscattering limit ($	heta \approx \pi$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to an idealized fixed-angle post-selected spin state, and some calculations neglect forward-scattering interference terms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the angular dependence of $U_A$ and $S(ho_A)$ for varying entanglement parameters, and density plots show the relationship between these quantities in the $(	heta, \mu)$ plane.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by defining the initial entangled state, calculating the relevant quantum information measures ($U_A, S(ho_A), G_B, G_C$), and then analyzing the behavior of these measures in specific physical limits, such as high-energy backscattering.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate spin-outcome correlations and memory-assisted entropic uncertainty in tree-level Bhabha scattering, where an incident electron $A$ scatters with a positron $B$ initially entangled with a spectator electron $C$. For the fixed-angle post-selected final state, we compare the total memory-assisted uncertainty $U_A$ for three alternative Pauli measurements on $A$ with the entanglement entropy $S(ρ_A)$ across the $A|BC$ partition. We resolve $U_A$ into the separate uncertainties $U_B$ and $U_C$ and evaluate the corresponding outcome-memory mutual-information sums $G_B$ and $G_C$. This separates changes in the randomness of the outcomes on $A$ from changes in their correlations with each memory. In the parameter regions studied, enhanced $A|BC$ entanglement is accompanied by lower $U_A$, most prominently near high-energy backscattering. An analytic treatment of this limit shows that $B$ factorizes from $AC$: $G_B$ vanishes, whereas $G_C$ increases with the initial $B$-$C$ entanglement. An entropic complete complementarity analysis characterizes the accompanying loss of local helicity predictability in $ρ_A$ and changes in the coherence, predictability, and mixedness of the interacting pair $ρ_{AB}$. These results show that initial $B$-$C$ entanglement can lower the total memory-assisted uncertainty in high-energy backscattering by strengthening spin-outcome correlations with the spectator $C$, thereby identifying the distinct roles of the interacting particle and the spectator as quantum memories.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces the Symmetric Mode Ansatz (SyMA) to theoretically describe the low-energy magnon excitations in Chern and fractional Chern insulators found in Moiré materials. By applying the SyMA to Hubbard models, the authors derive rigorous quantum geometric bounds on the magnon gap. This provides a powerful, unified theoretical tool for understanding magnetism stabilized by topological band structures.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous derivation of bounds on the magnon gap using topological invariants (Chern number, Berry curvature) connects fundamental concepts from band theory and topology to the stability of magnetic order in strongly correlated systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to clarify the nature and origin of the magnon gap in Chern insulators (CIs) and fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) stabilized by ferromagnetism in Moiré materials.

**Main result.** The Symmetric Mode Ansatz (SyMA) provides a highly accurate theoretical description of the low-energy magnon spectrum, leading to quantum geometric bounds on the magnon gap.

**Method.** The authors develop and apply the generalized single-mode approximation (SyMA) to the magnon Hamiltonian derived from Hubbard-type models.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on Moiré materials, specifically twisted MoTe2, which host FCIs due to spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking. The theoretical framework is tested using Hubbard models and the First-Harmonic (FH) model.

**Key observables.** Magnon spectrum/gap ($\Delta$), Chern number ($C$), Berry curvature ($F(k)$), and quantum metric ($G$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Filling fractions ($
u$), magnetic coupling strength ($U$), and the twist angle ($	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The SyMA is assumed to be exact or highly accurate for certain solvable Hubbard models; approximations are made when neglecting single-particle terms in the low-energy magnon analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the exact magnon spectrum against the SyMA predictions across various fillings ($
u$), showing agreement at integer filling and providing gap energy dependence on $
u$.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the SyMA theory, tests it on analytically solvable Hubbard models to derive general bounds, and then applies it to the specific FH model of MoTe2 to analyze the magnon gap across integer and fractional fillings.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Moiré materials host integer and fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) where time-reversal is broken spontaneously by flat band ferromagnetism. In twisted MoTe2, unlike in quantum Hall, opposite spins carry opposite Chern numbers and realize Ising ferromagnetism with gapped magnon excitations. Clarifying the nature of these collective modes and the origin of the magnon gap is key to understanding the stability of the Chern magnets in these materials. To do so, we develop a generalized single-mode approximation, which we call the symmetric mode ansatz (SyMA), to describe the low-energy magnon spectrum. We find it to be in exceptional agreement with numerical calculations at integer filling, and qualitatively accurate across fractional fillings including FCIs. To explain the accuracy of the SyMA, we present two families of Hubbard models (including the Haldane model and continuum ideal bands) whose collective modes are analytically solvable and for which the SyMA is either exact or an accurate approximation. For a class of these models where SyMA is exact, we prove two-sided bounds on the zero-momentum magnon gap in terms of the Chern number, Berry curvature, and quantum metric, revealing that uniform quantum geometry is sufficient for stabilizing magnetism in Chern bands.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors demonstrate a novel method to probe quantum-spin-ice correlations by coupling them to Weyl semimetal surface states via a synthetic Kondo lattice interface. By measuring the angular magnetoresistance, they observe a unique twelvefold symmetry reconstruction only when coupled to a quantum spin-ice candidate ($	ext{Tb}_2	ext{Ti}_2	ext{O}_7$). This confirms that the electronic transport acts as a sensitive transducer for the underlying multipolar quantum magnetic order.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly tunable, solid-state platform to probe exotic quantum magnetic correlations (multipolar moments) by mapping them onto measurable electronic transport symmetries, which is relevant for understanding strongly correlated interfacial physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to demonstrate a method to encode and detect quantum-spin-ice correlations, particularly those involving multipolar degrees of freedom, into measurable electronic transport properties.

**Main result.** The quantum-spin-ice interface ($	ext{Tb}_2	ext{Ti}_2	ext{O}_7$) exhibits a unique $	ext{6-fold} 	o 	ext{12-fold} 	o 	ext{6-fold}$ reentrant anisotropy in the angular magnetoresistance, a signature absent in the classical spin-ice reference ($	ext{Dy}_2	ext{Ti}_2	ext{O}_7$).

**Method.** The research uses in-plane and out-of-plane angular magnetoresistance measurements on a synthetic Kondo lattice interface at ultra-low temperatures.

**Model / system.** The platform is a synthetic Kondo lattice interface formed between a Weyl semimetal ($	ext{Eu}_2	ext{Ir}_2	ext{O}_7$) and a quantum-spin-ice candidate ($	ext{Tb}_2	ext{Ti}_2	ext{O}_7$), allowing the coupling of itinerant Weyl surface states to frustrated local moments.

**Key observables.** Angular magnetoresistance ($	ext{MR}$), specifically the symmetry reconstruction observed as a transition from sixfold to twelvefold anisotropy ($	ext{MR}_{12}/	ext{MR}_6$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Ultra-low temperatures ($	ext{20 mK}$), varying magnetic field strength, and the comparison between quantum ($	ext{Tb}$) and classical ($	ext{Dy}$) spin-ice couplings.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The electronic transport is sensitive to the specific magnetic degrees of freedom (dipolar vs. multipolar) present in the adjacent spin-ice material.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the structural interface, the field evolution of angular magnetoresistance showing the $	ext{6-fold} 	o 	ext{12-fold} 	o 	ext{6-fold}$ sequence for the quantum case, and direct comparisons with the classical case.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical system, details the measurement techniques (ADMR), presents the key comparative results showing the distinct symmetry signatures ($	ext{12-fold}$ vs. $	ext{2-fold}$), and concludes by establishing the synthetic Kondo lattice as a transduction route.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum spin ice hosts collective excitations and quantum fluctuations that are largely electrically silent because the materials supporting them are insulating. Coupling this magnetic environment to surface-localized Weyl states offers a route to encode its correlations directly into Fermi-arc transport. Experimental access to this regime, however, has remained largely unexplored. Here, we realize a synthetic Kondo lattice interface between the Weyl semimetal $\mathrm{Eu_2Ir_2O_7}$ and the quantum-spin-ice candidate $\mathrm{Tb_2Ti_2O_7}$, and demonstrate that quantum-spin-ice correlations are imprinted on Weyl Fermi-arc transport. At ultra-low temperature, electronic transport evolves from a sixfold anisotropic response at low field into a twelvefold response over an intermediate field window, before entering a reentrant sixfold anisotropy at high field. No analogous twelvefold response occurs at the classical-spin-ice interface. The quantum--classical contrast shows that the same itinerant electronic channel acquires qualitatively different symmetry information when interacting with the quantum-fluctuating Tb moments, consistent with an interfacial coupling between the Weyl surface states and the transverse, multipolar degrees of freedom, in addition to the longitudinal, dipolar contribution. Our work establishes synthetic Kondo lattice interfaces as a route for transducing frustrated quantum magnetism with multipole correlations into distinct Weyl Fermi-arc transport responses.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper solves a major theoretical hurdle in quantum gravity by developing the algebraic Petz map to reconstruct information trapped inside a black hole's 'island' from Hawking radiation. It achieves this by leveraging advanced tools from modular theory, bypassing the need for direct causal connections between the interior and the exterior. The result provides a concrete, computable dictionary proving that black hole information is preserved and accessible.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on gravity, the reliance on modular theory, algebraic reconstruction, and the mapping between different quantum algebras provides deep mathematical tools applicable to open quantum systems and entanglement structure in general.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the black hole information paradox by providing an operational, algebraic method to reconstruct quantum operators trapped inside a black hole's 'island' from measurable Hawking radiation.

**Main result.** The authors construct a rigorous dictionary using the algebraic Petz map, demonstrating that information inside the black hole is mathematically recoverable from the asymptotic radiation.

**Method.** The reconstruction relies on Tomita–Takesaki modular theory, mapping the island operators to their algebraic complement, and then using a sequence of modular conjugations and a $ho$-dual map to project them onto the radiation algebra.

**Model / system.** The system is an evaporating black hole coupled to a non-gravitating bath, analyzed using the framework of quantum field theory in curved spacetime and holographic duality (AdS/CFT).

**Key observables.** Island operators ($\phi_I$), Hawking radiation operators ($\Phi_R$), and the resulting reconstructed mirror operators ($\Phi_A$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The Page time, the large-$N$ limit, and the background quantum state $|\psi_gangle$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method assumes the relevant state is cyclic and separating, and it relies on the algebraic duality relation $A'_I = ar{A}_I$ to bypass the need for a direct global isometry.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the reconstruction protocol by first establishing the failure of standard entanglement wedge methods, then introducing the algebraic Petz map via modular theory, and finally demonstrating its application to yield the mirror operator structure.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The island proposal guarantees a unitary Page curve for evaporating black holes, implying that operators deep behind the horizon must be fully reconstructable from asymptotic Hawking radiation. However, because the interior is causally disconnected and highly dynamical, standard entanglement wedge reconstruction methods, relying on global isometries or continuous modular flow, fail to provide this mapping. We resolve this by constructing a protocol for island reconstruction using the algebraic Petz map. By using modular theory, we reflect island operators into the accessible complement, transport them to the boundary, and map them into the radiation algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this purely algebraic derivation naturally yields the structure of Papadodimas-Raju mirror operators. This framework provides a rigorous operational dictionary for the island formula, proving that information trapped inside a black hole can be decoded.

</details>

**Summary.** This work establishes a powerful structural property called 'mutual linearity' for the activities of complexes in chemical reaction networks. It proves that this linearity holds exactly, even far from equilibrium, provided the network has zero deficiency. This relationship serves as a powerful diagnostic tool, as its violation signals structural flaws like non-zero deficiency.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical chemical kinetics, the mathematical machinery—relating structural invariants (deficiency) to algebraic constraints (linearity)—is highly relevant to understanding constraints in open quantum systems or quantum field theories where non-equilibrium steady states are studied.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates finding exact, non-linear relationships (mutual linearity) describing how a system far from equilibrium responds to changes in its reaction rate constants.

**Main result.** Mutual linearity holds not for species concentrations, but for the activities of the reaction complexes ($\psi_c$), yielding a three-term linear relation independent of the controlled rate constants.

**Method.** The proof utilizes concepts from Markov chain theory, specifically analyzing the coplanarity of spanning-tree polynomials derived from the complex-space Laplacian.

**Model / system.** The system is Chemical Reaction Networks (CRNs) operating under mass-action kinetics, analyzed in the context of jump processes and complex-balance equations.

**Key observables.** Stationary activities of complexes ($\psi_c$), which are mass-action monomials; the relationship $\Delta_{bc}\psi_a + \Delta_{ca}\psi_b + \Delta_{ab}\psi_c = 0$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Zero deficiency ($\delta=0$) and the condition of having a single linkage class are crucial structural requirements for the theorem to hold.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the network is zero-deficiency and that the controlled reaction is bidirectional and not a bridge.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the theorem using a Michaelis-Menten cycle, showing the linear collapse of the mutual linearity product. Figure 2 demonstrates the relation holding for a complex network and its violation when the deficiency increases.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem of non-equilibrium response, proves the existence of mutual linearity in complex activities for specific network structures, derives the general linear relation, and uses this relation to test structural invariants like network deficiency.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Exact statements about how a system far from equilibrium responds to changes in its rate constants are scarce beyond linear response, yet they are central to the control of biochemical networks. A notable exception is mutual linearity: in a jump process, controlling the rates of a single transition makes any two stationary probabilities obey an exact affine relation, arbitrarily far from equilibrium. With nonlinear mass-action kinetics, and conservation laws in place of a normalization, chemical reaction networks seem to defy mutual linearity since species concentrations obey no such relation. We show that it was there all along, in the complexes' activities (mass-action monomials) rather than in the concentrations of species. For zero-deficiency networks with a single linkage class, controlling one reaction makes any three stationary activities obey a linear relation whose coefficients are independent of the controlled rate constants, the conserved quantities (hence the initial state), and even of the stoichiometry of complexes. This predicts hidden activities and bounds the activity ratios the control can reach, while a violation signals nonzero deficiency or multiple linkage classes.

</details>

**Summary.** This review surveys the field of quantum optical sensing, detailing the shift from solid-state quantum emitters like NV centers to bio-integrated systems using fluorescent proteins. It highlights the advanced techniques used to measure physical parameters like temperature and magnetic fields at the nanoscale. The paper emphasizes that while progress is rapid, overcoming environmental noise and ensuring scalability remain key challenges for clinical translation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it bridges quantum optics and condensed matter physics into a tangible application domain (biomedicine), requiring deep knowledge of open quantum systems, decoherence mechanisms, and solid-state defect physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper reviews the evolution of quantum optical sensing platforms, tracking the transition from isolated solid-state spin defects to bio-integrated systems for biomedical applications.

**Main result.** Significant progress has been made in integrating quantum sensors, utilizing platforms like NV centers, SiV centers, and fluorescent proteins, for nanoscale measurements in complex biological environments.

**Method.** The review synthesizes various experimental techniques, including Optically Detected Magnetic Resonance (ODMR), T1 relaxometry, and specialized readout methods like OADF, applied across different physical systems.

**Model / system.** The core systems discussed are solid-state spin defects (e.g., NV centers in diamond, $	ext{V}_{	ext{B}}^-$ in hBN) and engineered biological systems (fluorescent proteins). These platforms are used to probe local fields like temperature, strain, and magnetic fields.

**Key observables.** Temperature, strain, electric fields, magnetic fields, longitudinal relaxation time ($T_1$), and spin-photon interactions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Room temperature operation, nanometer-scale resolution, and coherence time in aqueous environments.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary challenge is maintaining quantum coherence and reliable sensing functionality when moving from controlled solid-state environments to complex, noisy biological media.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the various optically accessible spin defects (NV to hBN) and their diverse applications, ranging from radical detection to nanoscale NMR.

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured as a perspective review, first establishing the historical progression of quantum sensing platforms, detailing the physics and advances in solid-state defects, then covering the integration into bio-compatible systems, and finally summarizing current challenges and future outlook.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum optical sensing has evolved from isolated solid state spin defect platforms to increasingly bio-integrated systems designed for biomedical applications. This review presents a perspective on this transition, spanning nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond to emerging fluorescent protein based spin qubits. Advances in diamond fabrication have enabled photonic cavities, nanomechanical resonators, and microstructured devices that enhance spin photon interactions and room temperature sensitivity. Exploration of spin defects in alternative materials further expands the sensing landscape. Parallel progress toward biological compatibility includes chip based architectures for in vitro and in vivo studies, microfluidic integration, and minimally invasive nanodiamond probes capable of intracellular nanothermometry and nanorheometry. Improvements in surface functionalization have enhanced coherence and sensing reliability in complex environments. Collectively, these advances highlight the progress and remaining challenges toward application oriented quantum sensing for the life sciences.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a non-perturbative method to model how molecular vibrations are excited by strong, time-varying electric fields. By mapping the dynamics onto a complex phase-space coordinate, the authors provide a unified description that accurately predicts vibrational populations in both resonant and non-resonant regimes. This framework is crucial for understanding and controlling molecular energy transfer in intense light fields.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, non-perturbative phase-space picture for controlling molecular vibrations using intense light fields, which is central to ultrafast spectroscopy and quantum control.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a non-perturbative quantum framework to describe vibrational excitation in molecular systems driven by arbitrarily time-dependent external electric fields.

**Main result.** The dynamics are exactly mapped onto the evolution of a complex phase-space coordinate, yielding a Poisson distribution for vibrational populations that correctly captures both resonant enhancement and non-resonant suppression.

**Method.** The authors utilize an exact coherent-state solution for the driven harmonic oscillator, allowing the analysis to remain valid in the strong-field regime where standard time-dependent perturbation theory fails.

**Model / system.** The system models a single normal mode of a molecule with a harmonic potential and a linear dipole coupling ($\mu(q) = \mu_0 + \mu'_0 T \cdot q$) interacting with an external electric field $\vec{E}(t)$.

**Key observables.** Vibrational populations ($P_n(t)$), the time-dependent phase-space displacement ($S_t = |z_t|^2$), and the phase-space trajectory governed by $z_t$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Resonant vs. non-resonant driving ($\omega$ vs. $\omega_0$), field strength ($E_0$), and detuning ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The dipole operator is approximated by an affine function of the normal coordinate ($q$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase-space trajectories for resonant (outward spiral) and non-resonant driving, and compare the results of the exact coherent-state method against Time-Dependent Perturbation Theory (TDPT) in both weak and strong-field limits.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the non-perturbative coherent-state formalism, derives the closed-form expression for the phase-space coordinate $z_t$, analyzes the distinct behaviors in resonant and non-resonant regimes, and validates the approach by showing its reduction to TDPT in the weak-field limit.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a non-perturbative framework for the quantum treatment of vibrational excitation in molecular systems driven by electric fields with arbitrary time dependence. For harmonic potentials with linear dipole coupling, the field-induced dynamics is exactly described by a displaced coherent state, whose evolution is completely determined by a complex phase-space coordinate. Closed-form expressions for this coordinate reveal a clear distinction between resonant and non-resonant regimes. The resulting vibrational populations follow a Poisson distribution determined by a dimensionless time-dependent phase-space displacement, for both resonant and non-resonant driving. Resonant driving results in an enhanced phase-space displacement, whereas finite detuning between the driving and vibrational frequencies leads to an exponential suppression of the phase-space displacement and vibrational excitation. While the approach reduces to the standard time-dependent perturbation theory in the weak-field limit, it remains valid in the strong-field regime, where perturbative treatments fail. Our results provide a transparent phase-space picture of vibrational control and enable non-perturbative state preparation in ultrafast spectroscopy.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenge of efficiently simulating flow models on quantum computers by leveraging the formal connection between flow dynamics and quantum wavefunction evolution. The authors propose replacing the resource-heavy Quantum Read-Only Memory (QROM) technique with a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) for data encoding. This results in a method that maintains high simulation accuracy while drastically reducing the required quantum circuit depth and gate count.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the computational bottleneck of simulating continuous physical processes (like quantum evolution or fluid dynamics) on near-term quantum hardware by integrating advanced generative ML techniques (flow matching) with quantum circuit design.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to develop an efficient quantum circuit implementation for simulating flow models, which are used to model probability path transport.

**Main result.** The authors successfully propose a method using a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) to replace the resource-intensive Quantum Read-Only Memory (QROM) framework, maintaining simulation accuracy while significantly reducing circuit resources.

**Method.** The core method involves simulating wavefunction flow, which is connected to flow models via a continuity Hamiltonian, using a phase kickback framework enhanced by QNNs for data encoding.

**Model / system.** The system involves flow models generating trajectories via an ODE solved by a velocity field, which is formally linked to quantum dynamics via the continuity Hamiltonian driving Schrödinger evolution.

**Key observables.** Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Wasserstein-1 distance, and KL divergence are used to compare the final simulated probability density against the target distribution.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The efficiency is analyzed by comparing circuit resources (CNOT gates) between QROM-based and QNN-based implementations, and by varying temporal ($\Delta t$) and spatial ($\Delta x$) discretizations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that replacing QROM with a trained QNN can maintain the accuracy of the wavefunction flow simulation while drastically reducing the exponential resource scaling associated with QROM.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of simulated vs. reference final probability densities across different time steps ($\Delta t$), and show particle visualizations demonstrating successful transport from an initial state to a target distribution using the learned potential.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical link between flow models and quantum dynamics via the continuity Hamiltonian. It then details the simulation using QROM-based phase kickback, identifies the resource bottleneck, and proposes the QNN replacement for QROM, concluding with numerical experiments validating the efficiency and accuracy of the QNN-based approach.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Flow models generate trajectories from an initial distribution to a target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation defined by a velocity field. Flow matching learns this velocity field by modeling the transport dynamics between the two distributions. Wavefunction flow establishes a formal connection between flow models and quantum dynamics by introducing a continuity Hamiltonian, which drives the Schrödinger evolution of quantum states. In this paper, we investigate accurate and efficient quantum simulation of the wavefunction flow, thereby realizing the efficient implementation of flow models on quantum computers. We first leverage a quantum read-only memory (QROM)-based phase kickback framework for the wavefunction flow simulation, generating probability densities that closely match those produced by the corresponding conventional flow model. To address the high circuit-resource cost, we further incorporate a trained quantum neural network (QNN) into the phase kickback framework, replacing QROM for data encoding. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed method implements flow models on quantum computers more efficiently, since it maintains the accuracy of wavefunction flow simulation compared with the QROM-based framework, and significantly reduces the circuit resources.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes how periodically modulating inter-species interactions can stabilize matter-wave vector solitons in two-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates. By deriving an effective, averaged equation, the authors show that the resulting nonlinear quantum pressure counteracts the collapse tendency inherent in the system. Numerical simulations confirm that this management technique substantially prolongs the soliton's lifetime.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the stability of matter-wave solitons in BECs, a core topic in AMO physics. The concept of 'nonlinearity management' provides a novel, controllable mechanism to stabilize quantum states against collapse, which has implications for realizing robust quantum matter-wave devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the nonlinear management of matter-wave vector solitons in two dimensions, specifically addressing the mechanism by which this management prevents collapse.

**Main result.** The nonlinear quantum pressure arising from the averaging process arrests the collapse, leading to the existence of stable vector solitons whose lifetime is significantly prolonged compared to the unmanaged case.

**Method.** The analysis employs averaging techniques over fast temporal modulations of the inter-species interaction, leading to an effective Hamiltonian, which is then analyzed using variational methods and numerical simulations.

**Model / system.** The system models a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) governed by coupled Gross-Pitaevskii equations. The dynamics are analyzed under periodic modulation of the inter-species interaction, leading to an effective, averaged nonlinear quantum pressure term.

**Key observables.** Mean square radius ($ar{X}(t)$), soliton width ($w(t)$), and the effective energy functional ($ar{H}(L)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Modulation strength ($\sigma^2$), coupling constants ($g_{ij}$), and the finite width ($L_{\min}$) where stable solitons exist.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the modulation is strong and rapid, allowing for the derivation of an averaged system via a near-identity transformation; the rigorous proof of collapse arrest is limited to this averaged model.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the time evolution of width and density profiles for managed vs. unmanaged systems, showing stable oscillations when management is active and collapse when it is switched off.

**Paper structure.** The paper first derives the averaged system by averaging the time-dependent GPEs. It then uses variational analysis to map the dynamics to a mechanical system with an effective potential. Finally, it compares the predictions of the averaged model with full numerical simulations to confirm the stabilization effect.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The evolution of matter-wave vector solitons in two dimensions under nonlinearity management is studied. The averaged over strong and rapid modulations in time of the inter-species interactions vector Gross-Pitaevskii equation is derived. The averaging gives the appearance of the effective nonlinear quantum pressure depending on the population of the other component. Using this system of equations, the dynamical stabilization of the two-dimensional vector matter-wave solitons under the management of the mean-field nonlinearity is investigated. It is shown that the nonlinear quantum pressure arrests the collapse in the averaged system, giving rise to stable vector solitons. Full numerical simulations of the original, time-dependent system of Gross-Pitaevskii equations confirm that the management strongly prolongs the lifetime of these solitons compared to the unmanaged case.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work analyzes the nonlinear transport of both electric and heat currents in 1D SNS junctions using a scattering approach. By comparing different models for energy-dependent transmission, the authors demonstrate that the junction's response to temperature gradients is critically dependent on the microscopic details of the normal metal region. This provides a crucial microscopic reference for understanding energy transport in mesoscopic fermionic superfluid junctions.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed study of non-equilibrium transport in superconducting mesoscopic junctions provides a rich theoretical framework for understanding energy and charge flow in quantum systems, relevant to superconducting quantum devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the phase-independent DC components of electric and heat currents flowing through one-dimensional Superconductor-Normal-Metal-Superconductor (SNS) junctions.

**Main result.** The nonlinear response of both electric and heat currents to temperature differences is highly dependent on the specific transmission profile (e.g., QPC vs. quantum-dot type) used in the normal region.

**Method.** The authors employ a scattering approach derived from the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, incorporating Multiple Andreev Reflections (MARs) while retaining energy-dependent transmission.

**Model / system.** The system is a 1D SNS junction connecting two superconducting reservoirs via a normal metal. The analysis compares three transmission profiles: energy-independent, Lorentzian (quantum-dot), and QPC-like.

**Key observables.** Electric current ($J_{ele}^{DC}$) and Heat current ($J_{heat}^{DC}$)

**Important parameters / regimes.** Bias voltage ($V$), temperature difference ($\Delta T$), and the specific transmission profile $T(E)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on the phase-independent DC components ($\phi=0$) and utilizes the Andreev approximation, although limitations regarding unitarity near this limit are noted.

**Figures summary.** Figures are mentioned to illustrate scattering amplitudes in the normal region and the bias dependence of the currents for the different transmission profiles.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the physical system and the scattering formalism (Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations) to deriving the current expressions via field-operator expansion and solving recurrence relations for scattering amplitudes.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the phase-independent dc components of the electric and heat currents through a one-dimensional superconductor-normal-metal-superconductor (SNS) junction subject to chemical-potential and temperature differences between two superconducting reservoirs. Using a scattering approach based on the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, we incorporate multiple Andreev reflections while retaining the energy dependence of transmission through the normal region. We compare energy-independent, quantum-dot-type, and quantum-point-contact transmission profiles. At low bias, both currents exhibit nonlinear features associated with the superconducting gap and multiple Andreev reflections. Their responses to a temperature difference depend remarkably on the transmission profile. At a small finite bias, the electric current depends weakly on the temperature difference for the energy-independent and quantum-dot-type profiles, whereas the quantum-point-contact profile produces a pronounced nonlinear response. The heat current depends nonlinearly on the temperature difference for all three profiles over the parameter range investigated. These results highlight the role of the transmission profile in nonlinear electric and heat transport through SNS junctions and provide a microscopic reference for related transport studies in mesoscopic fermionic superfluid junctions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes the stability of learned representations in VAEs by treating the ELBO as an effective free energy. It develops a theory showing that latent dimension collapse occurs in a predictable 'spectral cascade' governed by the residual spectrum. This provides a rigorous, physics-based understanding of information loss in deep generative models.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between information geometry (VAE collapse) and spectral stability criteria mirrors concepts in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, particularly phase transitions or stability boundaries in complex systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the physical principles governing how learned representations, modeled by Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), lose latent degrees of freedom through successive collapse.

**Main result.** It derives a spectral cascade interpretation where the loss of latent dimensions occurs sequentially at points of spectral marginality, governed by the residual spectrum.

**Method.** The analysis formulates dimension-wise posterior collapse as a fluctuation theory around partially collapsed states, treating the negative Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) as an effective free energy functional.

**Model / system.** The model is a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) analyzed using statistical physics techniques. The latent space fluctuations are treated via a Gaussian theory derived from the quadratic expansion of the ELBO, leading to a Hessian matrix acting as a mass matrix.

**Key observables.** Residual spectrum ($\Lambda(A)^*$), local reactivation direction, and the stability criterion ($\sigma'^2 \geq \Lambda(A)^*$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Decoder variance ($\sigma'^2$), the residual spectral upper edge ($\hat{\Lambda}(A)^*$), and the number of active latent dimensions ($|A|$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on expanding the free energy around a stationary state and assuming a Gaussian theory for fluctuations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spectral cascade showing a staircase pattern of dimension loss as the decoder variance ($\sigma'^2$) is varied, alongside the comparison between the stability margin and the residual spectral upper edge.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by formulating the collapse as a fluctuation theory, deriving the residual spectrum using a conditional residual operator, establishing the stability criterion, and finally demonstrating the spectral cascade interpretation through numerical continuation experiments.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Learned representations can lose latent degrees of freedom successively, suggesting a cascade of transitions whose underlying stability principle remains unclear. Here we formulate dimension-wise posterior collapse in variational autoencoder (VAE) as a fluctuation theory around partially collapsed states. Interpreting the negative evidence lower bound as an effective free energy, its quadratic expansion defines a Gaussian theory whose Hessian acts as a mass matrix for latent fluctuations. We show that the collapsed directions form an invariant fluctuation sector and derive its exact mass spectrum in terms of a conditional residual operator. A local reactivation direction lowers the free energy when the decoder variance falls below the residual spectral upper edge, with equality marking marginality. The criterion recovers principal component thresholds in the linear Gaussian VAE limit. Viewed in reverse along continuously connected branches, the reactivation boundary provides a local criterion for successive collapse. Numerical continuation experiments show successive loss of latent dimensions near these spectral marginalities. These results support a spectral cascade interpretation governed by residual information left unexplained by the surviving representation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a rigorous mathematical framework by decomposing the quantum momentum into real and imaginary components. It proves that the expectation value of the imaginary momentum vanishes, while showing that the entire quantum potential is structurally determined by the imaginary component. This provides a gauge-invariant, geometric understanding of quantum dynamics applicable to various physical settings.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical treatment of the momentum decomposition and the derivation of the quantum potential from $\mathbf{p}_I$ offers a novel, geometrically grounded perspective on non-linear quantum dynamics, which is relevant for understanding complex many-body systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper establishes a rigorous functional-analytic framework to decompose the quantum momentum operator into real ($\mathbf{p}_R$) and imaginary ($\mathbf{p}_I$) components and analyze the physical consequences of this decomposition.

**Main result.** The expectation value of the imaginary momentum component ($\langle \mathbf{p}_I angle$) vanishes identically for physically admissible states, and the Bohm quantum potential arises entirely from $\mathbf{p}_I$, leading to connections with Fisher information.

**Method.** The analysis employs Sobolev spaces and functional-analytic techniques, utilizing the Gauss–Green theorem to evaluate expectation values and derive density identities.

**Model / system.** The study concerns quantum mechanics for a wavefunction $\psi$ in a domain $\Omega$, extending to curved Riemannian manifolds and incorporating magnetic minimal coupling.

**Key observables.** Complex weak momentum ($\mathbf{p}_Q$), imaginary momentum ($\mathbf{p}_I$), Bohm quantum potential ($\langle V_{qu} angle$), and Fisher information ($I[ho]$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is valid for $\psi \in H^1(\Omega)$, and results are shown to be gauge-invariant under magnetic minimal coupling.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on the boundary conditions (e.g., decay at infinity) to prove the vanishing of $\langle \mathbf{p}_I angle$.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining the complex momentum decomposition, proving the vanishing of $\langle \mathbf{p}_I angle$ using boundary integrals, and then deriving structural identities linking $\langle V_{qu} angle$ to $\langle \mathbf{p}_I^2 angle$ and the Fisher information.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We establish a rigorous functional-analytic framework for the imaginary component $p_I$ of the complex weak momentum $p_Q = p_R + ip_I = \frac{\hbar}{i}\nabla\lnψ$. For every wavefunction in the Sobolev space $H^1(Ω)$, including those with nodal sets, we prove that the expectation value of $p_I$ vanishes identically, as a consequence of the regularity of $ρ= |ψ|^2$ and without appeal to the polar form $ψ= Re^{iS/\hbar}$. We further show that \textnormal{(i)} the Bohm quantum potential arises entirely from $p_I$ and satisfies $\langle V_{\mathrm{qu}}\rangle = \langle p_I^2\rangle/2m$, from which the known Fisher information relation follows as a corollary; \textnormal{(ii)} the group velocity of a Bloch band is the density-weighted average of $p_R/m$, with no contribution from $p_I$; \textnormal{(iii)} the decomposition is gauge-invariant under magnetic minimal coupling, the vector potential acting only on $p_R$; and \textnormal{(iv)} the results extend to curved Riemannian manifolds.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work explores superconductivity in a magnetic Wigner crystal realized in graphene. By modeling the electron-phonon interaction, the authors demonstrate that the crystal's own vibrations can induce a pairing attraction strong enough to cause superconductivity. The resulting superconducting state is predicted to exhibit chiral p-wave pairing, providing a theoretical pathway for understanding electronic crystallization and pairing in correlated 2D materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state physics, the methodology of using collective excitations (bosons) to mediate pairing in a strongly correlated, non-equilibrium system shares conceptual links with how bosonic mediators are treated in some AMO contexts, though the physical system is distinct.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether collective vibrational modes (phonons) within a magnetic Wigner crystal can mediate an attractive interaction strong enough to induce electron pairing (Cooper instability).

**Main result.** The calculations show that the phonon-mediated attraction exceeds the pairing threshold, leading to the prediction of chiral p-wave pairing as the leading superconducting instability.

**Method.** The authors employed a combination of Hartree-Fock and time-dependent Hartree-Fock approximations to derive an effective fermion-boson Hamiltonian, which was then solved using the quasiboson approximation for the two-electron Cooper problem.

**Model / system.** The system is a magnetic Wigner crystal formed by electrons in the first conduction band of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene. The model treats the interaction via coupling to the crystal's collective bosonic excitations (phonons and plasmons).

**Key observables.** Pairing susceptibility, binding energy ($E_b$), and the momentum-space phase texture ($\chi_0(k)$) which exhibits a winding consistent with chiral p-wave pairing.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Electron density ($n = 0.8 	imes 10^{12} 	ext{ cm}^{-2}$); the comparison between the phonon-mediated attraction and the finite pairing threshold.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to the two-electron Cooper problem and relies on approximations such as the quasiboson approximation and neglecting retardation effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the single-particle bands, the particle-hole excitation spectrum showing collective modes (phonon, plasmon), and the real-space pair density, confirming the chiral p-wave nature.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from initial observations in graphene to constructing an effective fermion-boson Hamiltonian, solving the two-electron problem using approximations, and finally determining the superconducting pairing symmetry.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Recent scanning tunneling microscopy has directly imaged electronic crystals in rhombohedral hexalayer graphene, and magnetotransport measurements suggest that superconductivity and charge-density-wave order emerge from a common spin-valley-polarized ferromagnetic metal at nearby carrier densities. Motivated by these observations, we ask whether collective modes in a magnetic Wigner crystal can mediate pairing in this setting. We address this question by studying the Cooper problem for two electrons in the first conduction band of the Wigner crystal. Unlike conventional phonon-mediated pairing, the collective mode (boson) energies and single-particle (fermion) dispersion are comparable scales controlled by the electron density, leaving no small parameter for an adiabatic expansion. Moreover, because the magnetic Wigner crystal is not time-reversal invariant, the usual Cooper logarithmic divergence in the pairing susceptibility is absent, so the attraction must exceed a finite threshold for pairing to occur. These unusual features motivate a numerical experiment to see whether the crystal's own vibrations can bind electrons. We obtain the crystalline ground state and its collective mode spectrum within Hartree--Fock and time-dependent Hartree--Fock approximation, and derive the electron--phonon Hamiltonian using the quasiboson approximation. Solving the resulting two-electron problem, we find that phonon-mediated attraction exceeds the pairing threshold, with chiral $p$-wave pairing as the leading instability. Within these approximations, we show that collective modes of a Wigner crystal can indeed favor chiral pairing despite broken time-reversal symmetry. Our results provide an encouraging starting point for developing a full many-body theory to study electronic crystallization and superconductivity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a high-resolution numerical mapping of the phase boundary for the spin-1 Blume-Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice. Using advanced simulation techniques, it precisely locates the tricritical point and determines critical exponents. The work demonstrates strong internal consistency across multiple simulation methods, providing a detailed understanding of the system's phase transitions.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the use of advanced simulation techniques like multicanonical sampling and density of states estimation is highly relevant to simulating complex quantum many-body systems where phase boundaries are critical.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to map the phase boundary and precisely locate the tricritical point of the spin-1 Blume-Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice.

**Main result.** The tricritical point is located at $(\Delta_t, T_t) = [1.4819(2), 0.4022(7)]$, and the analysis yields consistent estimates for critical exponents and scaling parameters.

**Method.** The research employs advanced numerical simulation techniques including Wang-Landau estimation of the joint density of states, histogram reweighting, and multicanonical simulations to analyze phase transitions.

**Model / system.** The system is the spin-1 Blume-Capel ferromagnet defined on a honeycomb lattice, described by a Hamiltonian involving nearest-neighbor interactions and a quadratic term ($\sigma_i^2$).

**Key observables.** Joint density of states $\Omega(E_1, E_2)$, tricritical point coordinates $(\Delta_t, T_t)$, interface-tension exponent $\mu$, and critical exponents $y_t$ and $y_g$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coordination number $z=3$ (honeycomb lattice), and the field-mixing parameter $r \approx -1.587$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on extrapolating finite-size scaling results and assumes consistency across multiple independent simulation methods (WL, HR, MUCA).

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the phase diagram in $(\Delta, T)$ space, show the size dependence of interface tension ($\Sigma(L)$), and illustrate the extrapolation of the coexistence line and critical exponents.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the phase diagram by first using Wang-Landau methods to map the first-order line and locate the tricritical point. It then uses histogram reweighting and multicanonical simulations to confirm these results, determining critical exponents and scaling parameters through finite-size scaling analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a high-resolution numerical study of the spin-1 Blume--Capel ferromagnet on the honeycomb lattice ($z=3$). Wang--Landau estimates of the joint density of states $Ω(E_1,E_2)$, combined with field mixing, are used to map the first-order transition line and locate the tricritical point at $(Δ_t,T_t)=[1.4819(2),\,0.4022(7)]$. Histogram reweighting of Metropolis simulations for $L=36$ and $48$ provides an independent consistency check, with a crossing temperature near $0.4039$, compatible with the Wang--Landau extrapolation. From the field-mixing analysis we obtain $r=-1.586(19)$, while the slope of the multicanonical coexistence line yields the consistent and more precise estimate $r=-1.587(5)$. Normalizing by the zero-temperature field $Δ_0=zJ/2$, the available honeycomb, square, triangular, and simple-cubic estimates cluster near $r/Δ_0\simeq-1.06$, corresponding to a magnitude about $6\%$ larger than the mean-field value $-1$; no systematic dependence on coordination number or dimensionality is resolved over the range examined. Finite-size scaling of $σ_Q$ gives $y_t=1.795(7)$, consistent with the tricritical Ising value $9/5$, while the fourth-order cumulant scaling is compatible with $y_g=4/5$. Deep in the first-order regime, the cumulant approaches the expected two-phase limit $U_Q\to2/3$. Multicanonical simulations up to $L=64$, using weights constructed directly from the Wang--Landau density of states for $L\le24$ and rescaled and refined for larger systems, yield an interface-tension exponent $μ=1.265(26)$, consistent with the tricritical prediction $(d-1)/y_g=5/4$. Finally, we map the continuous branch of the phase boundary from the same density-of-states data, obtaining $T_c(Δ=0)=1.157$; estimates sufficiently close to the tricritical point are affected by crossover from Ising to tricritical scaling.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper derives a lower bound showing that performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes requires an ancillary qubit overhead scaling as $	ilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ in the worst case. This result demonstrates a fundamental space-time tradeoff, indicating that achieving complete measurement addressability demands a significant increase in physical resources relative to the code size.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides fundamental theoretical limits on the resource overhead (ancilla qubits) needed to perform complex quantum operations like lattice surgery, which is crucial for scaling up fault-tolerant quantum computation architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to establish a lower bound on the ancillary qubit overhead required to perform lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes, especially when measuring multiple logical operators.

**Main result.** The worst-case overhead for this surgery is shown to be $	ilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ ancillary qubits, implying that constant overhead ancillas limit the measurable logical subspace fraction for large codes.

**Method.** The authors develop a 'no-go theorem' using symplectic embeddings and bounding techniques (Lemma 2, 4, 5) to relate the number of measurable subspaces to the required ancilla qubits.

**Model / system.** The work analyzes quantum error correction using stabiliser codes, modeling the measurement process via a symplectic embedding involving ancillary complexes. The focus is on the theoretical overhead associated with the lattice surgery technique.

**Key observables.** The minimum number of additional ancilla qubits ($N_\star$) required for parallel surgery, and the size of the set of measurable logical subspaces ($|F|$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The code dimension parameter $k$, the sparsity parameter $\omega$, and the total number of qubits $n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the existence of ancillary complexes $D(l)$ for all desired measurements $l \in F$, and the bounds rely on the sparsity ($\omega$) of the associated maps.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds towards a lower bound by formalizing the measurement process via symplectic embeddings and then applying combinatorial and algebraic tools (Lemmas 2, 4, 5) to derive the scaling of the required ancilla qubits.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that performing lattice surgery on sparse stabiliser codes with sparse ancillas requires $\tildeΩ(k^2)$ ancillary qubits in the worst case. As a result, for codes with large $k$, constant overhead ancillas can only realise a small fraction of possible measurements.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper investigates the Higgs amplitude mode in strongly coupled superconductors, showing that phonon retardation effects lift the mode's degeneracy from the pair-breaking threshold. Using the Eilenberger equations on the real frequency axis, the authors predict the mode becomes a sharp, undamped subgap excitation, causing a measurable transfer of spectral weight from the continuum.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a detailed, quantitative theoretical prediction for a collective mode in superconductors, linking microscopic electron-phonon coupling effects to observable spectral weight changes, which is highly relevant to understanding pairing mechanisms beyond simple BCS theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To determine if retardation effects from phonon dynamics in strong-coupling superconductors lift the degeneracy of the amplitude (Higgs) mode from the pair-breaking threshold ($2\Delta_g$).

**Main result.** The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge, becoming a sharp subgap excitation with a binding energy predicted to be $2\Delta_g - \omega_H = 0.028 \Delta_g^2/\Omega$ in the intermediate-coupling regime.

**Method.** The frequency is determined by evaluating the longitudinal pair susceptibility directly on the real frequency axis using the Eilenberger equations within the Migdal-Eliashberg theory framework.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on superconductors described by a complex order parameter, utilizing the Migdal–Eliashberg theory with an Einstein phonon spectrum to model strong electron-phonon coupling.

**Key observables.** Amplitude mode frequency ($\omega_H$), spectral weight transfer, and the time-domain oscillation signature.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Intermediate-coupling window ($0.56 \le \Delta_g/\Omega \le 0.90$), the ratio $\Delta_g/\Omega$, and the gap edge $2\Delta_g$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculation requires using the real-axis Eilenberger-Keldysh approach, as the imaginary axis calculation fails to resolve the necessary small energy shifts.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the time-domain signature, contrasting the BCS prediction of $t^{-1/2}$ decay with the predicted undamped pole, and showing the spectral weight transferred from the continuum to the discrete level.

**Paper structure.** The paper contrasts the BCS prediction (algebraic decay) with the strong-coupling prediction (detachment). It details the theoretical machinery using Eilenberger equations on the real axis to locate the pole, derives the quantitative binding energy formula, and discusses the physical consequence of spectral weight redistribution.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the BCS theory of superconductivity the amplitude (Higgs) mode is degenerate with the pair-breaking threshold: its frequency coincides with $2Δ$, so it is an edge singularity rather than a true collective mode. This is why after a sudden weak perturbation at $t=0$ its oscillations decay algebraically as $1/\sqrt{t}$. We show that the retardation effects due to the phonon dynamics in the strong-coupling theory lift this degeneracy. The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge $2Δ_g$, set by the spectral gap, and becomes a sharp subgap excitation. We determine its frequency from the longitudinal pair susceptibility evaluated directly on the real frequency axis, using the Eilenberger equations for Migdal--Eliashberg theory with the Einstein phonon spectrum. The response of the mass renormalization supplies at least two fifths of the displacement, and possibly all of it: with it switched off, the binding falls below the resolution of the calculation. Its consequences, however, are significant because a percent-level shift transfers about a quarter of the spectral weight of the amplitude channel out of the two-quasiparticle continuum into a discrete energy level. What experiment sees is therefore not the displacement itself but its consequence: amplitude oscillations that persist instead of decaying as $1/\sqrt{t}$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper details a case study on using large language models to autonomously migrate quantum code benchmarks from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. The research demonstrates that while LLMs can significantly reduce human effort in this complex task, the process is improved by distilling reusable 'skills' from the initial migrations. This work advances the state-of-the-art in automated quantum software engineering.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the focus is on software engineering rather than fundamental physics, the successful automation of complex quantum algorithm implementation across platforms is crucial for realizing quantum hardware, directly impacting the practical application of quantum information science.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of autonomously migrating quantum algorithms and benchmarks from one programming framework (Qiskit) to another (CUDA-Q). This is necessary because quantum software requires specialized abstractions that differ significantly from traditional programming languages.

**Main result.** LLMs successfully generated satisfactory code ports with significantly reduced human effort, and distilling 'skills' from these migrations improved agent performance on unseen benchmarks by reducing required model turns by up to 85%.

**Method.** The authors used large language models (Opus, GPT, Gemini) as agents to port thirteen QED-C benchmark methods from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. They then tested knowledge transfer by creating and applying reusable 'skills' derived from these initial migrations.

**Model / system.** The work operates on quantum computing platforms, specifically comparing the Qiskit and CUDA-Q frameworks. The benchmarks cover diverse quantum algorithms including amplitude estimation, variational optimization, and factoring.

**Key observables.** Model turns required for porting, token usage, fidelity of generated code, and the percentage reduction in model turns/tokens when using distilled skills.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The benchmark suite includes 13 methods spanning foundational algorithms, Monte Carlo, and optimization tasks.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes that algorithmic intent can be preserved across framework abstractions, though it notes that this is not guaranteed and that agents can use 'shortcuts.'

**Figures summary.** The notes reference a figure detailing the two pathways: autonomous migration (Pathway 1) and knowledge transfer using reusable skills (Pathway 2). Tables quantify the percentage reduction in model turns and token count achieved by these skills.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a case study structure: first, performing the autonomous migration of the QED-C benchmarks across multiple LLMs; second, analyzing the resulting challenges and inconsistencies; and finally, developing and testing a knowledge-transfer mechanism using 'skills' to improve future agent performance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum programming requires concepts and intuition that differ substantially from those used in traditional programming languages. Multiple quantum programming frameworks address these requirements through different abstractions and execution models, creating tradeoffs in programmability, portability, and performance. Because quantum software is less prevalent in the training data available to large language models, autonomous coding agents might be expected to face additional challenges when working with these frameworks. We present a case study in autonomous migration of the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmarks from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. Opus, GPT, and Gemini models were each tasked with porting thirteen benchmark methods spanning foundational algorithms, amplitude estimation, Monte Carlo methods, variational optimization, linear-system solving, and factoring. In all cases, the models were able to generate satisfactory ports with little direct coding help and there was a drastic reduction in the time required compared to a human engineer. However, in all cases, the agents resorted to shortcuts when implementation challenges surfaced and multiple prompts were required to force appropriate coding directions. Assessment of the generated implementations showed that no single model consistently produced the best port across all benchmarks, indicating that multi-agent ensemble strategies could mitigate challenges associated with quantum software. The effort resulted in publicly available, near-complete CUDA-Q support in the QED-C benchmarks along with model-generated skills designed to improve agent performance when implementing CUDA-Q applications. When tested on an unseen benchmark, these skills reduced the required model turns by up to 85% and token usage by up to 96%. We conclude by distilling lessons from the case study.

</details>
